General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 36 min read (7249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~36 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource1.
  • Recent findings suggest that the global imperative to transition towards sustainable energy systems has intensified research and development in renewable energy technologies.
  • Sources indicate that despite their promise, the harsh hydrodynamic environment presents an important barrier to the economic viability of this renewable energy source.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource1. However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs2,3. Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.

Recent findings suggest that the global imperative to transition towards sustainable energy systems has intensified research and development in renewable energy technologies. Among these, tidal energy presents a uniquely predictable and substantial resource. Unlike other renewables such as wind and solar, tidal currents are governed by an astronomical cycle, which offers a consistent and forecastable power source4,5. The scale of this resource is significant. Tidal power is estimated at 50 TW h yr−1 in Europe6 and as much as 220 TW h yr−1 in the USA alone7. Near-term deployment targets are 1 GW by 2035 in the UK3, with international roadmaps project deployments eventually exceeding 300 GW worldwide by 20508. These highlight the potential of tidal energy in contributing to energy security and renewable energy portfolios.

Sources indicate that despite their promise, the harsh hydrodynamic environment presents an important barrier to the economic viability of this renewable energy source. A primary challenge is the hydrodynamic load fluctuations that arise from large variations in flow velocity, turbulence, turbine yaw with respect to the incoming stream, velocity shear along the water depth2, wave-induced oscillating currents9, and wake interaction within turbine arrays10. These fluctuating loads are a primary design consideration and are associated with accelerated fatigue, reduced operational lifespans and unplanned downtime. These reliability concerns result in blade and turbine designs with high capital costs, which directly increase the levelized cost of energy (LCOE)3.

To address the challenge of the dynamic loads, various mitigation strategies have been developed. Active control typically deploys systems to actively regulate the pitch11 or camber12 of the blades, therefore, to regulate power output, control mean loads and improve start-up performance. Although the active control systems are effective in certain operational envelopes, the reliability of sophisticated sensors and actuators in the harsh undersea environment remains a concern. Furthermore, the response times of the activator limit effectiveness against rapid, high-frequency load fluctuations13,14.

Recent findings suggest that to address these concerns, there has been an increased focus on developing passive control mechanisms. Passive control is mainly realized in two ways: introducing changes in the blade pitch or modifying the blade camber. Passive pitch control involves designing blades that can rotate around their spanwise axis in response to changing hydrodynamic loads, thereby altering their angle of attack. This is typically achieved by incorporating a pre-loaded torsional spring mechanism at the blade root. Theoretical work in refs. 15,16 are among the first to introduce the concept. Both demonstrated that complete cancellation of the load fluctuation is possible without compromising the mean power. This is followed by a numerical study in ref. 17, which confirmed more than 80% load fluctuations can be reduced in sheared flow conditions, with additional benefits such as faster wake recovery, which improves turbine array performance. Reference 18 has contributed a general framework for the design of passive pitching systems, identifying the locations of the pivot point for maximizing load mitigation. Experimental validations in ref. 19 have confirmed the ability of passive pitching systems in the reduction of time-averaged loadings.

Sources indicate that passive pitching systems are effective for low-frequency, large-scale adjustments and power regulation by adjusting the global angle of attack of the blades. However, the added inertia due to the displacement of the pitching axis required by effective pitching systems, as well as the bearing friction, limits the response of the system to high-frequency disturbances, such as turbulent eddies or rapid shear variations. Moreover, despite being simpler than active control systems, passive pitch blades still introduce extra moving parts and potential failure points in harsh undersea environments. Research has identified that for wind turbine applications, most of the failures originate from the pitch system20, highlighting the significant operational advantage of a robust, passive design.

According to recent reports, an alternative design philosophy can be found in nature, where organisms from fish to trees passively reconfigure their shape through distributed material compliance to manage fluid dynamic forces21,22. Drawing from these biological principles, passive morphing flexible blades offer an alternative strategy, where flexibility is distributed along the blade, allowing each blade section to adapt automatically through fluid–structure interaction. Therefore, a faster response time can be achieved with a fixed-pitch blade that does not require hinges and bearings. Passive morphing blades are common in wind energy applications23,24, in which the blade twists to feather in response to a wind gust. This technique, known as aeroelastic tailoring, requires ad hoc structural design, whose scalability and reliability for large tidal turbines is yet to be demonstrated. In fact, for similar power-rated turbines, the bending moment experienced by tidal turbines is higher than that of wind turbines. Therefore, the need for a scalable, reliable, passive system that can mitigate both rapid, localized turbulent fluctuations and slower, large-scale changes in inflow velocity on large-scale tidal turbines remains unmet.

Industry observers note that this study directly addresses this challenge by proposing a blade with chordwise flexibility, rather than spanwise flexibility, as in aeroelastic tailoring. The frontal and thickest part of the blade, which provides structural integrity, is rigid. Instead, the trailing edge is flexible from root to tip. Specifically, we provide the first comprehensive experimental demonstration that a carefully designed chordwise-flexible blade can achieve both control of the mean power and thrust with the quasi-steady variations of flow velocities over the tidal cycle (for example, the diurnal tidal cycle) and mitigation of the high-frequency (turbulence) hydrodynamic load fluctuations on tidal turbines, while enabling the same yield as a conventional rigid blade equipped with active pitch control. To demonstrate this potential, we experimentally evaluated the performance of these chordwise-flexible blades against a rigid baseline in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh. The turbine was tested across a range of nominal inflow velocities u∞ = 0.5–1.0 m s−1, and tip-speed ratios (λ) from 3 to 9, with the flexible blades designed for optimal performance at u∞ ≈ 0.85 m s−1. Our analysis first addresses the low-frequency load mitigation over a tidal cycle before examining the high-frequency load fluctuations and the underlying physical mechanisms of the deformation of the blade. Overall, we demonstrated a new pathway to enhance turbine reliability and survivability, reducing capital costs associated with the active pitch system, and reducing maintenance costs by removing hinges, bearings and actuators, ultimately reducing the LCOE.

Industry observers note that the structural design of a tidal turbine is primarily dictated by low-frequency loads, which, in this context, refers to the quasi-steady hydrodynamic loads that change as the mean inflow velocity varies over a tidal cycle. To investigate the potential for load control in this regime, the time-averaged performance of the flexible blades was compared against a rigid baseline. Figure 1 demonstrates the time-averaged power (CP), thrust (CT), and root bending moment (CM) coefficients as a function of tip-speed ratio λ, at all tested inflow velocities. The results demonstrate that the introduction of blade flexibility does not compromise the primary function of energy capture of the turbine. As shown in Fig. 1a, at the rated velocity (uR = 0.878 m s−1) and above, the power coefficient of the flexible blade closely matches that of the rigid blade, achieving a comparable peak CP of approximately 0.37. Notably, the limited value of the maximum CP of both the rigid and flexible blades compared with full-scale state-of-the-art turbines is due to the low Reynolds number at which the model-scale turbines were tested (Methods).

The key advantage of the flexible blade design is its ability to passively regulate peak loadings. At the rated velocity, the thrust coefficient of the flexible blade is comparable to that of the rigid blade near the optimal power-producing tip-speed ratio (λ ≈ 5.5−6), as shown in Fig. 1b. However, the performance of the flexible blades diverges from rigid ones for λ values beyond this optimal range. This high λ region is typically explored by the turbine control strategy to cap power when inflow velocity exceeds the rated velocity. Under these conditions, the flexible blade thrust passively decreases, whereas the rigid one increases. This demonstrates a load-shedding mechanism that can protect the turbine structure during the most demanding high-flow conditions and will be discussed in detail in the next section, in which we simulate the power and thrust a tidal turbine experiences over a tidal cycle. However, at off-design conditions, the flexible blade exhibits higher CT and CM values than at its design speed. While this results in higher thrust coefficients at lower velocities, the absolute forces, which scale with velocity squared (\(F\propto {u}_{\infty }^{2}\)), are much smaller during lower flow periods and are not as notable for the structural design of the turbine as the peak loads experienced at or above rated velocity. Therefore, the ability of the flexible blade technology to match power performance while simultaneously offering a passive mechanism to reduce the most important structural loads represents a marked advancement for designing more durable and cost-effective tidal turbines.

a–c, Time-averaged coefficients of power (a), thrust (b) and root bending moment (c) as a function of the tip-speed ratio for rigid and flexible blades at different flow speeds.

Recent findings suggest that to quantify the practical benefits of the passive load mitigation of the chordwise-flexible blade in realistic inflow, we simulate the performance over a representative tidal cycle and compare it against a rigid blade turbine with the same control strategy and a state-of-the-art, actively pitch-controlled turbine (see Supplementary Note 2 for modelling of the active pitch-and-speed control turbine). The sinusoidal inflow velocity represents the flow seen by a tidal turbine during a tidal cycle is shown in Fig. 2a, which is.

In a recent development, a–d, Time history over a simulated tidal period of the freestream speed (a), the quasi-steady power (b), the tip-speed ratio (c) and the quasi-steady thrust (d). Data are presented for a rigid-blade turbine with only an active speed controller, a state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed controller, and rubber blades with an active speed controller. All data are divided by the corresponding rated value.

Sources indicate that the cut-in velocity of the turbine is selected at u∞/uR = 0.2. The turbine operates at λ = 5.5 when the velocity is lower than rated. At the rated speed, all turbine configurations are operated at the same tip-speed ratio (λR) and provide the same quasi-steady power (PR) and thrust (TR). At higher than rated velocities, λ is such that P/PR = 1. The maximum velocity is set at u∞/uR = 1.2, representative of typical tidal turbine operating conditions.

The simulation first confirms that the passive design of the flexible blade does not compromise its primary function of energy capture. The normalized power profiles shown in Fig. 2b coincide for the rubber blade with speed control and the state-of-the-art active pitch control turbine, where the turbine speed is shown in Fig. 2c. As the total energy harvested is proportional to the integral of the power curves over the tidal cycle, the overlap of the curves confirms a negligible difference in overall energy yield. This demonstrates that the load-mitigation benefits of flexible blades can be achieved without a penalty to energy capture in a real-world setting.

The advantage of the flexible blade design is revealed by the differences in the quasi-steady thrust (Fig. 2d) between the turbine configurations. The state-of-the-art active pitch system limits structural loads by actively feathering the blades into the flow while maintaining the rated rotational speed. For a rigid blade, using only an overspeed-control strategy, the fixed geometry cannot adapt to the increasing flow; solely increasing the tip-speed ratio results in an increasing thrust that peaks at approximately 1.65 times the rated value (Fig. 2c). By contrast, with a comparable speed-control strategy, the passive system of the flexible blade achieves the same quasi-steady power and similar quasi-steady thrust as the active control.

It is also important to note that flexible blades show a slightly higher thrust coefficient at lower, off-design velocities (Fig. 1b) than the baseline rigid blade. However, the absolute thrust force, which scales with velocity squared, is smaller during these periods than the peak values over the tidal cycle. As the maximum loading dictates the primary structural design requirements of a turbine, the nearly identical peak thrust of the passive flexible blade to that of the complex, state-of-the-art active pitch system suggests comparable outcomes for turbine longevity and maintenance costs, representing a marked advancement towards more durable and cost-effective tidal energy systems. Overall, these results indicate that the chordwise-flexible blades can offer a compelling and robust alternative to the state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed control turbine system.

According to recent reports, an effective passive system must also address high-frequency load fluctuations, which are a primary driver of fatigue damage. In this context, high frequency refers to the unsteady load components that occur at frequencies of the order of the period of revolution, such as those induced by turbulence, velocity shear or wake interaction, and so on. Figure 3 quantifies the effectiveness of the flexible blades by presenting the standard deviation of load fluctuations relative to the reference rigid blades at rated velocity. To reflect realistic conditions over a tidal cycle, the data for u∞/uR ≤ 1 are presented at the optimal tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5) for maximum power extraction, whereas the data for conditions above the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06) are presented at the higher tip-speed ratio (λ = 8) that is used to cap power. Figure 3 shows a substantial reduction of unsteady loads for all three components when the turbine is operating under its most demanding conditions. At the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.0), where the turbine operates at its optimal λ for maximum power extraction, the flexible blades provide effective fluctuation reduction across power, thrust and root bending moment (mitigated by approximately 18%, 23% and 28%, respectively). Furthermore, even when the inflow velocity increases beyond the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06), the load fluctuation mitigation remains substantial. This demonstrates the powerful and robust damping ability of the flexible blades during both the maximum-power and power-capping phases of operation, when the absolute magnitude of fluctuating forces is greatest. At the lowest velocities (for example, u∞/uR = 0.51), where the blade operates in a stalled condition, fluctuations are known to increase relative to the rigid blade. However, their absolute magnitude is small, reaching only about 15–35% of the fluctuation level of the rigid blade at its rated velocity. A more detailed analysis, presented in Supplementary Note 3, confirms that this mitigation is robust across a wide range of tip-speed ratios under these high-flow conditions.

It has been revealed that a–c, Standard deviation of power (a), thrust (b) and root-bending moment (c) of flexible and rigid blades, for the optimum tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5). All quantities are divided by those of the rigid blade at rated velocity.

In a recent development, to illustrate the physics of the passive load regulation mechanism demonstrated previously, the deformation of the flexible blade is visualized at the tip section. Figure 4 highlights the phase-averaged digital image correlation (DIC) measurements of the tip of the same flexible blade at a constant azimuthal angle, in which the blade is horizontal with downward velocity. The successful application of this technique using fully submerged cameras represents a significant experimental achievement, as most underwater DIC studies to date have been performed through observation windows rather than submerging the camera in the fluid25. In this way, complex optical distortions and refractive index mismatches associated with viewing ports are avoided, thereby achieving a more accurate measurement. In this study, the DIC system measured the deformation of the suction side of the blade. The full blade profile was then reconstructed by adding the known thickness distribution of the undeformed blade to the measured deformed chord line.

Phase-averaged profiles of one blade tip measured with DIC when the blade span is horizontal, and the tangential velocity is pointing downwards. Coordinates x, y are normalized by the chord length at the blade tip with origin at the quarter chord.

In a recent development, the measurements demonstrate the mechanism of the passive morphing concept. The undeformed flexible blade was designed with a significant initial camber, noticeably higher than that of the conventional rigid blade profile. The high camber present in both the initial blade shape and the subsequent deformed shape before reaching the designed operating point is the primary reason for the higher thrust force generated by the flexible blade operating off-design. Under hydrodynamic loading, the flexible trailing edge deflects upwards, causing the entire profile to flatten into a shape with less camber. This passive feathering becomes more pronounced with higher inflow velocities, which is the mechanism that reduces the thrust coefficient at high tip-speed ratios and velocities.

Sources indicate that DIC measurements of different blades (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2) show that blades with lower flexural rigidity undergo greater camber reduction and exhibit stronger load shedding. Specifically, for blades with the same mould geometry, a too-stiff blade results in a too-low pitch and too-high camber, and thus high mean and unsteady thrust. Conversely, a too-soft blade results in an over-pitched blade and low power capture.

Recent findings suggest that the observed mean load-shedding behaviour shown in Fig. 1 arises primarily from quasi-steady passive morphing, and not from dynamic blade deformation resulting in hysteresis, vortex dynamics, and so on. DIC reconstructions of each individual blade at the same azimuthal position reveal only a narrow spread about the mean shape, corresponding to a standard deviation of the pitch variation of approximately ±0.2° (Extended Data Fig. 3).

Recent findings suggest that to further verify that the mean load-shedding behaviour is due to a quasi-steady morphing, we compare the measured blade deformations (Fig. 4) and the corresponding power and thrust (Fig. 1) with those computed with an in-house fluid–structure interaction solver based on a quasi-steady low-order model (Methods). The blade shapes computed with this program are in good agreement with those measured experimentally, and so are the predicted power and thrust for different tip-speed ratios (Extended Data Fig. 4). Because the numerical solver assumes the blade is in static equilibrium under hydrodynamic loads, these results confirm that the governing physics is quasi-steady.

Industry observers note that the fluid–structure interaction of the flexible blades is governed by two non-dimensional groups such as the Reynolds number (Re) and Cauchy number (Ca) (defined in the Methods). The experiments are performed at sufficiently high Re that the hydrodynamic load coefficients are about the same as those at full scale, as shown by the almost identical values for the rigid blade tested at different velocities in Fig. 1. To ensure geometric similarity between the model and the full-scale strain of the flexible blades, the Young modulus E of rubber must be scaled up to maintain the same Ca across scales. As discussed in Supplementary Note 4, rubber features a sufficiently high range of E for full-scale applications. Furthermore, rubber has the advantage of matching the mass density of water, enabling the design of buoyancy-neutral blades and preventing mass-related load fluctuations.

In a recent development, to demonstrate the scalability of the present results, numerical simulations are performed using the in-house fluid–structure interaction solver to model a utility-scale turbine. A rated speed of u∞ = 3.0 m s−1 and a 20-m diameter turbine is selected consistently with modern, state-of-the-art commercial turbines26 and typical energetic tidal sites27. Simulations performed at the respective Re and the same Ca confirm that power and thrust coefficient curves are similar at model and full scale (Extended Data Fig. 5), and therefore the present results are applicable to utility-scale turbines. Although E of the steel spar can be scaled up in numerical simulations, this is not possible in practice. Therefore, different full-scale spar design options are discussed in Supplementary Note 5.

Industry observers note that finally, rubber features high fatigue endurance. Preliminary calculations in Supplementary Note 6 show that the fatigue life of a full-scale rubber blade would substantially surpass the 20 years of service expected by state-of-the-art turbines.

Overall, by allowing similar control on power at thrust above rated speed than active pitch control systems, and mitigating load fluctuations, this technology offers a viable pathway to lower the LCOE. Furthermore, the reduction in load fluctuations enables deployment in energetic, highly turbulent sites previously deemed unviable due to the high fatigue loads. Further analysis of the potential industrial impact of this technology is presented in Supplementary Note 7.

Recent findings suggest that this experimental investigation has evaluated the performance of tidal turbine flexible rubber blades with passive chordwise flexibility, compared against conventional rigid blades. Our results confirmed that the power coefficient of the flexible blade at the design tip-speed ratio is comparable to that of its rigid counterpart, demonstrating that load mitigation benefits are achieved without penalty to the primary function of the turbine as an energy harvester.

In a recent development, the main advantage of the flexible blades is their ability to deform, shedding the excess of load at off-design conditions. This reconfiguration allows control of power by manipulating the angular velocity of the turbine, while achieving passive mitigation of the high-frequency fluctuations that drive fatigue damage.

Recent findings suggest that therefore, the chordwise-flexible blades offer a compelling and robust alternative to state-of-the-art active pitch control. By mitigating loads with a much simpler setup, the flexible blade eliminates a significant source of potential failure and maintenance costs in offshore renewables.

The mechanism for load mitigation is confirmed through DIC measurement and a quasi-steady low-order code, which shows that the stiffness and initial geometry of the blade produce a controlled ‘feather’ as loads increase. The no-flow geometry and stiffness of the blade are designed so that, under flow conditions approaching the design point, it deforms toward the reference rigid-blade configuration.

Looking ahead, this work opens up new pathways for tidal turbine design and cost reduction. The demonstrated reductions in peak and fatigue loading could allow a reduction in structural requirements for both the blades and their supporting structure, lowering capital costs and enabling higher generator ratings, which in turn improve rated capacity per unit mass. Moreover, the increased robustness from the removal of the pitching system reduces operational and maintenance costs. These factors contribute to a lower LCOE of tidal turbines, addressing the primary barrier to the large-scale deployment of tidal energy farms. By making the technology more financially viable, this technology offers a realistic and attractive option for renewable energy production.

All experiments were conducted in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh, a circular combined wave–current basin designed for scaled testing of offshore renewable energy devices. The tank has a diameter of 25 m and, for the present campaign, was operated in current-only mode with a working water depth of 1.92 m. A schematic of the facility is shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a. The experiments were performed at six inflow velocities in the range u∞ = 0.444–0.923 m s−1, corresponding to a diameter-based Reynolds number,.

from 0.49 × 106 to 1.16 × 106, where ν is the kinematic viscosity and d is the turbine diameter. See Supplementary Note 4 for a discussion on the Reynolds number scaling.

Industry observers note that floWave turbulence is between 8% and 9%, and integral length scales of about 25% of the water depth28. These turbulent characteristics are consistent with energetic tidal sites such as, for example, the Fall of Warness29. There, the turbulence intensity is between 5% and 11%, with integral length scales of approximately 30–50% of the channel depth. The mean vertical shear in FloWave is approximately a power law with a 1/12 exponent (Extended Data Fig. 6b), which is only slightly weaker than the 1/10 power-law profile commonly used to represent tidal flows30. Extended Data Table 1 summarizes the comparison between FloWave and the representative tidal sites.

Industry observers note that A three-bladed horizontal-axis turbine with a rotor diameter d = 1.26 m was installed in the tank centre, at hub height zhub = 0.876 m. The turbine is equipped with a brushless d.c. motor and a 25:1 planetary gearbox. The main components of the turbine are outlined in Extended Data Fig. 7.

The results presented in the main text refer to four sets of blades: one set of rigid blades used as a baseline and three sets of rubber blades. The baseline rigid blades are CNC-machined (SS316) using a modified NACA 63-415 hydrofoil profile along the span. The profile was modified to ensure a blunt trailing edge, as specified in ref. 31. These blades exhibited negligible flapwise and edgewise deformations. Notably, utility-scale tidal turbine blades exhibit some structural compliance. However, here the model-scale rigid blade was deliberately made rigid to provide a defined geometry.

Recent findings suggest that the main text presents the results for the rigid blades and one set of rubber blades with the optimal stiffness. Conversely, the Extended Data figures also include results for the other two sets of rubber blades, with higher and lower stiffness than optimal. The flexible blades were manufactured by injecting a proprietary rubber mixture into a mould and around a steel spar. All rubber blades have the same mould geometry. See Extended Data Fig. 8 for schematics of the rubber blade. The aeroelastic properties of the blade are tailored along its span by varying the ratio of the rigid spar width to the local chord length, which increases from the tip towards the root with an average of 45%.

Industry observers note that the thrust and torque are measured by a force transducer installed between the turbine rotor and the motor shaft (Extended Data Fig. 7). The transducer is bespoke, manufactured by Applied Measurements, rated for an axial load of 1,300 N and a torque of 100 N m, and a resolution of 0.005 N and 0.0004 N m, respectively. In this study, thrust is the net force measured by the hub transducer along the streamwise direction, and torque is the net edgewise moment about the hub axis. Moreover, each blade root was instrumented with a flapwise custom root-bending-moment sensor. Calibration matrices for each sensor were obtained in situ before the test by applying known weights at four points along the cantilever beam attached to the sensor. All force signals were transmitted to a National Instruments NI 9203 acquisition system through a slip ring. The load cells were zeroed without flow before each set of measurements. For each measurement, loads were recorded at a sampling frequency of 128 Hz for 300 s. Rotor angular velocity was measured using an inductive proximity sensor that emitted one pulse per blade pass (three pulses per revolution), enabling determination of the revolution period and computation of the angular velocity.

The principal measured quantities were torque (Q), thrust (T), flapwise root-bending moment (M) and angular velocity (ω). Measured loads and power are non-dimensionalized using standard turbine coefficients:.

The tip-speed ratio is defined as.

where ω is the turbine angular velocity in radians per second.

It has been revealed that sensor accuracy and calibration uncertainties were propagated to the non-dimensional coefficients using standard bias-limit uncertainty analysis32, including thrust-torque transducer manufacturer specification (0.1% of full-scale capacity) and primary uncertainties in u∞, ω and geometric parameters. For the present setup, the maximum total bias limits is of order 10−2 for CP and of order 10−2 for CT (representative values). Supplementary Note 1 provides the full derivations and tables.

Blade deformation was measured using phase-locked DIC with underwater cameras and LED illumination (LaVision). The camera system had a fixed focal length of 1.1 m and a field of view of approximately 0.87 m × 0.56 m, sufficient to capture the full blade span (0.56 m). Phase locking was achieved by using the proximity-sensor signal to trigger image acquisition as a blade passed a fixed azimuthal position, with a horizontal span and a downward tangential velocity. For each condition, between 89 and 447 instantaneous deformation fields were recorded over a 300 s period, depending on u∞ and λ.

Images were processed in LaVision DaVis 11 using a subset size of 21 × 21 pixels and a grid step size of 2 × 2 pixels, resulting in a spatial resolution of approximately 0.68 mm near the blade tip (approximately 2% of the tip chord). A reference image in quiescent water was acquired before each set of measurements. In the present configuration, DIC was used to measure the deformation of the suction-side surface of the blade. The full blade profile was reconstructed by combining the measured chord-line deformation with the known undeformed thickness distribution.

A bespoke fluid–structure interaction (FSI) solver was developed for the present study. The solver couples an in-house code based on blade element momentum theory (BEMT), with a panel method with an integral boundary-layer formulation (XFOIL), and a finite element analysis commercial software (Abaqus). The code uses a two-level iterative process, as schematically shown in Extended Data Fig. 9. The process begins with an initial blade geometry. In the outer loop, the BEMT solver is used to calculate the axial and tangential induction factors on a finite number of blade sections at different radial coordinates. Then, the flow velocity and angle of attack experienced by each blade section are computed. These values are used as initial conditions for the inner FSI loop. First, the pressure distributions around each blade section are computed with XFOIL. Then, the pressure distributions from each blade section are combined to obtain a three-dimensional pressure distribution on the blade, which is used as input to Abaqus, in which a upcoming deformed shape is computed. The Abaqus model includes the steel spar. This new shape is then discretized into sections and returned to XFOIL to recalculate the pressure field. This iterative process continues until the blade shape converges. This deformed blade geometry at equilibrium is then fed back into the outer BEMT loop to revision the induction factors. This entire two-level process is repeated until convergence. The power and thrust coefficients of the whole turbine are then computed by integrating the loads computed with XFOIL for each blade section and multiplying by three to account for the three-bladed turbine.

This code was used to design the stress-free mould shape for each blade stiffness, ensuring that the equilibrium blade shape matches the reference rigid blade at the design flow speed and tip-speed ratio. The model-scale simulations in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 are initialized with the mould geometry and use the actual stiffness of the metal spar and of the rubber. In the full-scale simulations (Extended Data Fig. 5), the stiffness of both the spar and the rubber is 10.6 times higher than at model scale to ensure that the model and full-scale Cauchy number for both the spar and the rubber is the same, where.

where ρ is the fluid mass density and E is the Young’s modulus.

Industry observers note that the mould geometry Xi,j is used as input, where i = 0 and j = 0 indicate the iteration number of the inner and outer loop, respectively. The lift and drag coefficient curves (\({C}_{{{\rm{L}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\), \({C}_{{{\rm{D}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\)) are computed with XFOIL for various blade sections, and the induction factors (\({a}_{i,j},{a}_{i,j}^{{\prime} }\)) are computed with BEMT. Then the pressure distribution (pi,j(x)) around each blade section is computed with XFOIL and assembled into a three-dimensional load condition for Abaqus, where the new geometry is computed (Xi,j, with i increased by one). The inner loop is repeated till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi−1,j∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵi. If converged, the new geometry is Xi,j, where j is increased by one. The outer loop is repeated from the computation of the lift and drag coefficient for the new geometry, till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi,j−1∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵj.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christian Comotto is one of the brightest gems to emerge from the AC Milan youth system in recent years, but he could stop shining.

In the summer, there was plenty of interest in Comotto. After a strong season with Spezia in Serie B, the youngster was ready to make the step up to Serie A and several clubs came forward offering themselves as potential destinations to aid his growth.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Industry observers note that yet, Milan made the decision to keep him, believing they could offer him the mentorship and minutes to raise his level and ceiling. However, it’s not played out that way, with the Italian hardly playing so far.

With who is in front of him, it’s understandable, but that doesn’t make his lack of minutes any less frustrating.

Speaking to Sportitalia after Italy U-20’s win against Portugal, he admitted that he was happy with the minutes he’d received, but didn’t deny that he wanted more, as MilanPress relayed.

“I’m only 18, so it’s understandable that with players like Modric and Rabiot ahead of me, it can be more difficult to find space,” he noted.

Industry observers note that “I’m happy to have made my debut in both Serie A and the Europa League. I’m an ambitious guy and I expect more playing time in the coming months. As for everything else, we’ll see later.”.

Highly-rated Reading youngster agrees out-of-window loan move

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (498 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reading youngster Tyler Sackey has featured only in cup matches for the club over the past three seasons.
  • Aside from his EFL Trophy appearances, Sackey has played for the U21s in Premier League 2, operating from central midfield.
  • In a recent development, pete O’Rourke states that Reading have agreed to send Sackney on loan to National League side Aldershot Town.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reading youngster Tyler Sackey has featured only in cup matches for the club over the past three seasons. His three senior appearances this term have come in the EFL Trophy, and the 20-year-old has impressed in his outings.

Aside from his EFL Trophy appearances, Sackey has played for the U21s in Premier League 2, operating from central midfield. He impressed last term, and now looks set for a chance to prove his abilities on the senior stage away from Leam Richardson‘s squad.

In a recent development, pete O’Rourke states that Reading have agreed to send Sackney on loan to National League side Aldershot Town. It will give him a chance to play frequent first-team football for the first time in his promising career.

Sackey signed a new contract at the Berkshire outfit in the summer, keeping him tied down until 2029.

Industry observers note that on Sackey’s senior debut, he scored in a 3-1 EFL Trophy win against West Ham United U21s. He also scored against Walsall in the same competition in the 2024/25 season.

The Reading prospect has recent experience against National League sides, including scoring against Woking in a pre-season friendly with a composed left-footed finish this summer.

According to recent reports, sackey offers a creative presence in central midfield and further forward as a No. 10. He has made 158 successful passes in the Premier League 2 this term while winning 59.5% of his duels and having 270 touches. Combined with 27 defensive contributions, it reveals the Royals youngster’s well-rounded game and his work rate out of possession in winning the ball back and showing to receive the ball.

This will be Sackey’s first chance at regular senior minutes, so he needs to be given time to adjust to the physical demands of the game and settle into his role in the team and dressing room at Aldershot.

Reading aren’t afraid to trust youthful creative midfielders, so Sackey has the potential to pave his way into the first team.

Charlie Savage is a prime example of this, following a youth career with Manchester United and a brief loan with Forest Green Rovers. He quickly became a key influence, and Bristol City loanee Josh Stokes has been entrusted with a similar role, having provided three assists so far this season.

Sackey will hope to impress with Aldershot Town to soon replicate those performances for his parent club.

#14799. So much pace and potential, not enough positive impact... surely Scotland must now redefine the role of Ben Gannon-Doak?

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1188 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

So much pace and potential, not enough positive impact... surely Scotland must now redefine the role of Ben Gannon-Doak?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 12:41 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:14 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • In an age where much of the football on show in the English Premier League is so robotic as to be almost unwatchable, flashes of individual brilliance are increasingly becoming things to be cherished.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 12:41 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:14 EST, 14 November 2026.

In an age where much of the football on show in the English Premier League is so robotic as to be almost unwatchable, flashes of individual brilliance are increasingly becoming things to be cherished.

Across his time at Liverpool and Bournemouth, Ben Gannon-Doak has sporadically distinguished himself as someone who can light up a game by doing something out of the blue and out of the ordinary.

It has been revealed that as many a defender will testify, that electric burst of pace across a short distance makes him unplayable at times. He has an X-factor which sets him apart from the crowd.

What a shame that injuries have restricted his number of appearances to this point. Since moving south from Celtic in 2022, including a loan spell with Middlesbrough, Gannon-Doak has played fewer than 50 times.

At the very time in his career when he could have done with smoothing off the rough edges, he’s spent far too long rehabilitating from one setback or another.

In the build-up to Friday’s match with North Macedonia, Sebastien Pocognoli spoke about how encouraged he was that the player was finally seeing more game time on the south coast, partly as a result of the team’s maiden voyage in Europe.

Ben Gannon-Doak started in a right wing-back role and had an energetic yet frustrating night.

According to recent reports, the hope of all concerned was that the recent run of matches which the winger had so evidently needed would translate into a more accomplished display in a Scotland jersey. Alas, this proved to be wishful thinking.

Even against very ordinary opposition, Gannon-Doak’s display proved to be another frustrating watch for the Tartan Army.

Time and time again, he brought them to the edge of their seats by facing up a white jersey and seemingly disappearing in a puff of smoke towards the line. Rarely, however, did the end product materialise.

For a winger with such blinding speed to continually struggle with the all-important final ball is a difficult thing to repeatedly witness.

We shall never know, of course, if the player’s crossing ability would be better by this stage if he hadn’t endured such wretched luck with injuries. But you suspect it’s now just about as good as it’s ever going to be.

The trouble for Pocognoli is that the quality of the delivery from wing-backs into the penalty box is arguably the most crucial facet of his preferred 3-4-3 system.

When it breaks down, as it did so often against the group outsiders, the whole thing threatens to grind to a halt.

Gannon-Doak's crossing remains an area of concern for Scotland given his wide position.

According to recent reports, on his record-equalling 102nd cap, Andy Robertson was also guilty of being wasteful on the other flank. Given we know what the skipper has delivered down the years, though, we can write that off as merely a bad night at the office.

The difference with Gannon-Doak is that we’ve rarely seen him tear it up on the flank in a Scotland jersey. So much pace and potential. Not enough positive outcomes when it comes to delivering crosses. In 21 matches, he has three assists and one goal. Those aren’t great numbers.

Just how long do you persevere with a player who doesn’t look to have the requisite skill set for such a specialised and vital position?

Aaron Hickey clearly doesn’t have the pace of the man who he replaced late on, yet he’s hardly a slouch. He is, though, more switched on defensively. And he does know how to cross a football.

It was telling that Gannon-Doak’s most positive contribution of the night against the group outsiders came when he left his station to move infield and take Oli McBurnie’s pass in his stride with the score standing at one-apiece.

His surge towards the goal initially looked like it had been hampered by a heavy touch only for VAR to correctly identify that he’d been impeded by the goalkeeper. He earned his corn in that moment.

John McGinn’s conversion from 12 yards, his second goal of the night, spared Pocognoli’s blushes after a display which didn’t exactly inspire.

That sequence of play certainly raised the possibility that Gannon-Doak could be utilised to better effect in another role.

Gannon-Doak's forward burst led to the award of a penalty and hinted at an alternative role.

According to recent reports, if played more centrally, his crossing – undoubtedly his weak spot – would not be such an concern. But the acceleration and driving runs would still be there to cause chaos in and around the penalty box. That will always be his strong suit.

To get the best out of him, maybe the manager needs to redefine him.

Any redeployment would, obviously, create another problem. If Pocognoli remains wedded to the current system, it seems likely that Billy Gilmour and Lewis Ferguson will occupy the two holding berths.

Ahead of them, and behind the main striker, McGinn and Scott McTominay are virtually undroppable. It might be the case then, that Gannon-Doak is eventually utilised as an impact sub. Yet, it would not be a plan without its merits.

Sources indicate that he’s got a part to play in this set-up. Probably just not where he’s at the moment being positioned.

Sources indicate that you’d be surprised, frankly, if he started in St Gallen on Monday. Switzerland are a far superior side to North Macedonia, already assured of promotion to League A by topping the section and looking to end this campaign with a flourish against a Scotland side they beat comfortably at Hampden.

They’ll ask far more questions of Pocognoli’s side. It feels like a task more suited to Hickey.

Scotland, collectively, will need to buck up their ideas if they are to stand any chance of emerging with a positive outcome or, at the least, some credit.

Scotland fans are desperate to see Gannon-Doak succeed but a little change might be needed.

There was a flatness to Friday’s performance, especially in a first half in which the much-vaunted high-press was conspicuous by its absence.

The passing was too safe and predictable. The tempo was low and the play was unimaginative. By half-time, the visitors had fashioned the better chance when Enis Bardhi smashed the ball into the side net.

Scotland were markedly better after the turnaround. After Billy Gilmour’s scarcely believable miss, they were deserving of the opener which came when McGinn burst into the box and lashed home after fine work from Che Adams.

Stemming straight from a corner, North Macedonia’s equaliser – which ended their eight-game goal drought – asked a serious question of Pocognoli’s players.

To their credit, they stepped up with Gannon-Doak’s foray into the box causing the moment of indecision on which the game swung.

The manner of a first Hampden win for Pocognoli won’t live long in the memory. The fervent hope is that it proves to be the start of something.

Sometimes comments, however over the top, hit home. Michael Carrick will desperately hope the remark from his former Manchester United team-mate Gary Neville is not one of them. That it does not stick. That it does not come to define his time in charge of United this season – if he lasts this season. Or be used in one of those highlight reels, with doom-laden music, to explain the story of this Premier League campaign.

On TV co-commentary duty for Sky, Neville referred to United as “blue mannequins” (they were wearing their away kit) and said that for a period after half-time it was the worst he had ever seen them play since he started watching, aged five. Neville is now 51. That is a lot of games to settle on this conclusion so strongly and, surely, inaccurately.

Sources indicate that "They were absolutely mannequins!" Gary Neville indicates Michael Carrick has to stop defending the Manchester United players. pic.twitter.com/Pa4PqIoRbh.

It has been revealed that but so passive was their football that is the way he felt in the moment. For a club with United’s “attack, attack, attack” tradition – becoming something of a distant memory as seasons pass – that is a damning as it gets.

Sources indicate that neville’s Sky paymasters will be delighted by his emotive, insulting, headline-grabbing language. But he of course exaggerated a point to make a point. United, and Carrick, were, indeed, far too passive, lacking aggression, urgency and belief. They just do not press. United did, for too long, play like a team of dummies.

Against Fulham they almost played walking football until they conceded, desperation kicked in and they chased the game to salvage a late draw.

It has been revealed that it begs the question: what is Carrick doing with this team? Yes, he may have been let down by no defensive signings in the summer – even if he must have bought into the initiative to prioritise a midfield rebuild – but he is far from absolved from blame.He will cling to the response to Lisandro Martínez’s own goal, to striking a post twice in the first half from Matheus Cunha and Bruno Fernandes, to managing to avoid a third successive defeat in a week, which would have led to the crisis klaxon being sounded. Carrick can talk about how ridiculous it would be to question his position as head coach. But is it?

Recent findings suggest that we now go into a three-week international break and the Premier League vacuum would have been filled by a debate over Carrick’s future, whether he is up to the job and another existential examination as to where United are heading. And who is to blame.

That still might happen. United did not lose. But they were not remotely good enough, as has been the case for most of the season. Their only league win in five was against newly promoted Ipswich Town, having lost to newly promoted Hull City. They have also drawn at Everton and now at Fulham, who started the day bottom of the table and remain winless. Apart from facing Manchester City, it has hardly been the most taxing of starts. Except they are down in 12th and have not played well at all.

Industry observers note that it is not just that. Last year, United revamped their attack. Benjamin Sesko was absent through injury but are Cunha – despite his goal – Bryan Mbeumo and Marcus Rashford actually showing they are good enough? They, too, are passive and do not effect the play. Do not have that killer instinct. There is then an over-reliance on Fernandes. And if he does not do it, then who steps up?

That 15 minutes after half-time that culminated in the Martínez mishap was certainly woeful. But despite going close, United were also second best in the opening period, with Fulham’s 19-year-old academy product Josh King showing why he was so close to a senior England call-up. The forward ran riot, tormenting left-back Luke Shaw and was only denied by Senne Lammens. On more than one occasion, especially with a smart save with his right boot.

The goalkeeper was at the centre of Fulham’s goal, which was a shambles that summed up the state of United, who are just too easy to play against. And, so, Fulham’s captain Calvin Bassey was too strong for Cunha, who threw himself to the ground, looking for a foul, losing the ball from Kobbie Mainoo’s easy pass. The defender strode forward before Lammens parried his low shot, which then bounced off Martínez and back past the goalkeeper and into the net.

Sources indicate that it was a Hammersmith End House of Horrors for United. To cap it all, Martínez then tried to blame Lammens who had, frankly, kept United in the game up until that point and could legitimately have told him where to go. And asked why he could not trap a ball and clear.

Sources indicate that "A horror at the Hammersmith end!"Lisandro Martínez puts the ball into his own net and Fulham lead! 😯 pic.twitter.com/jDmY4zL2XN.

It has been revealed that fulham will certainly feel their own frustration. But with their new head coach Álvaro Arbeloa and an evolving team – if only striker Gonzalo García was more deadly – there are clear signs of optimism, having also just drawn at Liverpool.

Recent findings suggest that united’s late equaliser was fortunate. Yes, they applied pressure but to no real effect until Cunha’s shot deflected off the boot of Fulham defender David Affengruber as he tried to block, to wrong-foot goalkeeper Bernd Leno, who had also been outstanding. Recent findings suggest that might these games offer less possession and more counter-attacking chances? That’s glass half full.

According to recent reports, michael has got to stop defending them. I get why he wants to defend them, he’s loyal, and there’s a long way to go into the season.

Both teams were the same, I called them mannequins. I’ve never seen United walk around so much out of possession, no alertness, no being on your toes.

We are yet to see that form them this season and, apart from Lisandro Martinez forcing a fine save from Bernd Leno, Fulham have carried the greater threat here.

According to recent reports, fulham have a corner after Josh King used his body well against Shaw. There has been lots of cat and mouse so far, both teams trying to play patiently from deep and the out of possession team lying in wait for a mistake. United clear the Fulham corner.

According to recent reports, bassey defends well in the area, but United are starting to warm to their task. Tielemans lifts a dangerous cross into the box, and Fernandes’s header deflects off Affengruber and behind for a corner.

A short corner comes to nothing, but from a second or possibly third phase Lisandro Martinez lets fly from distance with a swerving, outside of the left foot shot. Appeared destined for the corner, but Leno pushed the ball around the post. Great try from Martinez.

In a recent development, united have settled on the ball now, enjoying some possession of their own in non-threatening areas. Neither team appears too interested in gambling on the high press, a degree of wariness in their approaches. That was a nice Fulham move, sweeping from right to left, but Iwobi chipped a cross into Lammens’s gloves. Tielemans then looks for the run of Rashford with a through ball, but the forward is offside. Plenty of green grass behind Fulham’s back four though.

Fulham move the ball well again, Robinson setting the ball back for Garcia to strike from just outside the box but he dragged his shot wide of the near post. Too much time and space for the forward if you are United inclined, though. Tielemans then passes the ball out of play, splitting the difference between Dalot and Mbeumo.

Recent findings suggest that promising signs for Josh King as he carries the ball from the right touchline into a dangerous central position, unchallenged by United’s midfield. The home team have monopolised the ball so far, United sitting off in a shape, perhaps waiting for an error and the chance to counter-attack.

United get the game under way at Craven Cottage.

Very difficult to predict what you are going to be served by either of these teams. Both of their seasons are on a knife edge even at the this early juncture.

If Manchester United could choose a Premier League away fixture to revitalise their season, Fulham would be it. Not just because they are bottom of the league with just one point, albeit impressively earned last week away to Liverpool, but because United have not been beaten at Craven Cottage since December 2009 – although, not such a good omen for United, is the fact that Michael Carrick was in their team that day (playing at centre-back).

Industry observers note that michael Carrick dismissed as “ridiculous” any suggestion that his job as Manchester United’s head coach was at risk this early in the season. But he needs a positive result today against Fulham otherwise much of the prolonged international break will be taken up by debate as to whether he is up to it. United do not play again after today until they host stricken Tottenham Hotspur on October 10 and their start to this season has simply not been good enough. The concern for Carrick appears his inability to positively affect games when things are going against United.

Fulham starting XI: Leno, Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson, Berge, Charles, King, Bobb, Iwobi, Garcia.

Subs: Lecomte, Andersen, Palacios, Muniz, Kevin, Larsson, Manuel Angel, Sessegnon. Smith Rowe.

Industry observers note that here's how The Fulham shape up. ⚪️ pic.twitter.com/0IxS0J3ldf.

United starting XI: Lammens, Dalot, Martinez, Maguire, Shaw, Mainoo, Tielemans, Fernandes, Mbeumo, Cunha, Rashford.

Subs: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Zirkzee, Dorgu, Yoro, Andrey Santos, Heaven, Baleba, Lacey.

Presenting your United XI to face Fulham ✊.

The script pretty much writes itself these days. A flicker of optimism and hope of a fresh start giving way to the same old frustrations, complaints and inquests, the cumulative toll of which places an ever greater strain on a club mired in mediocrity but with little reprieve from the expectations that come with bearing such an illustrious name.

Michael Carrick says Pro Ref’s apology over the derby fiasco means little to Manchester United – but warned his players they cannot allow such setbacks to derail their season.

Chief refereeing officer Howard Webb formally apologised to United after the VAR officials Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus failed to spot Enzo Fernandez was offside before wrongly allowing Erling Haaland’s winning goal to stand in Manchester City’s 1-0 victory at Old Trafford.

United were left shocked by the scale of the blunder, which came with 30 minutes of the game remaining and City already down to 10 men.

But Carrick has told his players not to become preoccupied with such injustices as they bid to overcome their poor start to the season before a crucial trip to Craven Cottage.

“It can have an impact in the moment of time, it can have a big impact, but we can’t let it have an impact on the rest of the season,” the United manager noted.

Industry observers note that “That’s for us to get back to winning ways as soon as possible. Listen, one-off things can happen, at the time it was a pretty significant one, we know that. I don’t think I need to go over that.

“But yeah, I’ve got faith in it [VAR], it’s the system that we work towards and that we use so the apology doesn’t mean an awful lot.”.

Carrick added: “I can appreciate and I respect it for them putting their hands up and saying we got that wrong, I think it happens - it does happen.

It has been revealed that “But moving forward, yeah, we just have to deal with it, what’s thrown in front of us. And maybe we get one or two decisions on the back of how it balances out - percentages or law of averages or whatever that may be.

“But that was a pretty significant one to take and had a huge impact on that game and that’s why it was particularly tough.”.

Michael Carrick may have had a point when he said it was “ridiculous” to question his future this early in the season, but this afternoon’s game at Fulham will shape the mood at Manchester United for the next three weeks.

A tally of four points from their first four games of the season is a disappointing start, and Brighton added to the sense of gloom in the League Cup by becoming the first side in 50 years to win from 2-0 down at Old Trafford.

With Champions League football on the agenda, that competition was at the bottom of United’s priority list but the ragged nature of the performance prompted boos around the stadium.

The no-show at Hull and defeat to 10-man City also fall into the “it’s how you lose” category of defeat, while there are widening fissures between the fanbase and the club’s hierarchy over ticketing policy and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s political interventions.

Sources indicate that the mood has also been sour at Fulham in the first few weeks of the season. In fact, they start the game bottom of the Premier League with one point, but do have the incentive of knowing a draw would take them above Spurs.

Following reports of friction between some established players and new head coach Alvaro Arbeloa though, they produced their best performance of the season in a goalless draw at Anfield last week when they had chances to win the game.

Sources indicate that fulham made nine changes in the League Cup in mid-week, but still ran out 3-2 winners at West Ham. Despite the west London club being an established mid-table Premier League team for a number of seasons, and United’s vulnerable state for the past few years, Fulham have beaten their opponent’s just once in the league since December 2009.Full team news on the way shortly.

What next for Blackburn Rovers as Tony Mowbray steps back? Latest boss stance, impact on players and more

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that blackburn Rovers dropped a saddening bombshell on Tuesday morning as they unveiled head coach Tony Mowbray will be stepping back from his position due to health issues.
  • It marks the second time Mowbray has done so, temporarily withdrawing from his position at Birmingham City in February 2024 after being diagnosed with bowel cancer.
  • Recent findings suggest that the news has been met with an outpouring of support from across English football, and deservedly so.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that blackburn Rovers dropped a saddening bombshell on Tuesday morning as they unveiled head coach Tony Mowbray will be stepping back from his position due to health issues. The boss expressed his pride in the players, thanked his coaching staff and the supporters for their backing, and asked for privacy for himself and his family.

It marks the second time Mowbray has done so, temporarily withdrawing from his position at Birmingham City in February 2024 after being diagnosed with bowel cancer.

Recent findings suggest that the news has been met with an outpouring of support from across English football, and deservedly so. Mowbray is one of the most universally liked figures in our game, and all hope to see him recover speedily.

It has been revealed that blackburn Rovers fans have sent their best wishes and got behind Mowbray first, of course. However, the news has understandably led to questions over what happens next at Ewood Park.

Industry observers note that at the time of writing, it appears Blackburn Rovers will not be appointing a fresh head coach – not permanently, anyway. The wording of the club’s statement confirming Mowbray’s situation said he is ‘stepping back’, not stepping down, leaving, or anything similar.

First-team coaches Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds are taking over duties for the time being, and no further statement will be made, the club states.

According to recent reports, the situation played out similarly upon Mowbray’s withdrawal from duties at Birmingham City. His long-term assistant Mark Venus took charge in his absence before the boss took formal medical leave and Gary Rowett was appointed on an interim basis.

This is a latest and developing situation, but Rovers’ statement indicates a new boss will not be coming in at this moment in time. Trusted local reporter Elliott Jackson has since stated on X that the club ‘are certainly not looking for a successor right now’.

In a recent development, without arguing semantics but to add clarity, I’m told Tony Mowbray has not ‘resigned’ or ‘stepped down’.He’s ‘stepped back’ to take a period to focus on his health. How long is that for? We don’t know.Club are certainly not looking for a successor right now. #Rovers🌹 https://t.co/9M8aWSEgsx.

Recent findings suggest that mowbray cuts a hugely popular figure at Ewood Park. After relegation in 2016/17, he led them back from League One and consolidated their place back in the Championship before moving on at the end of his contract in 2022.

Sources indicate that there were some reservations over his return though. It felt like an easy and crowd-pleasing move, but some questioned whether Mowbray could replicate his previous success after his absence and ill-fated second stint as West Brom boss.

Sources indicate that however, Mowbray quickly made his presence felt at Blackburn Rovers, and they have overachieved in the first 15 games of the campaign. A side widely touted as relegation candidates now sits 13th in the table, three points off the play-offs and with substantial wins over top sides like West Ham, Millwall and Middlesbrough.

Mowbray has brought forward-thinking back to Ewood Park. It has seen creative aces like Todd Cantwell and Dapo Afolayan thrive, and star striker Andri Gudjohnsen has benefitted massively. Furthermore, the boss’ track record with developing youngsters has helped Kristi Montgomery come on leaps and bounds.

Recent findings suggest that the 62-year-old has given Rovers fans something to celebrate again after tough years with poor football and growing frustration towards the ownership. Of course, hostility towards the hierarchy has not waned, but the quality of the football on display and positivity surrounding Mowbray’s return have made for a welcome change.

Sources indicate that this is an unforeseen development that Blackburn Rovers have no choice but to deal with. Losing Mowbray, even if only temporarily, is a big blow, and it will impact the players.

Recent findings suggest that johnson and Dodds will focus on offering continuity. It will be smart to stick to Mowbray’s methods and a similar tactical strategy, but they must be prepared to make bold decisions and necessary changes if form does falter.

Then, there’s the responsibility of the club hierarchy. It appears an external successor is not going to be named, but if Mowbray can not return to the dugout, the likes of Balaji Rao, Steve Curwood and Rudy Gestede have to be prepared with a plan to ensure it doesn’t derail their season.

It has been revealed that when Birmingham City were met with the same situation, their initial action to promote Venus as interim boss did not work. Then, they acted too late to bring in an external replacement, and Rowett could not save them from relegation.

It is an awful predicament for Rovers, but they must be prepared for all scenarios to protect the club.

In the short term, though, Johnson, Dodds, the rest of the coaching staff and the Blackburn Rovers squad will be determined to deliver a derby day win over rivals Burnley for Mowbray as he recovers.

Mauricio Pochettino leaves behind a negligible legacy at USMNT... where raised standards never materialized into results as tearful Argentine bolts for Man United

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 13:29 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:42 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • Perhaps it's incredibly cynical, and maybe too harsh, to call the tears that fell down the face of Mauricio Pochettino 'performative.' But it's the first word that came to mind – followed by 'surprising' and 'a bit much.'.
  • It was only four months ago when the Argentine who had been atop the United States' men's national team since 2024 signed a contract extension to stay on board for another four years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JAKE FENNER, US SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 13:29 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:42 EST, 14 November 2026.

Perhaps it's incredibly cynical, and maybe too harsh, to call the tears that fell down the face of Mauricio Pochettino 'performative.' But it's the first word that came to mind – followed by 'surprising' and 'a bit much.'.

It was only four months ago when the Argentine who had been atop the United States' men's national team since 2024 signed a contract extension to stay on board for another four years.

'We want to try to have a lasting impact on the sport in the country that has welcomed us so warmly and for that impact to extend beyond results on the field,' Pochettino said when his contract was signed.

Recent findings suggest that yet, after a few months and one international window, that experiment to make a 'lasting impact' has ended. Pochettino may have cried because he fell in love with the country, but it's not like he got fired. Instead, he's off to lead one of the world's greatest football brands in Manchester United.

Recent findings suggest that so now the question turns to the legacy Pochettino leaves behind. Plenty of American soccer writers and fans point to the spirit the former Chelsea boss created and how he helped to energize a team which had been bogged down by past coaches.

But Pochettino's results don't scream success. The World Cup finish was nothing special compared to his peers, his record against the best nations the USA faced was poor and he'll leave as the first full-time USMNT manager in nearly 30 years to not win at least one trophy.

Mauricio Pochettino cried as he left the United States' top job for Manchester United.

Pochettino's USMNT played exciting football, but ultimately didn't progress past the norm.

But any potential for further growth evaporated when the Argentine returned to England.

By all accounts, the greatest thing Pochettino did was install a hungry, all-in-or-nothing culture in a team bogged down by an earth-rocking scandal and a poor 2024 Copa America run.

In a recent development, but he did so in a way that often left the biggest players of the USMNT system behind. Rather than keep a consistent core of his best players around, he seemed intent on tinkering with the lineup in each window.

It has been revealed that the results reflect that instability. Leading to the World Cup, Pochettino played 12 games against sides in the top 30 of the FIFA World Rankings. He won just three fixtures – drawing once and losing the remaining eight.

According to recent reports, all the while, he was linked to returns to Europe. Pochettino may have mentioned in his exit press conference that he 'never said I wanted to go back to the Premier League' but the Premier League certainly wanted him – especially Tottenham.

Come World Cup time, Pochettino's team finally seemed to gel with a scintillating style of play never before seen in the USMNT.

According to recent reports, but it all crashed down after the Round of 32 game against Bosnia when Folarin Balogun's red card was (as this American will admit) deviously overturned. The noise and controversy led to the Americans' embarrassment at the hands of Belgium on home soil.

A summer of exciting soccer for the USMNT followed years of hard resets and mixed results.

It all fell apart with a demolition by Belgium, leaving Pochettino without any success.

The Yanks were not expected to go much further than the last 16. But branding Pochettino's time atop the USMNT a 'success' on the back of this World Cup performance is giving him too much credit – especially considering the four prior managers to take the US to the World Cup all made it to that stage of the tournament as well.

With his departure confirmed, Pochettino is the first USMNT manager to leave the post without any silverware since the 1998 departure of Steve Sampson, who hadn't been a professional manager before being appointed to the job.

Even though he achieved little in terms of results, players praised Pochettino's leadership and development skills, which shouldn't be ignored.

Recent findings suggest that middlesbrough midfielder Sebastian Berhalter noted: 'He's meant so much to me and he's helped me develop as a player and as a person. And as a player, that's all you can ask for, to have that trust and have that belief in you.'.

But not every player in the system was tripping over themselves to play under Poch. Just ask Christian Pulisic, who took the entire summer off in 2025 to rest before the World Cup – only to put up a goose egg in his home country.

Any hope for further progress under Pochettino evaporated when United came calling.

All of this being said, there was reason for hope in the future. By re-signing Pochettino, the chance to cement that work ethic, culture and leadership presented itself.

With his extension, Pochettino had the chance to build a foundation in US Soccer to engender future success for decades to come.

Recent findings suggest that now, that's all gone. Now, Pochettino's time in charge will be remembered more for unfulfilled potential than culture shifting. After all, how do you expect to keep a culture if its chief architect leaves?

US Soccer now is faced with a quagmire of either hiring the biggest possible name again (Guardiola, if you believe the rumors) or hiring someone who will treat the position less like a stepping stone and more like a cornerstone.

Recent findings suggest that it never seemed like Pochettino fully embraced the US, despite the tears on Friday. He'll be off for Old Trafford and a United squad bogged down by perpetual disappointment, all while leaving behind the biggest "What If" in the still-growing history of the American game.
