#14753. Manchester City found guilty of 114 charges

📅 25 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2091 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Manchester City found guilty of 114 charges

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules.
  • City face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League.
  • If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules. It is a decision that, if upheld, would equate to one of the biggest scandals in football history.

City face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League. Or a combination of all, under rule W51 of its handbook. No punishment has yet been announced.

If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.

The charges can be broken down into five categories and relate to a period from 2009-23 in which City won six League Cups, three FA Cups, seven league titles and the Champions League. There is the provision for removing past titles, but that would appear remote.

City have been the dominant force in English football for most of that time, but that status is under threat with a verdict that will send shockwaves around Europe and could have huge ramifications for the club.

That is unless they can win an appeal, with sources cautioning it still may take up to another two to three years for the case to be resolved, following on from an already five-year investigation.

The Premier League’s rules provide for an independent appeal board with broad powers, including the ability to uphold, vary or overturn the independent commission’s decision.

Industry observers note that it would therefore appear that despite the verdict, the case is far from being resolved and punishment decided. The details of the commission’s findings, when published, will be crucial to determining what happens next.

But if it is upheld, the verdict also opens up the possibility of City facing legal action from other clubs who feel they missed out on trophies and even merit money from league placings.

It is understood Premier League clubs are already discussing legal action and possible compensation claims as a result of the guilty verdict.

Each of those cases would have to be held individually, potentially leading to years more of litigation. Conversely, if City win their appeal, they too could take legal action against the Premier League the damage caused to their reputation.

Sources indicate that there has not yet been an official confirmation of the independent panel’s verdict from the Premier League. The Premier League declined to comment.

However, several sources have told Telegraph Sport that the panel has found City guilty of all but one of the charges they faced. The one that has not been proved is noted to be one of the most serious of the 115.

The damning verdict for City is a major new test of fragile UK relations with the United Arab Emirates, with whom bilateral trade was worth £25bn last year. Redacted freedom of information documents, seen by Telegraph Sport, show Abu Dhabi hosted UK government officials including Lord Stockwood, then investment minister, as recently as February. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the City chairman and trusted adviser to the UAE president, was present at the meeting. Government notes from the meeting recorded that he “noted they are very proud of what they have achieved through their investments in Manchester”.

The Government previously caused acrimony among senior leaders in Abu Dhabi after putting forward legislation to ban foreign states from owning UK newspapers and news magazines. The intervention prompted the collapse of a takeover of The Telegraph in April 2024, which was largely funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the owner of City and vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

Sources indicate that the previous UK government has admitted its embassy in Abu Dhabi and the Foreign Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) in London discussed the charges levelled at City by the Premier League. However it refused to disclose the correspondence.

According to recent reports, city have steadfastly maintained they are innocent, promising “irrefutable” evidence in support of their position, and had assembled some of the most expensive lawyers in the country to argue their case. Despite the verdict, the club are understood to be confident that it will win the argument in the end. Senior figures are said to be calm about the latest development, as significant as it seems.

Industry observers note that city rebuilt their team this summer and it is understood that signings were brought in on conventional player contracts, rather than terms including clauses triggered in the event of a heavy punishment. Given the club have consistently denied breaching financial regulations, and their deals for new players to work with head coach Enzo Maresca underlines their position.

On Friday, a City spokesman noted: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

“The club have diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”.

Sources close to Pep Guardiola, the former City manager who stepped down last summer after 10 years of remarkable success at the club, including a treble triumph in 2023 and an unprecedented fourth straight league title in 2024, insist he has not been informed of any verdict.

In the days after City were first charged, Guardiola mounted a fierce defence of the club, claiming: “I am fully convinced we will be [proved] innocent.”.

The verdict vindicates the Premier League’s decision to launch an investigation after explosive allegations that City had routinely broken financial rules were first made in Der Spiegel in 2018 based on the Football Leaks documents.

Uefa previously accused City of breaches of its financial regulations and confirmed in 2020 that it was suspending the club from the Champions League for two years for “overstating” sponsorship revenue between 2012 and 2016.

Sources indicate that city denied the Uefa charges and, after an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the two-year ban was overturned. Cas found that a number of the claims brought by Uefa had fallen outside a five-year “time bar” and others were “not established”.

Recent findings suggest that it did, however, still impose a €10m fine after ruling that City failed to cooperate with investigators. City had previously also agreed a settlement with Uefa of €20m in 2014 following an investigation into their finances.

Sources indicate that legal experts agreed that the commission’s verdict is far from the end of the case. Yasin Patel, barrister at Church Court Chambers, mentioned: “City’s lawyers will now analyse this decision and look at the options open to them to appeal, which may include procedural impropriety, wrongful interpretation of law, and legal errors – importantly, they can guarantee an appeal.

“Sanctions could include a major fine, points deduction, relegation or even all three. Factoring in whether titles and trophies should be stripped, whether other clubs have been robbed of further revenue and opportunities due to City’s wrongdoings and losses incurred, we safely say that this is only the first chapter of a long-running legal saga that will not end any time soon.”.

In a recent development, ian Hargreaves, partner with specialist disputes firm Quillon Law, said the verdict was “not the end of the story but the beginning of a new phase”, and added: “There is also the question of whether the panel’s decision can withstand a hard-fought appeal, and on what grounds any challenge might be brought. Much will depend on the detail of the panel’s findings and reasoning, which will inevitably be closely scrutinised by both sides.”.

Former Manchester City midfielder Rodri, who won the Ballon d’Or during his trophy-laden spell at the club, mentioned he believed the club were innocent.

Industry observers note that “For the players, it’s different than it is for journalists. I can understand all opinions, but we try to stay positive,” the Spain midfielder said while on international duty.

“When you see all the people who worked hard at City to achieve success, you know what we achieved can’t be taken away. It wasn’t paid for with money, but with effort and teamwork. Everything we achieved was deserved; we marked one of the great eras of English football. I believe in the club’s innocence – we already went through this in 2020.”.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, remarked: “I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions.”.

Zohran Kwame Mamdani, the mayor of Newly introduced York, posted “114” in relation to the charges while former Manchester United players David de Gea and Rio Ferdinand both asked whether they should be due winner’s medals from past seasons.

The Premier League statement in February 2023 said that “a number of alleged breaches” had been referred to an independent commission. It then detailed each specific rule against each season in which the alleged breach took place. The precise number was not clear from the statement and led to varying reports between 115 and 130. Friday’s news suggested the figure was 115.

All the way to 2009-10, the first full season following the club’s takeover by Sheikh Mansour, who is a member of the Abu Dhabi Royal family and the vice president of the United Arab Emirates. There were charges relating to all 14 seasons until the Premier League completed their investigation during the 2022-23 campaign. In that time, City won seven Premier League titles, six League Cups, three FA Cups and the Champions League. They have since won another league title – the first club to do so four times in a row – as well as the Uefa Super Cup, the Fifa Club World Cup and the FA Cup and League Cup double last season.

They can be split into five groups. The biggest relates to the seasons from 2009-10 until 2017-18 and the requirement for clubs to provide accurate financial information and act in the utmost good faith.

It has been revealed that the next set of rules concern the full disclosure of manager and player payments. The alleged manager breaches related to the period between 2009-10 and 2012-13, when Roberto Mancini was leading the team. The alleged breaches with respect to player payments relate to all of the seasons between 2010-11 and 2015-16.

Industry observers note that as well as providing financial detail, clubs were required to meet Uefa and Premier League rules which were designed to bring a club’s spending broadly in line with their income by placing set limits on losses. City were charged with breaches of Uefa’s licencing and financial fair play rules from 2013-14 until 2017-18, and the Premier League’s profit and sustainability rules from 2015-16 until 2017-18.

The final set of charges spanned the five seasons during which City were being investigated by the Premier League and rules that require members to cooperate in the utmost good faith by providing information and documents.

It has been revealed that A full picture will only emerge when the commission publishes its findings but we know that the Premier League investigation began in December 2018 following allegations in the German newspaper Der Spiegel based on the Football Leaks documents. These included alleged payments to former manager Mancini for consultancy work at an Abu Dhabi-based club that was separate to his regular contract at City.

In a recent development, we also know that City were alleged to have breached rules over setting out image rights payments to players in their club contract. Der Spiegel reported that the Premier League investigation also focused on payments to under-age players, as well as whether club sponsors were paying for commercial deals themselves or a significant proportion was in fact effectively coming from owner Sheikh Mansour.

In a recent development, city have always denied breaking any rules. In response to the Premier League statement about the alleged breaches, they stated that they have “irrefutable evidence” to support their position and “look forward to this matter being put to rest once and for all.”.

At the start of the hearing in September 2024, Guardiola also remarked: “Wait for the independent panel. We believe we have not done anything wrong.”.

Of the Football Leaks documents, City remarked: “We will not be providing any comment on out-of-context materials. The attempt to damage the club’s reputation is organised and clear.”.

By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER and CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 16:03 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 16:48 EST, 14 November 2026.

Thomas Tuchel was dragged into a bitter race row on the eve of England's Nations League showdown with Spain.

Tuchel had been asked before England's departure for Spain about England's protocols in case their players suffered racist abuse at the Metropolitano Stadium on Sunday evening.

England players were notoriously subject to racial abuse at the Bernabeu in 2004 and England have not played in Madrid since.

But Spain manager Luis de la Fuente reacted angrily when he was told that Tuchel had addressed the subject.

Sources indicate that 'Tell Tuchel that there is no racism in Spain,' de la Fuente noted. 'Just like in England. We are not racist.'.

The row then deepened when a Spanish journalist told Tuchel about De La Fuente's reaction and the England coach grew exasperated with the line of questioning.

Tuchel had been asked before England's departure for Spain about England's protocols.

'Tell Tuchel that there is no racism in Spain,' de la Fuente said. 'Just like in England. We are not racist.'.

'I was polite enough to answer a question from your colleagues,' Tuchel mentioned, 'and you run and ask Spain's coach and tell them that I talked about racism in Spain.

According to recent reports, 'I never talked about racism in Spain. I answered a question politely. I never expect racism. The dressing room is the most anti-racist place in the world. This is a perfect example of how you create confusion out of nothing.'.

Industry observers note that tuchel had earlier said: 'It's important that the players know about the protocol. And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch.

According to recent reports, 'We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]. There is a protocol in place.'.

England midfielder Declan Rice said that Tuchel had not yet addressed the group about racism protocols but that they were clear about what they would do if any England players were abused.

England's game against Bulgaria in Sofia in 2019 was halted after allegations of racism against England players but the game was completed.

Thomas Tuchel has revealed that James Trafford will face world champions Spain on Sunday night, raising questions over Jordan Pickford’s status as England’s No 1.

It was assumed that Pickford, who the head coach maintains is his first choice, would keep the jersey given the identity of the opposition and the chance for England to top their Nations League group with victory here in Madrid.

However, Tuchel will hand Leeds stopper Trafford his fifth cap at the Metropolitano Stadium.

’We want to try and see how far Traff is,’ said Tuchel, who rotated his keepers during last month’s international break. ‘So he gets a highly competitive match. We had some changes in the back four in the last match (2-1 win over Croatia on Thursday), so we went for more stability and more experience with Pickers.

It has been revealed that ‘Tomorrow is a high-pressure match, on the biggest stage, and it's exactly what we need to see where we are with him (Trafford). Hopefully he's not too over-excited or overly nervous, because there's no need to be. We trust him. But it is different to play for England than to play for your club.

'To have the opportunity to play matches where it really matters is the best way to show up, and to show that you're ready.’.

It was put to Tuchel that it would make more sense to play the goalkeeper he believes is his No 1 in the biggest game from this round of fixtures.

’It was the circumstances of the last match, that we had some changes in the back four, and that was the decision in the goalkeeping team,’ he said. 'Jordan is at the moment our No.1. I have a very clear picture in high-pressure moments. He played in tournaments and played for me in the World Cup.’.

Meanwhile, centre back Ezri Konsa is also set to start after recovering from a knee concern.

‘I’m very pleased with how he has fitted in seamlessly at Arsenal,’ said Tuchel. ‘It just looks like he's always been there. For us, it’s amazing that he plays on the highest level, competes for every title, is in an atmosphere and in a situation where it really matters that you stay focused and you show up every three days. It's only positives for us.’.

PROBABLE ENGLAND XI: Trafford; White, Quansah, Konsa, Hall; Anderson, Rice; Rogers, Jude Bellingham, Gordon; Kane.

Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis

⏱️ ~123 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1,2,3.
  • Industry observers note that gene expression profiles classify breast cancers into luminal A or luminal B (hormone-receptor-positive (HR+)), HER2-positive and basal-like subtypes.
  • According to recent reports, chromatin organization, mediated by DNA and histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), facilitates the acquisition of epigenetically distinct cellular states in genetically identical cells10,11,12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1,2,3. Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival4,5,6,7. Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse.

Industry observers note that gene expression profiles classify breast cancers into luminal A or luminal B (hormone-receptor-positive (HR+)), HER2-positive and basal-like subtypes. Among these, basal-like subtypes largely overlap with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)2,3. These classifications guide treatment management and prognosis. Luminal HR+ breast cancer generally responds to endocrine therapy with favourable outcomes, yet many patients relapse8. Single-cell and spatial studies have revealed substantial intratumoural heterogeneity among subtypes, which potentially drive treatment resistance and recurrence4,5,6,7,9.

According to recent reports, chromatin organization, mediated by DNA and histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), facilitates the acquisition of epigenetically distinct cellular states in genetically identical cells10,11,12. Although single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell chromatin-accessibility sequencing (scATAC–seq) delineate intratumour heterogeneity13,14,15,16, the contribution of chromatin patterns remains unclear17. Single-cell profiling of histone marks, such as trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me3), implicates chromatin states in breast tumour heterogeneity and treatment resistance18,19. However, these methods measure a limited number of chromatin marks, which hinders analyses of complex patterns and interactions. We developed a cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) method to systematically profile multiple histone PTMs and decode population-specific chromatin patterns to examine heterogeneity among cancer cells20,21,22,23.

Tumour epigenetic states are also reflected in blood. Cell-free, plasma-circulating nucleosomes, released mainly by dying normal and cancer cells, retain tissue-of-origin epigenetic patterns24,25,26,27. Our single-molecule imaging platform, epigenetics of plasma isolated nucleosomes (EPINUC), captures multiple epigenetic features on plasma nucleosomes28. This method detects colorectal cancer, including low-burden early-stage disease28, and enables minimally invasive molecular profiling and treatment monitoring of paediatric brain tumours29.

Here we present a holistic epigenetic analysis of primary treatment-naive breast tumours and blood cell-free nucleosomes. Linking recurrent intratumoural epigenetic patterns to circulating nucleosomes connects tumour epigenetic heterogeneity with its potential clinical implications. This work reveals epigenetic alterations as key mediators of intratumour heterogeneity and potential biomarkers for early diagnosis and prognosis.

It has been revealed that to assess heterogeneity in breast tumour histone modifications, we performed epigenetic focused CyTOF on fresh, surgically resected tumours from treatment-naive women and quantified histone modifications at single-cell resolution (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). The cohort included mainly luminal HR+ tumours and only one basal triple-negative (TN, HR–) tumour (n = 12; Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1a,b), as standard neoadjuvant therapy excluded most TN cases from treatment-naive eligibility. Following batch correction and normalization, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) analysis of all 12 tumours revealed that tumour cells largely occupied patient-specific regions, whereas stromal cells clustered together across patients. This result aligns with previous studies that measured single-cell genomic differences13,14 (Fig. 1b, Methods and Supplementary Fig. 2a). Partial overlap among luminal tumour cells from different patients probably reflects shared lineage-specific epigenetic programs. As expected, stromal cells expressed vimentin and αSMA, whereas tumour cells expressed the epithelial keratins, EpCAM and E-cadherin (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2b,c). Notably, the basal TN tumour differed from HR+ tumours, showing low expression of the luminal marker GATA3 and high expression of the basal marker cytokeratin-5 (K5; also known as KRT5) and mesenchymal vimentin markers (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2d). Stromal and tumour chromatin patterns also differed, a result that underscores their role in dictating cellular identity (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2e). CyTOF analysis of MCF7 (luminal) and four basal-like TN cell lines validated that GATA3 and K5 expression patterns can differentiate luminal and basal-like identities. Moreover, SHAP analysis30,31 identified these two markers as the strongest discriminators of tumour type (Fig. 1e,f). Using multiple cell-identity markers, we derived a PermCell luminal signature (Methods) that accurately distinguished the identities of the cell lines (Fig. 1g).

It has been revealed that we next examined intratumour heterogeneity, focusing on the cancer cells of each luminal breast tumour separately. UMAP clustering and density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) across all features revealed three subpopulations in each tumour, which we termed cycling, luminal and basal-like (Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). These subpopulations were also conserved in two different luminal patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. This finding validates the observed heterogeneity as an inherent feature of luminal breast tumours and excludes contamination of normal cells (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 1c). MCF7 cells indicated similar luminal and basal-like heterogeneity, although most cells were cycling, as expected for a cell line (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In tumours, only a luminal subset cycled and expressed high levels of Ki-67, a result consistent with previous immunohistochemistry (IHC) and scRNA-seq studies14,32. CyTOF Ki-67 levels correlated with pathology estimates (Fig. 1k). Cycling cells also showed high levels of multiple chromatin modifications, both in raw measurements and following normalization to core histones (Fig. 1i, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Fig. 3). We validated this result by repeating CyTOF analyses of two tumours (14 and 18), adding the established cell cycle marker phospho-Rb (pRb). pRb-positive cells showed an increase in core histones, as expected from cycling cells, and a larger increase in histone PTMs (Supplementary Fig. 3). Accordingly, the epigenetically inferred cycling fraction strongly correlated with Ki-67 levels (Fig. 1l).

Most cancer cells strongly expressed GATA3 and scored highly for the luminal signature, consistent with clinical classification (Fig. 1h, Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Moreover, in each tumour, the PDX samples and the MCF7 cells, we identified a minor recurrent subpopulation that acquired basal-like identity, with high K5 expression and a reduced luminal signature (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4a). This phenotypic diversity is consistent with previous single-cell studies of human and mouse breast tumours14,21,33,34. Notably, luminal and basal-like cells also had distinct histone PTM signatures (Fig. 1h–j and Extended Data Fig. 1). Accordingly, UMAP plots based solely on histone modifications revealed separation of the subpopulations, which validated the epigenetic basis of this phenotypic diversity (Supplementary Fig. 4b). In MCF7 cells, epigenetic UMAP and clustering similarly identified several clusters, including a K5hi basal-like population (Fig. 1m). These basal-like cells with reduced luminal signalling appeared closer in UMAP space to the TN cell lines, which provided further support for their basal-like identity (Supplementary Fig. 4c). Independent CyTOF experiments, additional MCF7 parental cell culture and populations derived from independent single-cell clones revealed similar subpopulation patterns, a result that argues against a genetic basis for these effects (Fig. 1n and Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). Moreover, individual PDX tumours derived from the same donor and grown independently in different mice showed similar subpopulation proportions, which provides support for a dynamic and plastic relationship between cell states (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Overall, our data revealed inherent intratumour heterogeneity in luminal tumours, with epigenetic variability between distinct subpopulations.

Recent findings suggest that we further explored the characteristics of the cycling, luminal and basal-like subpopulations. Unsupervised clustering grouped corresponding subpopulations across patients, which confirmed their robustness and similarity (Fig. 2a). Across tumours, luminal cells expressed oestrogen receptor (ER), GATA3 and cytokeratin-8 and cytokeratin-18 (K8/18; also known as KRT8 and KRT18, respectively), whereas basal-like cells downregulated these luminal markers and highly expressed K5 (Fig. 2b). As these subpopulations also exhibited distinct and conserved chromatin patterns, we applied a machine-learning algorithm to predict intratumour classification35. In each tumour, a model trained on a random subset predicted the remaining cells with 94% accuracy, which confirmed the robust differences between subpopulations (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3a). It also assigned 78% of unclustered ‘noise’ cells with >95% confidence, generating classifications that aligned with the original clustering and UMAP positions (Extended Data Fig. 3b). SHAP analysis identified the features driving each subpopulation. In detail, histone PTMs, particularly the four acetylation marks, were leading predictors of cycling cells despite overlap of individual marks with basal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Polycomb-associated H3K27me3 and H2Aub also contributed to the features, a finding consistent with previously observed Polycomb deregulation and pro-proliferative activity in breast cancer36,37,38.

Luminal and basal-like separation was similarly epigenetic driven, with H4K20me3, H3K36me3 and H3K9me2 marks having the highest SHAP scores (Fig. 2d). Across tumours, basal-like cells consistently had increased H3K9me2 and H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation, whereas luminal cells had enhanced H4K20me3, H3K36me3, H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 marks (Fig. 2e). These results align with subtype-associated histone PTM signatures39 and reported roles for H3K4 demethylases, such as JARID1B, in luminal–basal transitions40. Both luminal and basal-like cells highlighted similar pRb distribution, which provide support for the conclusion that these results reflect distinct cell states rather than cell cycle differences (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Similar epigenetic signatures distinguished luminal and basal-like populations in PDX models (Extended Data Fig. 3f). Accordingly, epigenetic-only basal-like PermCell scores accurately captured basal-like cells in tumours, PDXs and MCF7 cells (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 4). Overall, our computational framework confirms that there is recurrent epigenetic heterogeneity in HR+ breast tumours and highlight chromatin patterns associated with basal-like K5hi cells.

Recent findings suggest that consistent with the CyTOF results, tumours with higher fractions of epigenetically defined basal-like cells had fewer ER-positive and progesterone receptor (PR)-positive cells, as measured by IHC (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b and Supplementary Table 2). Basal-like cells were also more abundant in worse-prognosis luminal B than luminal A tumours. This result is in agreement with studies showing that these tumours exhibit features shared with the basal-like subtype3,41,42,43 (Fig. 2g). Although tumour mutational burden was low across the cohort, it correlated positively with the CyTOF-defined basal-like fraction, which parallels the greater genomic instability typically associated with TNBC44,45 (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Table 2). TP53 mutant tumours likewise contained more basal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 5c), a finding reminiscent of single-cell studies of glioblastoma showing that genetic mutations may affect balance between cellular states46. Overall, these associations between pathological and molecular characteristics link the epigenetically distinct basal-like subpopulation to a more aggressive disease phenotype.

In a recent development, to characterize these cells functionally, we performed FACS to sort cells from tumour 19 and then low-input mass spectrometry. After excluding stroma through pan-cytokeratin staining, cells were sorted according to K5 levels to enrich for basal-like cells compared with the luminal population. K5low cells highly expressed luminal markers and proteins associated with oestrogen signalling, whereas basal-like K5hi cells expressed proteins involved in oncogenic pathways, such as MYC–mTOR signalling (Fig. 2i–k). Moreover, multiple chromatin regulators differed between these subpopulations, including the H3K4me1 methyltransferase SETD7 and histone demethylase KDM4A, consistent with the histone PTM differences observed by CyTOF47,48 (Extended Data Fig. 5d). KDM4A, enriched in K5hi cells, targets H3K9me3 and H3K36me3, which potentially accounts for their reduced levels and H3K9me2 accumulation in the basal-like population49. Comparisons with a normal mammary single-cell atlas50 revealed hormone-sensing programs in K5low cells and an alveolar progenitor signature in K5hi cells (Fig. 2l), a result consistent with their enrichment in luminal and basal TN tumours, respectively50.

Sources indicate that to gain a mechanistic understanding of these findings, we sorted MCF7 cells using K5-specific and GATA3-specific antibodies and performed transcriptomic profiling, comparing basal-like cells (K5hiGATA3low) to bulk MCF7 or extreme luminal cells (K5lowGATA3hi; Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Notably, basal-like cells were enriched for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes (P < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 5f). We then focused on differentially expressed cell surface markers to enable live sorting, which revealed that CD74 was significantly upregulated in basal-like cells in both MCF7 and tumour 19 proteomic analyses (Fig. 2m and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Live-sorted CD74hi cells exhibited increased migratory capacity in migration and wound-healing assays, which provided further support for the more aggressive phenotypes of basal-like cells (Fig. 2n,o and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Together, these single-cell and bulk proteomics and functional assays identify epigenetically distinct K5hi basal-like cells in luminal tumours associated with aggressive traits such as reduced luminal signalling, elevated oncogenic signalling and increased migratory potential.

Industry observers note that the distinct chromatin and phenotypic states of the basal-like subpopulation led us to explore whether intratumour epigenetic heterogeneity is also apparent in DNA methylation patterns. Thus, we conducted deep whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) on three luminal tumours from our cohort. DNA methylation patterns accurately capture breast cancer subtyping, as shown by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)51. We next jointly deconvoluted the TCGA and our WGBS data into functional archetypes (V1–V3), with each tumour positioned in the deconvolution space. Stratifying the data into three archetypes revealed the expected separation of basal (TN) tumours from luminal (HR+), with archetype V3 associated with basal tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Tumours 18, 19 and 23 from our cohort clustered with the luminal tumours, as expected from their bulk clinical subtyping. Correlation of the archetype contribution with RNA expression confirmed the association of V1 and V2 with luminal transcriptional programs, whereas V3 was associated with EMT, a result consistent with previous studies of TN tumours52,53,54 (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 5a). To improve resolution, we added a fourth archetype (V4). This analysis revealed another layer of diversity: basal TN tumours were strongly associated with V3, which corresponded with reduced oestrogen signalling and increased oncogenic signalling, whereas luminal tumours were more heterogeneous and spread across the V1 axis (Fig. 3a,b and Supplementary Fig. 5b). Notably, V1 was strongly enriched for EMT, thereby potentially capturing an intermediate-transitional state between luminal and basal-like programs. Moreover, the percentage of CyTOF-measured, vimentin-positive cells, indicative of EMT, in tumours 18 and 19 differed accordingly (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 5c). Tumour 19, with a higher V1 contribution, also comprised more vimentin-positive cells, as assessed by CyTOF. These results support the use of WGBS deconvolution to capture functionally distinct cellular states in tumours, such as luminal cells undergoing EMT.

To directly link the CyTOF-defined subpopulations with DNA methylation patterns, we sorted K5hi and K5low cells from tumour 5 and tumour 23, followed by enzyme-mediated methylation sequencing (EM-seq). Functional enrichment of differentially methylated promoters revealed hypermethylation of oestrogen-response programs in K5hi cells, whereas genes associated with aggressive and oncogenic features, including KRAS signalling and mesenchymal or basal-state transitions, were hypomethylated (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). We next derived a CpG island (CGI) methylation signature to distinguish the two states using CGIs that were concordantly differentially methylated across both tumours. In TCGA breast cancer data, this signature scored higher in basal-like tumours, which indicated that the K5hi methylation program resembles basal-like tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6e). K5hi samples also demonstrated higher contribution to the basal-associated and EMT-associated archetypes than K5low samples, in both the three-archetype and four-archetype models (Extended Data Fig. 6f,g). Thus, the CyTOF-defined basal-like population exhibits basal-like and EMT-related methylation programs, which reveals another layer of intratumoural epigenetic heterogeneity.

It has been revealed that having identified distinct DNA methylation programs associated with tumour cell states, we next assessed cell-to-cell variability by clustering read-level methylation patterns across 100-bp genomic bins and calculating empirical entropy as an estimation of cell-type heterogeneity55. Genes near high-entropy bins were associated with functional terms related to poor differentiation, tumour aggressiveness and basal compared with luminal identity (Supplementary Fig. 6a). This result suggests that empirical entropy, by capturing diverse DNA methylation states, can be used as a proxy for cell-to-cell heterogeneity and reveal functional differences between subpopulations. We next calculated the mean entropy for each CGI (Extended Data Fig. 7a). As expected, most CGIs were unmethylated across all cells56, thus showing zero entropy. The variable CGIs (entropy > 0) were functionally enriched for EMT and the related Hedgehog signalling pathways, which indicated that these are differentially regulated in tumours57 (Extended Data Fig. 7b). This analysis suggests that intratumour variability in methylation patterns may be associated with cell identity transitions.

To further explore intratumour entropy and its relation to cell identity, we leveraged a published multiomic study of luminal breast cancer that included single-cell expression and chromatin accessibility measurements13. Focusing on cancer cells, we observed intratumour heterogeneity in luminal and basal-like expression patterns, as previously described14,54 (Supplementary Fig. 6b). Using the ATAC–seq modality, we calculated the within-peak (WIP) fraction, a metric of epigenetic noise58, whereby a low-WIP fraction may indicate a destabilized or noisier epigenome, which supports cell plasticity. For each tumour, we correlated the WIP fraction with chromatin accessibility of basal-like and luminal gene signatures. Cells that scored high for EMT and basal-like identity demonstrated lower WIP fraction, a finding reminiscent of the higher DNA methylation entropy associated with these signatures (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 6c). Single-cell multiome analysis of a freshly resected independent luminal tumour reproduced the basal–luminal continuum and association between basal identity and reduced WIP fraction (Supplementary Fig. 6d,e). To explore whether the increased epigenetic noise is associated with higher transcriptional heterogeneity, we divided cells into quartiles according to a published basal–luminal index59 and basal-like and luminal gene sets (Methods). Indeed, across all tumours, cells with a high basal identity showed higher transcriptional heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 7c). In line with these observations, the CyTOF-defined basal-like subpopulation also showed higher epigenetic heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Moreover, read-level methylation entropy was higher in K5hi-sorted compared with K5low-sorted populations in both tumours analysed by EM-seq, with higher variability among the K5hi 200-cell replicates (Supplementary Fig. 6f,g). Together, our analyses across DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility and histone PTMs indicate that the basal-like subpopulation exhibts a noisy epigenetic landscape and increased transcriptional heterogeneity.

Our CyTOF analysis highlighted a global increase in several histone PTMs in the basal-like subpopulation, including H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation (Fig. 2e). To explore the genomic distribution of these marks, we conducted single-nucleus CUT&Tag (snCUT&Tag) on three luminal tumours from our cohort60. Similar to the CyTOF data (Fig. 1b), stroma cells clustered together across patients, showing H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 deposition on fibroblast and endothelial markers. By contrast, tumours clustered separately, which indicated inter-patient variability (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d).

In each tumour, malignant cells clustered into distinct H3K4me1-defined or H3K4me3-defined states (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). Differential analysis of H3K4me1 distribution between clusters highlighted a recurrent group of cells across tumours, annotated as ‘cluster 2’, with significant H3K4me1 enrichment at genes associated with basal-like identity and EMT (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 8g,i). In tumour 15, cluster 1 was also enriched for basal-like genes (adjusted P < 0.05), but not EMT. H3K4me3 similarly identified basal-like subpopulations in all tumours (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Accordingly, peaks associated with these clusters indicated enrichment for transcription factor motifs linked to EMT and basal-like identity (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Next, we trained a classifier to identify H3K4me1-marked and H3K4me3-marked genes that contribute to variation between the clusters. For both histone methylations, these genes were enriched in terms related to breast cancer cellular identity, including oestrogen signalling, basal-like and mesenchymal identity (Supplementary Fig. 7b–e). Overall, our analysis provides support for chromatin-defined cell states in luminal tumour cells, including a basal-like state distinguished by H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 distributions.

Industry observers note that the above snCUT&Tag results aligned with the heterogeneity observed by CyTOF, which led us to compare the single-cell datasets and integrating both genomic and protein information. CyTOF-defined basal-like cells highlighted global increases in both H3K4 methylation marks. We reasoned that sequencing reads per nucleus may reflect global levels of the target modification. Single-cell epigenomic analyses generally assume similar global modification levels, discarding read-count information, as in our analysis above61 (Fig. 3e–h). Departing from this convention, we examined whether read counts capture additional aspects of epigenetic heterogeneity. Across all three tumours and both modifications, read counts negatively correlated with luminal identity signatures and positively with basal-like and mesenchymal signatures (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Consistently, cells with high read counts, potentially indicative of elevated global levels of H3K4me1 or H3K4me3, showed less enrichment of these active marks at luminal identity genes. Although requiring further validation, this direct comparison suggests that read counts may serve as proxy for global levels of histone modifications to capture additional aspects of epigenetic variation.

To further integrate these datasets, we label-transferred the CyTOF classification (Figs. 1 and 2) onto the H3K4me1 snCUT&Tag dataset. CyTOF-predicted basal-like populations were enriched in the basal-like clusters identified by H3K4me1 genomic profiling (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 9b). For tumour 15, cluster 1 was also predicted to comprise basal-like cells, consistent with its higher H3K4me1 deposition on basal-like-associated genes (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 9c). CyTOF-predicted basal-like cells also showed higher H3K4me1 deposition at EMT and basal-like gene signatures, which further confirmed their distinct epigenetic and functional features (Extended Data Fig. 9d). To validate these results, we sorted luminal PDX models and MCF7 cells by K5 expression, followed by H3K4me1 CUT&Tag. K5low-specific peaks were enriched near oestrogen signalling genes, whereas K5hi-specific peaks were associated with basal-like and mesenchymal programs, which confirmed the distinct H3K4me1 landscapes between subpopulations (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Together, the protein abundance and genomic distribution data implicate H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 as epigenetic determinants of the basal-like subpopulation in luminal tumours.

The repressive mark H3K9me2 was also identified as a strong contributor to the epigenetic basal-like signature (Fig. 2d,e). Thus, we conducted H3K9me2 snCUT&Tag on tumour 8, which was also profiled for H3K4me1. Given that H3K9me2 occupies large genomic regions, its distribution is not readily interpretable in relation to gene activity, especially in low-coverage single-cell datasets. We therefore leveraged the H3K4me1 data and trained a classifier, assuming opposing genomic distributions of enhancer-associated H3K4me1 and repressive H3K9me2 chromatin62,63, to identify malignant versus stromal cells (Extended Data Fig. 9f). We next clustered tumour cells by H3K9me2 genomic distribution and applied the same H3K4me1-based inference framework. This approach predicted strong enrichment of basal-like cells in cluster 4, consistent with elevated H3K9me2 deposition on oestrogen-related genes (Extended Data Fig. 9g–i). This cluster also showed the highest H3K9me2 read counts per nucleus, which provided support for its correspondence to the H3K9me2hi basal-like cells identified by CyTOF (Extended Data Fig. 9j). Overall, these analyses highlight an epigenetically distinct basal-like population with globally increased and redistributed active and repressive histone modifications over genes associated with luminal-basal identity and EMT.

Our multimodal analysis linked the chromatin landscape to intratumoural cell-state diversity. We next aimed to translate our tissue-level findings to a liquid biopsy test based on our single-molecule EPINUC technology, which profiles the epigenetics of plasma-isolated nucleosomes28,29. We tailored EPINUC for breast cancer by developing single-molecule systems to quantify the breast-tissue-related proteins K5, L1CAM and MUC1, and added the histone PTMs H4K16ac and H4K20me3 (refs. 64,65,66,67) (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Table 5 and Supplementary Fig. 8a–c). Nucleosomes from plasma were captured and their combinatorial modifications imaged by TIRF microscopy, whereas protein biomarkers were quantified in parallel single-molecule antibody-capture assays (Fig. 4a). The expanded 29-parameter panel was applied to a cohort of plasma from 77 women with luminal breast cancer and 30 healthy women, and the results revealed significant differences (Supplementary Table 6). For example, cancer samples contained more H3K9ac and H4K16ac nucleosomes (Fig. 4b). As PTMs were normalized to nucleosome abundance, these differences reflect the epigenetic state rather than tumour burden. We also used EPINUC to measure PTM ratios and co-occurrence, which revealed increased bivalent (H3K4me3 and H3K27me3) nucleosomes, as previously observed in colorectal cancer and pancreatic cancer28. Indeed, bivalency is altered across cancers68, and can prime drug-tolerant persister programs in breast cancer19.

L1CAM and MST1 were also elevated in plasma from patients with breast cancer, a result in agreement with the association of high MST1 with poor prognosis in ER+ tumours69 (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 8d). Multiple parameters differed between healthy individuals and patients diagnosed with early-stage (T1) low-burden tumours, which demonstrated the early detection sensitivity of this method (Fig. 4b). Predictive power scores (PPS) revealed the contribution of the newly measured H4 PTMs, selected on the basis of the CyTOF analysis, which illustrates the value of matched tissue–plasma profiling (Fig. 4c). Principal component analysis (PCA) of predictive features separated healthy individuals from patients with breast cancer, which highlights the ability of EPINUC to capture differences between these groups (Fig. 4d).

We next applied machine-learning-based classifiers to diagnose luminal breast cancer from EPINUC data. SHAP analysis of XGBoost models trained on all patients, or only stage T1 cases, identified multiple histone PTMs and protein biomarkers as informative (Fig. 4e). Notably, both models emphasized combinatorial features, particularly H4K16ac and H4K20me3 co-occurrence, thereby highlighting the ability of EPINUC to quantify such combinations. In particular, H4K16ac activates transcription of transposable elements70, which reside in H4K20me3 heterochromatin71, and because transposable elements are often upregulated in cancer, elevated H4K16ac and H4K20me3 might be a cancer-associated phenomenon. Finally, we applied several classifiers to assess the diagnostic contribution of the expanded EPINUC panel in discriminating healthy individuals from patients with cancer. Use the original 20 EPINUC parameters28 produced an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.85 (Supplementary Fig. 9a), whereas the expanded 29-parameter panel achieved 0.95, including among patients with early-stage T1 cancer (Fig. 4f,g). Unlike mammography, the sensitivity of which declines with dense breast tissue72,73, the features and performance of EPINUC were unaffected by different BI-RADS breast density scores, including patients with heterogeneous and extremely dense breast scores (Supplementary Fig. 9b,c). To assess the robustness of the EPINUC-based classifier, we applied the model trained on the original cohort (MAYO-1; Fig. 4f) to an independent, separately processed set of plasma samples collected 6–12 months later (MAYO-2). Following batch correction (Methods), the pre-trained model accurately distinguished healthy from luminal breast cancer, achieving an AUC of 0.98 and high classification accuracy (Extended Data Fig. 10a,b).

It has been revealed that to generalize our findings, we analysed pretreatment plasma from patients with luminal breast cancer at two independent medical centres (Supplementary Table 6). EPINUC distinguished patients from healthy controls with high accuracy in both cohorts and highlighted comparable sensitivity and specificity in TNBC (Extended Data Fig. 10c–e). Pooling all luminal samples across centres (n = 188), a model trained on 75% of the data achieved an AUC of 0.96 and robustly classified the remaining 25% despite mixed sources and batches, a scenario that reflects real-world clinical settings (Fig. 4h, Extended Data Fig. 10f and Supplementary Fig. 10). Performance was similar for luminal A and luminal B tumours (Extended Data Fig. 10g). Although retrospective, these results support the use of high-resolution, multiparametric plasma epigenetic analyses for cancer diagnosis.

It has been revealed that MAYO-1 comprised preoperative samples with at least 5 years of clinical follow-up, which enabled stratification by 5-year recurrence (Fig. 5a). Already at diagnosis, several EPINUC features differed between patients who were disease-free and patients who had relapsed disease. H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation, associated with the aggressive basal-like subpopulation, were elevated in plasma of patients developing recurrent disease (Fig. 5b). H3K27me3 and H3K9ac were also elevated, perhaps reflecting other aggressive tumour or microenvironmental states, such as cycling cells that were particularly high for histone acetylations (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Nucleosomes modified with both H3K9ac and H3K4me1 were higher in the recurrence group, a result that further demonstrates the power of EPINUC in capturing these combinations (Fig. 5b). ER or PR status did not associate with relapse (Fisher’s exact test, P > 0.05), and the epigenetic signature persisted in tumours with the following characteristics: comparable ER and PR levels; only luminal A tumours; low-burden T1–T2 or grade 1–2 disease; and tumours without lymphovascular invasion (LVI). No EPINUC feature was significantly associated with histological grade, which indicates that there is prognostic information beyond known clinical parameters (Extended Data Fig. 11a–f).

To further explore the association between tumour and plasma epigenetic patterns, we analysed a small cohort of luminal tumours with histone PTM mass-spectrometry data39, which were similarly stratified by disease recurrence39. H3K4me1 and H3K9me2, which marked the basal-like cells in our CyTOF data, were significantly higher in patients who developed recurrence, a result that further links this subpopulation to aggressive tumour traits (Figs. 2e and 5c). Finally, for patients analysed in Figs. 1–3, we obtained preoperative blood samples, which enabled direct correlation of tumour (CyTOF) and blood (EPINUC) epigenetic patterns. Most histone PTMs correlated positively, with the recurrence-associated H3K4me1 and H3K9ac marks showing the strongest positive correlation, a result that provided further support for their prognostic value (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 11h). Although requiring larger validation, these data suggest that circulating nucleosomes report both the tumour presence and its epigenetic state, a finding with potentially important implications for clinical management.

It has been revealed that to examine the prognostic power of EPINUC to predict disease recurrence, we applied machine-learning classifiers on the multiparametric data. The best model achieved an AUC of 0.81, and outperformed predictions based on classical prognostic parameters such as stage, grade and subtype (Fig. 5e–g and Extended Data Fig. 11i). To assess reproducibility and to benchmark established assays, MAYO-2 was focused on samples with available OncotypeDX scores74. Despite its smaller size, EPINUC predicted recurrence with an AUC of 0.92 (Fig. 5h). Across patients with OncotypeDX data from both cohorts, scores did not differ between disease-free and relapsed groups, whereas EPINUC retained discriminatory power (Fig. 5i, Extended Data Fig. 11j and Supplementary Fig. 11). Combining assays did not improve performance, which indicated limited added value from OncotypeDX in this setting. Overall, the data suggest that epigenetic signatures of tumour cell subpopulations, such as basal-like cells, may be captured in blood and provide insight into disease biology beyond the static tissue-based prognostic window. Pending larger prospective validation, these findings provide support for the use of EPINUC for early diagnosis and recurrence-risk stratification.

Industry observers note that single-cell studies have revealed clinically relevant phenotypic diversity across cancers, yet the epigenetic mechanisms fuelling this heterogeneity remain poorly understood75,76. Our analysis of luminal breast tumours uncovered tumour cell diversity consistent with previous transcriptomic and proteomic approaches14,21,33,34,54. Quantitative mass-spectrometry also indicated differences in global histone modification levels between breast cancer subtypes, which provides support for the idea that chromatin regulates cell identity39,77,78. Altered H3K4 demethylation can drive loss of luminal identity40, which suggests that changes in ER signalling, even without ESR1 mutations, may promote luminal-to-basal plasticity. Here we performed single-cell profiling of histone PTMs in luminal breast tumours. By measuring multiple global chromatin modifications at single-cell resolution, we identified a recurrent epigenetic signature of K5hi basal-like cells across tumours, supported across modalities by single-cell genomic profiling of H3K4 methylation.

Sources indicate that reconstitution of the full heterogeneity spectrum in single-cell-derived MCF7 clones and independently grown PDX tumours provides support for epigenetically driven, interconverting states rather than genetically distinct clones. Subpopulation frequencies varied among patients and may be influenced by mutations that bias state acquisition, as reported in glioblastoma46. This plasticity may enable adaptation to therapeutic pressures, which then promotes resistance and progression. Accordingly, proteomic intratumoural heterogeneity increases with tumour grade independently of genomic heterogeneity, thereby implicating epigenetic mechanisms7. Whether epigenetic therapies can limit plasticity and state transitions remains to be tested.

It has been revealed that breast cancer prognosis depends strongly on early detection, yet accurate screening while minimizing false positives remains challenging79,80,81,82. Detection of molecular changes before clinical progression could guide treatment adaptation and maximize first-line benefit83. Tumour-level histone PTM signatures distinguished luminal breast cancer cell states, whereas EPINUC analysis of pretreatment plasma samples provided proof-of-concept for outcome prediction. Notably, H3K4 methylation marks were elevated in both basal-like tumour cells and in plasma from patients with recurrent disease, which suggests that there is a link between this subpopulation and disease outcome.

Unlike CyTOF, which resolves tumour cell populations, plasma measurements integrate signals from damage of healthy tissue, the tumour microenvironment and local and systemic immune responses29,84. Nevertheless, patient-matched histone PTMs analyses in tumours and blood revealed a positive correlation for most marks, with the highest correlation observed for the recurrence-associated marks H3K4me1 and H3K9ac, which provides support for their prognostic value. Overall, our tissue and plasma chromatin dataset reveals epigenetically driven intratumoural heterogeneity in breast cancer and supports the use of EPINUC as a potential approach for breast cancer diagnosis and prognosis.

Collection and analyses of breast cancer tissue samples and matching blood samples were approved by the Israeli Ministry of Health Ethics Committees (Helsinki applications KMC-0028-22), followed by approval of the Weizmann Institutional Review Board (IRB, 2314-3).

The breast cancer samples for histone PTM mass-spectrometry-based analysis, which comprise 21 tumours, were obtained from patients undergoing surgery at the European Institute of Oncology and are part of a study approved by the institute’s Ethical Committee (study UID 2550).

Recent findings suggest that plasma samples and data for luminal breast cancer patients were obtained from Mayo Clinic (IRB approval number 23-011311). Collection of plasma samples from breast cancer patients treated at the Sheba Medical Center was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB approval 7509-09). Plasma samples from healthy individuals were obtained from the Weizmann Institute of Science (IRB approval number 1850-1).

All studies were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. No direct identifying participant information is reported in this study. Participants’ information is detailed in Supplementary Tables 2 and 6. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. No randomization or blinding was performed in the collection, processing, or analysis of human samples.

All animal studies were approved by the Weizmann Institute’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), and they were performed in accordance with Israeli law. Mice were housed and handled in a pathogen-free, temperature-controlled (22 °C ± 1 °C) facility on a 12-h light–dark cycle. Animals were fed a regular chow diet (2018 Teklad Global 18% protein rodent diet) and given ad libitum access to food and water.

The TM00112 (PDX-1) and TM00386 (PDX-2) models were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory and implanted in 10-week-old female NSG mice (Jackson Laboratory). In brief, following euthanasia, tumours were removed from donor mice and cut into small fragments. A small pouch was made in the lower back of each mouse, and one fragment was inserted into the pouch. The wound was closed using a surgical clip. Clips were removed 4–5 days after surgery. Tumours were measured twice a week with a caliper, and body weight was measured once a week. The IACUC-approved maximum tumour size was 1,000 mm3. Mice were euthanized when tumours reached approximately 500 mm3, and tumours were collected for analyses. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample sizes. Animals were not randomized, and investigators were not blinded during the experiments.

MCF7 and MDA-MB-468 cell lines were obtained from the Tissue Culture Cell repository at the Weizmann Institute of Science. HCC70, HCC1937 and SUM149 cell lines were provided by I. Ben-Porath. HCC70 and HCC1937 cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% L-glutamine and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. SUM149 cells were maintained in Ham’s F-12 medium supplemented with 5% FBS, 1 µg ml–1 hydrocortisone (Sigma-Aldrich, H0888), 0.5 µg ml–1 insulin (Sigma-Aldrich, I5500), L-glutamine and penicillin–streptomycin. MDA-MB-468 and MCF7 cells were cultured in DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 41965-039) supplemented with 10% FBS (Sigma-Aldrich, F7524), 1% L-glutamine (Sartorius, 03-020-1B) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Corning, 30-002-CI). All cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2.

Single-cell-derived MCF7 clones and matching parental MCF7 cells were either provided by U. Ben-David89 or generated in-house by single-cell sorting into 96-well plates using a Sony SH800S cell sorter (Sony Biotechnology) and expanded for approximately 4 months before experiments.

Cell lines were not independently authenticated but were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination and were negative.

Owing to the limited number of dissociated cells available from each tumour sample provided for research, we were unable to profile identical samples using all the different methods described in the paper. The single-cell CyTOF-based epigenetic analysis of human tumours was the priority for each tumour (besides tumour 23, which was used for WGBS and not profiled by CyTOF). For tumour 18, both WGBS and snCUT&Tag were performed owing to the high availability of tumour cells. For the remaining samples, we did not have sufficient cells to perform both methodologies. Notably, although the additional analyses were not conducted on identical samples, each was performed on three independent tumour samples, which ensured the reproducibility of the conclusions from each approach. The focus of the analysis was on identifying common patterns in tumours, rather than comparing between tumours and patients.

Patient and tumour information was extracted from pathological reports. To quantify ER positivity, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour blocks prepared alongside sample collection for CyTOF analysis were retrieved, sectioned and stained for ER by IHC. Slides were scanned, and digital images containing DAB signals were analysed using QuPath software90. Tissue regions were first segmented using a pixel classifier to identify areas containing tissue (average channels < 245, sigma = 2, at 8.4 μm resolution). In these regions, epithelial and stromal compartments were segmented using a supervised pixel classifier, with a minimum object size of 1,000 µm2 and a minimum hole size of 5,000 µm2. The classifier was trained on representative regions from multiple slides using a multilayer perceptron (ANN_MLP) model implemented in QuPath, based on haematoxylin and DAB channels at 2.1 µm resolution and multiscale neighbourhood features (scales 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12). Cell nuclei in epithelial regions were segmented using Cellpose-SAM91. For each nucleus, the median DAB intensity was quantified. The distribution of nuclear DAB intensities was computed for each tumour sample and a per-sample thresholding was used to account for inter-slide staining variability. For each tumour, a kernel density estimate of the median nuclear DAB intensity was computed, constrained to the observed intensity range. Local maxima and minima of the density function were identified, and the threshold separating ER-negative and ER-positive nuclei was defined as the lowest local minimum between the two most prominent density peaks. Tumour-specific thresholds derived using this approach were applied to classify nuclei as ER-positive or ER-negative, and the percentage of ER-positive cells was calculated for each sample.

It has been revealed that DNA was extracted from FFPE blocks using a RecoverAll Total Nucleic Acid Isolation kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and stored at −20 °C. FFPE blocks were reviewed and annotated for tumour cellularity by a certified pathologist, with a minimum accepted tumour cellularity threshold of 20%. DNA concentrations were quantified using a Qubit 3 fluorometer using a dsDNA HS Assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Sources indicate that libraries were prepared using a TruSight Oncology 500 (TSO500) assay (Illumina) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, 100 ng DNA from each sample was sheared using a Covaris M220 ultrasonicator (Covaris). Genomic libraries were prepared using a Hamilton Microlab STAR system (Hamilton) and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq550 instrument with a High Output kit v.2.5 (300 cycles). Initial analysis was performed using DRAGEN TruSight Oncology 500 analysis software (v.2.6.2, Illumina).

Variants were annotated and classified according to AMP guidelines into tiers IA, IB, IIC, IID, III and IV92. Variants classified as tier IV, synonymous, non-coding or having no established biological impact were excluded using Velsera Clinical Genomics Workspace (CGW). Remaining variants were manually reviewed using in silico prediction tools (REVEL, CADD and SpliceAI) together with annotations from Franklin (Genoox), UCSC Genome Browser and Velsera CGW. Variants were reported only when sequencing coverage exceeded 100× and the variant allele frequency was >1%.

Sources indicate that the antibody panel combined breast-tissue-relevant cell identity markers33,34, histone PTMs spanning diverse chromatin states and the chromatin modifiers EZH2 and BMI-1 (Supplementary Table 1). The chromatin marks analysed were chosen on the basis of availability of highly specific and validated antibodies, and quantification of core histones was used for signal normalization.

According to recent reports, following surgery, a sample of the tumour tissue was kept in MACS Tissue storage solution (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-100-008), and dissociation into single cells was conducted using a human Tumour Dissociation kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-095-929) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Red blood cells were removed using Red Blood Cell Lysis solution (10x, Miltenyi Biotec, 130-094-183) and CD45+ cells were depleted using human CD45 MicroBeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-045-801). The cell suspension was then washed with PBS and either further processed for CyTOF analysis or nuclei were extracted for snCUT&Tag analysis (when the number of cells was suitable). For cell lines, cells were dissociated using Accutase (Sigma-Aldrich, STC-07922) supplemented with DNase I (Merck, 4716728001).

Sources indicate that for CyTOF analysis, cells were washed with Maxpar CyTOF PBS (Standard BioTools) and stained with 1.25 μM cisplatin (Standard BioTools) for 1 min. Cisplatin was neutralized with warm 10% FBS–DMEM. Cells were washed with Maxpar Cell Staining buffer (Standard BioTools) and blocked using TruStain FcX, Fc Receptor Blocking solution, human (422301, BioLegend), followed by 30 min of incubation with a cocktail of extracellular antibodies (Supplementary Table 1). For tumour samples, cells were washed with PBS, mildly fixed (1.6% paraformaldehyde (PFA)–PBS) for 30 min and frozen in 10% DMSO–FBS. When the number of cells allowed, aliquots of frozen cells from this step were used for additional applications (flow-cytometry-based sorting or WGBS). For cell lines, samples were directly stained for intracellular markers without mild fixation and freezing.

For intracellular staining and CyTOF measurements, tumour samples were thawed, all samples were washed with staining buffer, fixed and permeabilized using Maxpar nuclear antigen staining buffer set (Standard BioTools) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For multiplexed samples, barcoding was performed using a Cell-ID 20-Plex Pd Barcoding kit (Standard BioTools). In brief, each sample was resuspended in MaxPar Nuclear Antigen Staining Perm buffer (Standard BioTools) and mixed with freshly thawed barcode reagent. Samples were incubated for 60 min at room temperature with mixing every 15 min, washed twice with Perm buffer and all barcoded samples were combined into a single tube or well. Before antibody staining, cells were blocked using 10% FBS for 10 min and then incubated with the antibody cocktail (Supplementary Table 1) diluted in MaxPar Nuclear Antigen Perm buffer (Standard BioTools) for 30 min at room temperature. Cells were fixed with 4% PFA overnight. On acquisition day, samples were suspended in 4% PFA containing 125 nM Cell-ID Intercalator-Iridium (Standard BioTools), washed twice with staining buffer and twice with Maxpar Cell acquisition solution (201240, Standard BioTools). Samples were suspended in Maxpar Cell acquisition solution supplemented with 10% EQ Four Element Calibration Beads (201078, standard BioTools). Before acquisition on a CyTOF machine, cells were adjusted to about 300,000 cells per ml and filtered through a 35 μm mesh cell strainer. Data were acquired on a CyTOF Helios system (Standard BioTools).

Recent findings suggest that the CyTOF software by Standard BioTools was used for normalization. Several gates were applied using FlowJo software: normalization beads were gated out using the 140Ce channel; live single cells were gated using the cisplatin 195Pt, iridium DNA label in 193Ir, event length and the Gaussian parameters of width, centre, offset and residual channels. De-barcoding was done using CyTOF software93.

In a recent development, overall, 17 different tumour samples were analysed by CyTOF, with 5 samples analysed twice as either technical replicates in different batches to provide anchor information or with different antibody panels for the analysis of an additional cell-cycle marker (pRb). A total of 1,565,881 viable cells were measured (around 30,000–400,000 cells per sample; Supplementary Table 3). The remaining CD45+ cells were removed from the analysis. For PDX analysis, CD45+ cells were removed and only human cells were analysed by maintaining human CD298+ and mouse MHC class I-negative cells.

According to recent reports, as samples were measured in batches, anchor samples, identical tumour samples measured in different batches, were used to implement batch-effect correction. Batch effects were corrected using a Q-Q transformation based on the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF). This method non-linearly maps quantile values from one anchor sample to corresponding quantiles in another, which effectively aligns their distributions. This transformation was then applied to tumour samples in the first batch.

Notably, as Q-Q plot transformation is inherently restricted to the range of the anchor samples owing to its reliance on interpolation, for values outside this range, linear extrapolation—based on the mean and standard deviation of the samples—can approximate the transformation’s slope and intercept, which provides a reasonable estimate of the nonlinear mapping beyond the observed data range.

The transformation can be approximated by the following equation:.

Sources indicate that following batch correction, the full cohort was subsampled to roughly 10,000 cells per sample for subsequent analysis with stroma cells. Following the removal of stroma cells, the cohort was further subsampled to 5,000 cells per sample. Normalization and data scaling were performed on either all tumours as one batch or on individual tumours, as previously described22,23. In brief, cells were gated using the core histones (H3, H3.3 and H4), and the signals for intracellular proteins, including histone PTMs, was subsequently normalized using these core histone values to reduce systematic technical variation:.

Sources indicate that the coefficients were selected to minimize the sum of the variances of the core histones. UMAP representations show a random subset of data points (around 10%) to improve visualization.

To analyse the high-dimensional data generated from our CyTOF experiments, we first applied dimensionality reduction using UMAP94. This was followed by clustering with DBSCAN95. Clusters were then joined on the basis of similarity in expression patterns to define the three distinct cellular subpopulations: cycling, luminal and basal-like.

We quantified, for each cell and each predefined gene signature, whether the set was enriched relative to a competitive null that matches the signature size but samples features from the same cell’s remaining markers. The method returns per-cell z-scores, which were visualized on UMAP embedding.

Detailed computation is as follows:.

Let X ∈R(N × G) be the cell-by-feature matrix. For sets \(\,{\mathcal{S}}=\{{S}_{1},\ldots ,{S}_{S}\}\), each Ss has size m_s ms = |Ss|. Optional signed feature weights w{s,g} are supported (w{s,g} = 0 if g ∉ S_s).

We row-centred per cell to remove global level shifts as follows:.

Signed observed sum (unweighted) as follows:.

Signed observed sum (weighted) as follows:.

Absolute-magnitude observed sum (unweighted) as follows:.

Absolute-magnitude observed sum (weighted) as follows:.

Industry observers note that for competitive null (size-matched permutations or exact enumeration), for each set s, we formed a pool of competitor genes \({{\mathcal{P}}}_{{\rm{s}}}\). By default we used the complement in the current feature space, \({{\mathcal{P}}}_{s}=\{1,\ldots ,G\}\backslash {S}_{s}\) (exclude_set = True), enforcing a competitive null; if the complement was too small we fell back to all features. We then sampled m_s genes without replacement from \({{\mathcal{P}}}_{{\rm{s}}}\) to construct null sums for each cell:.

With b = 1,…,B permutations. When the number of combinations \(C(|{{\mathcal{P}}}_{s}|,{m}_{s})\) was below a threshold (default 5 × 104), we enumerated exactly in streamed chunks. For each cell and set, we estimated the null mean and variance (and analogues for the absolute variant) with numerically stable streaming updates; a small constant (10–6) was added to standard deviations to avoid division by zero.

Per-cell z-scores (signed and absolute) were calculated as follows:.
