To summarize effect size while preserving direction, we defined:.

Thus, Z_dir is large and positive when the set is consistently up (large absolute signal with positive net direction), and large and negative when consistently down.

In a recent development, the framework supports signed feature weights w_{s,g} ∈ ℝ. Positive weights required higher expression, whereas negative weights encoded markers expected to be low in the target program. The null maintained the same size \({m}_{s}=\sum _{g}{\mathbb{1}}[w\{s,g\}\ne 0]\) by drawing m_s unweighted competitors from \({{\mathcal{P}}}_{s}\), preserving the competitive interpretation. Observed signed sums used w{s,g}, whereas absolute-magnitude sums used |w{s,g}|.

In a recent development, we used B = 2,000 permutations per set (10,000 for final figures), exclude_set = True (competitive null), two-sided P when depletion was relevant and FDR control at 5%. For scRNA-seq, we recommend computing on log-normalized counts after library-size normalization and optional regression of technical covariates; for CyTOF, arcsinh or z-score scaled channels work well.

In each tumour, a training set of cells was constructed, including only cells that were successfully classified as luminal, basal-like or cycling, keeping class-distribution and size equal between samples. From each tumour, 80% of these cells were randomly assigned to the training set, and the remaining 20% were used as the validation set. We used an XGBoost model35, with a learning rate of 0.1, a maximum depth of 10 and 1,000 estimators. The model achieved a prediction accuracy of 94% on the validation set. The trained model was subsequently applied to cells that were not assigned to a subpopulation by DBSCAN (cluster –1), and cells predicted with >95% confidence were assigned to the corresponding luminal, basal-like or cycling subpopulation for downstream analyses (Extended Data Fig. 3b). The contribution of each feature to the XGBoost classification was evaluated using SHAP scores30,31, which reflect feature contribution to the classification rather than relative expression levels.

In a recent development, vendi scores96 were computed based on the epigenetic CyTOF panel (histone PTM and chromatin modifiers). For each sample, cells were stratified by class label. To control for differences in cell number across classes, we repeatedly subsampled m = ⌊n_min/2⌋ cells without replacement from each class, where n_min was the smallest class size in that sample. Marker intensities were first normalized using a global z-score computed across a balanced sample of cells from all datasets. For each rarefaction, epigenetic marker values were discretized into 20 uniform bins, and the normalized dual Vendi score was computed on the resulting cell-by-marker matrix. Reported values correspond to the mean across 5,000 rarefactions, with uncertainty intervals defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the rarefied score distribution.

Sources indicate that sample preparation for mass spectrometry analysis was optimized to enable intracellular staining before FACS with limited input material. Mildly fixed (1.6% PFA) breast tumour single-cell suspensions prepared for CyTOF were thawed and washed with Maxpar CyTOF PBS. Cells were fixed and permeabilized using Maxpar nuclear antigen staining buffer set (201063, Standard BioTools) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Staining was done in 10% FCS/CyTOF Nuclear Antigen Staining Perm with the following antibodies: K5–AF546 (Cell Signaling, 71536, in-house fluorophore conjugation) and pan-keratin–AF647 (Cell Signaling, 4528). Following three washes with PBS, cells were transferred to a new well, to minimize residual detergent content. Samples were read using FACS (BD Aria III), with 200 cells of each population (K5hi and K5low; Supplementary Fig. 12a) sorted directly into freshly prepared 3 μl lysis buffer-containing wells in a 96-well plate format (Eppendorf twin.tec PCR plates). With a sorter droplet volume of 3.33 nl, the sorting process contributed an additional 0.66 μl to the total volume per well.

Industry observers note that the cell lysis buffer was prepared by combining 5 mM tris-(2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP) as a reducing agent, 20 mM chloroacetamide (CAA) alkylation agent, 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) and 0.1% n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM). After sorting, the plate was briefly centrifuged to ensure cells settled into the lysis buffer. The plate was then sealed with PCR cap strips and incubated at 95 °C for 30 min in an Eppendorf ThermoMixer C, with the lid covered to prevent condensation. Following incubation, the plate was cooled, briefly centrifuged and 11 μl protein digestion buffer (50 mM ammonium bicarbonate buffer, 0.033 ng μl–1 sequencing grade modified trypsin (Promega) and 0.132 ng μl–1 Trypsin/Lys-C mix, mass spec grade (Promega)) was added to each well. The plate was resealed, briefly centrifuged and incubated overnight at room temperature for protein digestion. The next day, 20 μl solvent A (99.9% water and 0.1% formic acid) was added to each well to acidify the samples and halt the trypsinization process.

In a recent development, LC–MS analyses were performed on an Evosep1 liquid chromatography system (Evosep) coupled to the TimsTOF SCP mass spectrometer (Bruker). The samples were loaded onto a disposable Evotip C18 trap column (Evosep Biosystems) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, the workflow involved rinsing dry Evotips with 20 μl solvent B (99.9% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid), followed by centrifugation at 800g for 60 s. The tips were then conditioned by soaking in 100 μl 1-propanol until they appeared pale white. After conditioning, the tips were equilibrated with 20 μl solvent A, followed by centrifugation at 800g for 60 s. The protein samples were loaded onto the wet tips, followed by another centrifugation step at 800g for 60 s. To ensure cleanliness, the tips were washed with 20 μl solvent A, with centrifugation repeated. Finally, to maintain tip hydration, 100 μl solvent A was added, and the tips were centrifuged briefly at 800g for 10 s.

Industry observers note that peptides were separated on an Aurora Elite CSI 15 × 75 C18 UHPLC column (IonOpticks) using the Whisper 40 SPD method. Mass spectrometric acquisition was performed in a data-independent (DIA) PASEF mode. For the diaPASEF mode, the ion accumulation and ramp time was set to 100 ms, and precursors in an ion mobility range from 1/K0 = 1.45 V s–1 cm–2 to 0.64 V s–1 cm–2 were analysed over a mass to charge (m/z) range from 100 to 1,700. Precursor ions for MS/MS analysis were isolated based on diaPASEF window placement covering an ion mobility range from 1/K0 = 0.75 V s–1 cm-2 to 1.2 V s–1 cm–2 and a m/z range of 400–1,000. The estimated cycle time was 0.64 s with 1 MS ramp and 5 MS/MS ramps, resulting in 75 MS/MS windows. The collision energy was ramped from 20 eV at 1/K0 = 0.6 V s–1 cm–2 to 59 eV at 1/K0 = 1.6 V s–1 cm–2.

According to recent reports, DIA-NN (v.1.8.1) was used to analyse the mass spectrometric raw files97. Analyses of the files were performed using a library-based approach (spectral library provided by BRUKER containing 67,686 proteins and 13,827 genes). Library precursors were re-annotated using a FASTA database (FASTA files UP000000589_10090.fasta and UP000000589_10090_additional.fasta, version August 2022). Trypsin was selected as protease, with a maximum of one missed cleavage. DIA-NN default settings were used with the following exceptions: the charge range of precursors was set to 2–10, and the ‘unrelated runs’ option was selected. A total of 5,630 proteins were identified.

Functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed proteins was done using the enricher function (clusterProfiler package98) comparing to MsigDB hallmark gene sets85.

According to recent reports, single-cell suspensions of mildly fixed (1.6% PFA) cells derived from luminal PDX tumours or MCF7 cultures were stained as described above. For PDX samples, cells were stained with K5–AF555 (Cell Signaling, 72825) and pan-keratin–AF647 (Cell Signaling, 4528). Pan-keratin-positive epithelial cells were sorted on the basis of K5 expression levels into K5hi and K5low populations. For MCF7 cells, staining was performed using K5–AF555 and GATA3–Brilliant Violet (BioLegend, 653814). Cells expressing high K5 and low GATA3 were defined as K5hi and compared with the remaining cell population (K5low). Cells were sorted using a Sony SH800S cell sorter (Sony Biotechnology) with single-stain controls for compensation and to establish gating thresholds.

According to recent reports, following sorting, H3K4me1 profiling was performed using a CUT&Tag-IT Express Assay kit (Active Motif, 53175) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The H3K4me1 antibody (Cell Signaling, 5326) was used at a 1:50 dilution. Decrosslinking was performed by incubation for 1 h at 55 °C followed by 4 h at 65 °C. Libraries were sequenced on an AVITI platform (Element Biosciences) using paired-end 50 bp reads. Sequencing data were demultiplexed and aligned to the hg38 assembly. Peaks were called using MACS2 with the --keep-dup 1 parameter. Peaks unique to either K5hi or K5low samples were assigned to genes using the ChIPseeker R package. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using the enricher function from the clusterProfiler R package, using gene signatures detailed in Supplementary Table 4.

According to recent reports, EM-seq was adapted for low-input samples. Tumour single-cell suspensions were stained with K5 and pan-keratin antibodies as described above. In brief, 200 cells of each population (K5hi and K5low) were sorted directly into freshly prepared lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 200 mM NaCl, 10 mM EDTA, 0.5% SDS and 0.3 mg ml–1 proteinase K) and frozen. For each condition, four replicates were analysed.

It has been revealed that lysed cells were incubated at 55 °C for 3 h, followed by overnight incubation at 60 °C to reverse crosslinking. Tris-HCl and NaCl were added to reduce the SDS concentration to 0.33% before PCI extraction. The aqueous phase was recovered, NaCl was adjusted to 300 mM and glycogen added to 0.13 mg ml–1 following DNA precipitation with 2.3 volumes of ice-cold ethanol at −20 °C overnight. DNA was pelleted by centrifugation (21,000g, 45 min, 4 °C), washed once with 70% ethanol and resuspended in 10 mM Tris-HCl, 0.1 mM EDTA (pH 8.0).

DNA samples were enzymatically fragmented using a NEBNext UltraShear kit (M7634S, Latest England Biolabs) for 25 min at 37 °C. Libraries were prepared using a NEBNext Enzymatic Methyl-seq v.2 kit (E8015S, New England Biolabs) and NEBNext LV Unique Dual Index Primers Set 2A (E3390S, New England Biolabs) according to section 3 of the NEBNext UltraShear user manual, with the following modifications: unmethylated lambda and CpG methylated pUC19 DNA controls were diluted 1:500. Libraries for replicates three out of the four replicates were prepared with conversion controls. DNA denaturation before cytosine deamination was performed with formamide (4401457, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Libraries were amplified for 12 PCR cycles and purified by 2 rounds of bead cleanup with NEBNext Sample Purification Beads at 0.8× ratio. Library quality and fragment size distribution were assessed on an Agilent TapeStation with a High Sensitivity D5000 kit, which produced an average fragment size of about 500 bp. Libraries were sequenced on AVITI high-output flow cells (Element Biosciences), which generated 150-bp paired-end reads.

It has been revealed that paired-end sequencing reads were subjected to adapter and quality trimming using cutadapt99 (v.4.4; parameters: --quality-cutoff 20 --overlap 5 --minimum-length 25; Illumina TruSeq adapter ‘AGATCGGAAGAGC’ clipped from both reads), followed by trimming of 10 and 5 nucleotides from the 5′ and 3′ end of the first read and 15 and 5 nucleotides from the 5′ and 3′ end of the second read. The trimmed reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg19) using BSMAP100 (v.2.90; parameters: -v 0.1 -s 16 -q 20 -w 100 -S 1 -u -R). Duplicates were removed using the ‘MarkDuplicates’ command from GATK101 (v.4.6.2.0; --VALIDATION_STRINGENCY = LENIENT --REMOVE_DUPLICATES=true). Methylation rates were called using mcall from the MOABS package102 (v.1.3.9.6; default parameters). To assess similarity between sorted tumour populations, pairwise correlations of CpG methylation levels were calculated using only shared CpG present in all eight samples of a given tumour. Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated across these shared CpG sites.

In a recent development, differential methylation analysis comparing K5hi and K5low cells was conducted for each tumour separately, with replicates pooled to obtain higher coverage. WGBStools (https://doi.org/10.26508/lsa.202503514) was used to identify differentially methylated regions, which were assigned to genes based on promoter overlap (–2,000 to +500 from the transcription start site (TSS)). For each gene, promoter-associated methylation changes were aggregated, and only genes with an absolute difference >0.2 and FDR-corrected Fisher’s exact test <0.05 were considered. Genes were classified according to the predominant direction of methylation change.

Functional enrichment analysis was performed using the enricher function (clusterProfiler package), comparing to MsigDB hallmark gene sets or curated breast cancer cell identity signatures.

Replicate-pooled EM-seq methylation profiles were summarized at the CGI level for each tumour and state combination by calculating CGI methylation as the ratio of methylated reads to total coverage. TCGA BRCA DNA-methylation data (Illumina HumanMethylation450) were mapped to hg19 CGI coordinates, and CGI methylation for each tumour was defined as the mean β value across probes overlapping the corresponding CGI. A shared CGI feature space was constructed as the intersection between CGIs detected in EM-seq and those measurable in TCGA. In each sample (tumour 5 or tumour 23), differential methylation between K5hi and K5low states was calculated for each CGI, and CGIs showing concordant direction of change across the two samples were retained. The effect size for each retained CGI was defined as the median of the model-specific differences and used to assign a signed weight. TCGA CGI methylation values were standardized across tumours, and for each tumour, a signature score was computed as the weighted mean of standardized CGI methylation values across the retained CGIs. Signature scores were compared across PAM50 subtypes.

Recent findings suggest that read-level DNA methylation heterogeneity was quantified using the RLM tool103. For each replicate, BSMAP-aligned paired-end BAM files were analysed against the hg19 reference genome using parameters -m PE, -a bsmap, and -s all. Only loci with sequencing coverage ≥10 reads were retained for analysis. Entropy values from all loci were aggregated for each sample and compared between the K5hi and K5low in each tumour sample.

For bulk MARS-seq analysis, MCF7 cells were sorted into K5hiGATA3low and K5lowGATA3hi populations (as described above) to capture basal-like and extreme luminal subpopulations. Cells were dissociated using Accutase (Sigma-Aldrich, STC-07922) supplemented with DNase I (Merck, 4716728001), washed with PBS and viability assessment was conducted using Zombie Violet fixable viability dye (BioLegend, 423105 or 423113). Cells were incubated for 10 min on ice in the dark, followed by 2 washes with staining buffer (PBS containing 2% FBS and 2 mM EDTA). For intracellular staining, cells were fixed in 4% formaldehyde–PBS for 15 min at room temperature. The fixation reaction was quenched with glycine (final concentration 125 mM), and cells were centrifuged at 700g for 5 min at 4 °C, then washed once with ice-cold staining buffer and once with PBS. Cells were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS for 15 min at room temperature, washed twice with staining buffer, and blocked for 10 min on ice with blocking buffer (PBS containing 5% FBS and 2 mM EDTA). Cells were then stained with anti-GATA3-BV421 (1:10 dilution, BLG-653814) and anti-KRT5-Alexa Fluor 555 (1:20 dilution, CST-72825S) antibodies in staining buffer overnight at 4 °C protected from light, followed by two washes with sorting buffer. Flow cytometry was performed on a Sony SH800S Cell Sorter. Single viable cells were gated (Zombie dye exclusion). Intracellular GATA3 and KRT5 expression were quantified in viable cell populations using single-stain controls for compensation and to establish gating thresholds (Supplementary Fig. 12b).

It has been revealed that total RNA was extracted using a RNeasy Micro Kit (Qiagen, 74004) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and stored at −80 °C. Bulk MARS-seq libraries were prepared from extracted RNA following the published protocol104 and sequenced on a NextSeq 500 instrument using a NextSeq 500/550 High Output Kit v.2.5 (75 cycles). Differential expression analysis was conducted using UTAP transcriptome analysis pipeline105.

MCF7 cells were dissociated using Accutase (Sigma-Aldrich, STC-07922) supplemented with DNase I (Merck, 4716728001) and counted in culture medium. Cells were washed with PBS and viability assessment was conducted using Zombie NIR or Zombie Violet fixable viability dye (BioLegend, 423105 or 423113). Cells were incubated for 10 min on ice in the dark, followed by two washes with staining buffer (PBS containing 2% FBS and 2 mM EDTA). For surface marker staining, cells were incubated with anti-human CD74–FITC antibody (1:10 dilution in staining buffer; eBioscience, 11-0748-42, clone 5-329) for 45 min at 4 °C in the dark with intermittent mixing every 10 min, then washed twice with sorting buffer (PBS containing 1% FBS and 5 mM EDTA). Viable cells were sorted into collection medium containing 50% FBS and 50% DMEM supplemented with 1% penicillin–streptomycin. To enrich for cells of the basal-like population, the top 10% of cells with the highest CD74 expression (CD74hi) and, as a control, the bottom 10% of cells with the lowest CD74 expression (CD74low) were sorted based on CD74–FITC fluorescence intensity (Supplementary Fig. 12c). Cells were sorted using a Sony SH800S cell sorter (Sony Biotechnology) with single-stain controls for compensation and to establish gating thresholds.

Cell migration capacity was assessed using Transwell polycarbonate membrane inserts (6.5 mm diameter, 8.0 µm pore size; Corning, 3422) placed in 24-well plates. Sorted cells were seeded in complete culture medium and allowed to recover for approximately 20 h. Cells were then serum-starved in DMEM supplemented with 0.1% FBS for 5 h before the assay. Following serum starvation, cells were dissociated using Accutase, resuspended in DMEM with 0.1% FBS and counted. A total of 5 × 104 cells in 150 µl DMEM with 0.1% FBS were seeded into the upper chamber. The lower chamber was filled with 600 µl of medium containing 20% FBS and 100 ng ml–1 epidermal growth factor (EGF; PeproTech, AF-100-15) as a chemoattractant. Control wells contained DMEM with 0.1% FBS in both chambers to assess random migration.

Following a 20-h migration period, non-migrated cells on the top surface of the membrane were removed with a cotton swab, and migrated cells on the bottom surface were fixed with 4% formaldehyde (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 28906) for 15 min at room temperature and stained with 0.1% crystal violet (Sigma-Aldrich, C0775) in 20% methanol for 10 min. Membranes were washed with distilled water and air-dried. Owing to weak crystal violet signal intensity and high background noise that precluded accurate automated quantification, migrated cells were imaged using the Cy5 channel (excitation and emission of 640 and 670 nm, respectively) to detect crystal violet autofluorescence. This approach enabled reliable background subtraction and automated cell counting. The Cy5 signal revealed complete overlap with crystal-violet-positive cells, thereby confirming that autofluorescence accurately represented the migrated cell population. Quantification was performed using ImageJ software (v.1.53; National Institutes of Health), and results are expressed as the number of migrated cells per field.

Collective cell migration and wound closure were assessed using a two-dimensional wound-healing assay. Culture-Inserts 2 Well for self-insertion (ibidi, 80209) were placed in 6-well plates (Corning, CC-3516) under sterile conditions. Cells were seeded at 1 × 105 cells per well in 70 µl of complete growth medium and incubated for 24 h until a confluent monolayer formed. Culture inserts were carefully removed with sterile tweezers to create a defined cell-free gap of approximately 500 µm width. Wells were washed twice with PBS to remove non-adherent cells, and 2 ml of fresh medium was added. Images were acquired at 0 h, 20 h, 46 h and 54 h after wounding at ×10 magnification using an inverted microscope.

Wound areas were quantified from bright-field images using an interactive segmentation workflow based on the Segment Anything Model (SAM). For each image, the wound region was identified as the continuous cell-free area and segmented using user-guided point prompts placed in the wound and, when required, outside the wound to suppress surrounding tissue or background. The resulting binary mask was visually inspected and refined interactively until it matched the wound boundary. The wound area was then calculated as the number of pixels contained in the final mask. To account for differences in image size or field of view, the fractional wound area was computed for each image by dividing the wound-mask area by the total image area. When spatial calibration was available, pixel areas were converted to physical units (µm2) using the microscope pixel size. This procedure yielded both absolute and normalized wound-area measurements for comparison across experimental conditions.

According to recent reports, mildly fixed breast tumour single-cell suspensions prepared for CyTOF were thawed and DNA was extracted using a NucleoSpin Tissue kit. RNA was removed by the addition of 20 μl of 10 mg ml–1 RNase during the lysis step. The generation of dual-indexed libraries WGBS followed a modified protocol based on the NEBNext Ultra DNA Library Prep kit for Illumina (Newly introduced England BioLabs, E7442, E7445 and E7535), in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. The library input was 500 ng gDNA, quantified using a Qubit BR assay (Invitrogen, Q32853), and 1% unmethylated Lambda DNA (Promega, D1521) was added as a control for bisulfite conversion efficiency. Fragmentation of input gDNA to achieve an average insert size of 350 bp was done with a Covaris S220 Focused-ultrasonicator. Size selection was performed using SPRIselect beads, isolating fragments in the 300–400 bp range. Bisulfite conversion after size selection was done using an EZ DNA Methylation-Lightning kit (Zymo, D5030), following the manufacturer’s guidelines. For amplification after bisulfite conversion, Kapa HiFi Uracil+ (Kapa Biosystems, KK282) polymerase was used under the following cycling conditions: 98 °C for 45 s, followed by 8 cycles of 98 °C for 15 s, 65 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s, with a final extension step at 72 °C for 1 min. WGBS libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument using an S4 flowcell and a 150 bp paired-end dual indexed run, with 5% PhiX library control (Illumina). The resulting coverage ranged from 16.7× to 22.5×. The bisulfite conversion rate for unmethylated Lambda DNA averaged 99.8%.

Industry observers note that paired-end sequencing reads were pre-processed with Trim Galore! (v.0.6.5) before alignment with Bismark (v.0.24.2) and Bowtie2 (v.2.3.5.1)106 using the ‘non_directional’ option. A reference genome was generated for bisulfite-converted human hg19 (obtained from UCSC). The resulting alignment files were merged and sorted using Samtools (v.1.16.1) and further deduplicated with ‘deduplicate_bismark’, before calling of context-dependent methylation with ‘bismark_methylation_extractor’.

In a recent development, empirical entropy was calculated from read-level methylation patterns using ClubCpG package55. Read clustering of methylation patterns over 100 bp genomic bins was used to determine the observed empirical distribution of DNA methylation states, without imputation for reads that did not fully cover a given bin. As there is no reference methylation pattern for individual cell types in this dataset, we used an empirical entropy estimate to gauge the degree of cell type heterogeneity in each sample, using as the individual pattern probabilities the proportion of reads with that state, and normalizing Plog(P) over 2n, where n is the number of CpGs in the bin. Each bin was assigned a normalized entropy score. Genomic bins were associated with genes (±3 kb from the TSS) using ChIPseeker package107. A list of CGIs was downloaded from the UCSC table browser108 and bedtools intersect function was used to associate with genes (–1,000 bp from TSS – TES (transcription end site), n = 28,170)109. The average entropy was calculated for each CGI, and the functional enrichment for the associated genes was calculated using the enricher function (clusterProfiler package98) comparing with MsigDB genes sets85.

To deconvolute the DNA methylation data compared with the TCGA BRCA dataset51, the methylation status was calculated for each probe in the HumanMethylation450 array (Illumina) using the HumanMethylation450 v.1.2 Manifest File (https://emea.support.illumina.com/downloads/humanmethylation450_15017482_v1-2_product_files.html). The combined dataset (TCGA and this study) was then deconvoluted to different numbers of archetypes using the EDec package (https://github.com/BRL-BCM/EDec)110. The PAM50 information in the TCGA BRCA dataset was used to annotate tumours by subtype. The associated expression data available for the TCGA BRCA dataset were used to correlate expression patterns with each archetype. Genes were ranked according to the Pearson’s correlation coefficient for each archetype, which enabled us to associate each archetype with functional terms using GSEA and the MSigDB Hallmarks gene sets85,111,112.

Sources indicate that simultaneous profiling of chromatin accessibility and gene expression was performed using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression platform (10x Genomics) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Cryopreserved breast cancer cells were rapidly thawed, gradually diluted in RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS, washed in PBS containing 0.04% BSA and filtered through a 40 μm strainer. Nuclei were isolated using the 10x Genomics nuclei isolation workflow, washed in chilled nucleus wash buffer and resuspended in diluted nucleus buffer. Nucleus suspensions were filtered to remove aggregates and adjusted to the recommended concentration before loading. Approximately 500 nuclei per sample were loaded onto a Chromium controller for tagmentation, barcoding and GEM generation. Gene expression and ATAC libraries were generated according to the manufacturer’s protocol and indexed using 10x Genomics dual-index plates. Library quality and concentration were assessed using Qubit fluorometry and an Agilent TapeStation. Sequencing was performed on an Aviti platform according to 10x Genomics specifications. ATAC–seq data were processed with cellranger-arc (v.2.2.0) and mapped against human genome GRCh38. Gene expression data were processed using cellranger (v.10.0.0).

Previously published scRNA-seq and scATAC–seq data13 were analysed as described by the authors. Only cells annotated as cancer cells, as defined by RNA profiles, were included in the analysis. To visualize gene expression pattern, UCell scores for the indicated signatures were calculated. To account for dropout, the gene signatures were smoothed using a Gaussian kernel with a bandwidth set to the 5th percentile of the Euclidean distance of the point-to-point distances in the normalized gene space. For the basal–luminal index, the z-score difference between the down in luminal versus basal and the up in luminal versus basal signatures59 was computed. For the ATAC–seq data, peaks were called for each sample (only cancer cells) separately, and the WIP fraction was calculated. A lower WIP fraction, corresponding to a greater proportion of fragments outside called peaks, was interpreted as increased epigenetic noise58.

Following CD45 depletion, 1 × 106 cells were resuspended in antibody buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM spermidine, 0.05% digitonin, 0.01% NP-40, protease inhibitors and 1% BSA), incubated on ice for 3 min and centrifuged for 3 min at 600g to extract nuclei as previously described113. Nuclei were resuspended in antibody buffer supplemented with 10% DMSO and cryopreserved for further analysis.

For CUT&Tag, all washes were made with 500 µl unless otherwise stated and all centrifugations were done using a swinging bucket centrifuge at 600g for 8 min at 4 °C. Around 50,000 to 100,000 nuclei were resuspended in 50 μl antibody buffer (EDTA 2 mM, 20 mM HEPES pH 7.2, NaCl 150 mM, spermidine 0.5 mM, BSA 2%, NP-40 0.01%, digitonin 0.01% and proteases inhibitor 1×) with 1:50 antibody dilution (anti-H3K4me1 D1A9, 5326 and anti-H3K4me3 C42D8, 9751, Cell Signaling) or 0.3 μg (anti-H3K9me2 D85B4 80806, Cell Signaling) and incubated overnight at 4 °C with rotation. Nuclei were washed the next day with Dig-Wash buffer and resuspended in 100 μl Dig-300 buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.2, 300 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM spermidine, 2% BSA, 0.01% NP-40 and 0.01% digitonin) together with protein A–Tn5 fusion (Diagenode, C01070001, 1:250) and incubated for 1 h at room temperature with rotation. Nuclei were washed 3 times with Dig-300 buffer, resuspended in 300 µl Tag-Buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.2, 300 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM spermidine, 2% BSA, 0.01% NP-40, 0.01% digitonin and 10 mM MgCl2) and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. Tagmentation was stopped by addition of one volume of 1x diluted nuclei buffer (DNB, 10x Genomics) supplemented with 2% BSA and 12.5 mM EDTA. The nuclei were then centrifuged at 1,300g for 4 min at 4 °C and washed twice with 200 µl 1× DNB supplemented with 2% BSA. The nuclei were resuspended in 10–70 µl of DNB + 2% BSA. Nuclei were loaded on a 10x Chromium system using a 10X Chromium Single Cell ATAC–Seq kit v.2 (10x Genomics) as previously described113. GEM incubation, barcoding and amplification was performed according to the Chromium Single Cell ATAC Library kit manual with 17 PCR cycles. Libraries were amplified with 13 PCR cycles. snCUT&Tag libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina) in PE50 mode.

Raw sequencing files (Fastq files) were processed using an in-house pipeline (https://github.com/vallotlab/scCUT-Tag_10X) to generate fragment files and to count matrices. In brief, the barcodes are aligned to indexed reference libraries using Bowtie2 (v.2.5.4) and the genomic parts of the reads are aligned to the human reference genome (hg38) using STAR (v.2.7.8a). Duplicate reads, reads mapping to the ENCODE blacklisted regions and reads with low mapping quality (q20) were filtered out.

Next, 50-kb bin matrices were used to generate a joint UMAP representation of all three tumours samples. Tumour microenvironment and tumour cells were annotated based on H3K4me1 or H3K4me3 enrichment at known marker genes (Supplementary Table 7). Owing to the physical removal of CD45+ cells during tumour dissociation, no immune cells could be identified based on H3K4me1 or H3K4me3 profiles. Peaks were called using CallPeaks (Signac)114. Gene activity matrices were generated by aggregating counts across gene bodies and promoter regions extending (–2 kb from the TSS), following the standard Signac approach. These gene-level activity scores were used as features for dimensionality reduction and clustering. Count datasets were normalized using SCTransform115 for each tumour separately. Differential binding occupancies were calculated by two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test (FDR-corrected). Functional enrichment was conducted using the enricher function (clusterProfiler package98), with MsigDB gene sets85,116 as references. Epigenomic gene signature scores were computed using UCell117 for each gene set of interest, starting from SCTransform counts. For visualization of gene signatures in UMAP space, to account for dropout, epigenomic gene signature scores were smoothed using a Gaussian kernel with a bandwidth set to the 5th percentile of the Euclidean distance of the point to point distances in the normalized gene space.

To identify loci that contribute to epigenomic intratumour heterogeneity (either H3K4me3 or H3K4me1), the SHAP algorithm was used on a trained XGBoost classifier35. For each tumour, the most contributing genes that led to accurate classification (around 400 genes, about 90% accuracy) were compared against gene signatures from MSigDB85,116.

Recent findings suggest that pseudo-bulk coverage tracks were generated by aggregating fragment-level snCUT&Tag data from cells assigned to each cluster. For each sample and histone mark, fragments corresponding to the basal-like cluster and to all remaining clusters were pooled separately. To enable direct comparison, the non-basal-like group was downsampled to match the total fragment count of the basal-like population. Genome-wide coverage was computed from fragment intervals and normalized to counts per million (CPM), producing bedGraph files that were subsequently converted to bigWig format for visualization. Tracks were visualized using pyGenomeTracks.

Pseudobulk chromatin profiles were generated from single-cell data and used for peak calling with MACS3 (ref. 118), with narrow peak mode applied to H3K4me3 and broad peak mode to H3K4me1. Unified peak sets for each sample and histone modification were annotated using ChIPseeker107, and genomic feature distributions were summarized as percentages of total peaks per sample, with promoter subcategories merged before visualization. Differential association of peaks to clusters was evaluated in a one-versus-rest framework. For each peak, signal presence was binarized and detection fractions were compared between the target population (cluster) and remaining cells using a one-sided two-proportion z-test. Effect sizes were computed as log2 fold change of CPM-normalized mean signal. P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and peaks were considered significant at adjusted P ≤ 0.05, log2 fold change ≥ 0.25, and a minimum detection rate of 1%.

Recent findings suggest that motif enrichment analysis was performed using the Signac framework114 with transcription factor binding profiles obtained from the JASPAR database119. Motifs associated with a pre-defined list of EMT and basal-like state regulators, defined separately for enhancer (H3K4me1) and promoter (H3K4me3) signals, were examined, using a nominal significance threshold of P < 0.05. Multiple testing correction was computed using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure in the subset of tested transcription factors per sample, which reflect the reduced hypothesis space.

To compare the read count with gene activity, for each tumour the number of counts per cell (‘nCount_RNA’) per cell was correlated (Pearson’s) with the epigenomic gene signature score (UCell computed on TFIDF normalized115 data).

Industry observers note that using scGLUE120, we performed multimodal integration of the H3K4me1 snCUT&Tag dataset with the CyTOF dataset. For each of the cell-identity markers present in the CyTOF antibody panel, we identified the relevant gene in the gene activity matrix and used those to form the weakly informative connection for scGLUE. After running scGLUE, we trained an XGBoost classifier on the CyTOF data in the joint latent space to predict the cell label and used the classifier to perform label transfer to the snCUT&Tag modality.

Industry observers note that for cell annotation of the H3K9me2 dataset, the complementary H3K4me1 dataset from the same nucleus extraction was used. In brief, 20-kb bin matrices were generated for both H3K4me1 and H3K9me2 datasets, keeping cell labels derived from the H3K4me1 analysis. A classifier was trained on the labelled H3K4me1 dataset, which achieved >95% accuracy, and applied to the inverted z-score matrix of H3K9me2, using the generally opposing genomic distributions of H3K4me1-associated regulatory chromatin and H3K9me2-associated repressive chromatin as an inference framework62,63.

It has been revealed that for gene association analysis, H3K9me2 was analysed without peak calling, as this mark forms broad repressive domains rather than sharp focal peaks. Instead, promoter regions (–2 kb to +200 bp relative to the TSS) were tiled into 200 bp windows, and fragment counts were quantified across these promoter-proximal tiles to generate a promoter occupancy matrix. The resulting matrix was normalized using SCTransform115 and used for UMAP embedding and clustering. Because H3K9me2 is a repressive histone mark, high gene-set scores were interpreted as increased repressive occupancy over the corresponding loci rather than increased transcriptional activity.

Recent findings suggest that blood samples were collected in EDTA tubes and transferred ambient for processing. Plasma was separated by centrifugation and stored at −80 °C.

It has been revealed that PEGylated-biotin-coated and PEGylated-poly(T)-coated microscope slides were prepared as previously described28,29. In brief, glass coverslips were cleaned extensively (sonication rounds with acetone and Alconox), hydroxylated by incubation in 1 M KOH and passivated with amino-silanization chemistry (3% 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane, 5% acetic acid in HPLC ethanol). Surface functionalization along with the first passivation step was performed by applying mPEG: PEGylated-biotin/PEG-azide solution (10:1 ratio). PEGylated surfaces were further passivated with MS(PEG)4. Anchoring of dT50 to PEGylated-poly(T) surfaces was done via click chemistry (10 µM 5′heyxynyl-dT50 (IDT), 2 mM CuSO4).

Antibodies were labelled using a biotin conjugation kit (Abcam, ab201796) and Alexa Flour antibody-labelling kits (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A20181, A20183 and A20186) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Labelled antibodies were further purified by size-exclusion chromatography using Bio-Spin 6 columns (Bio-Rad, 7326200). Antibodies are listed in Supplementary Table 5a.

Quantification of the five protein biomarkers was conducted as previously described28. PEGylated-poly(T)-coated coverslips were assembled into a ChipSop flowcell (chip 2-28 mini Luer platform Fl. 342, 30001180), which generated a 14-lane flowcell. Streptavidin solution (0.2 mg ml–1 in PBS) was added to the surface for 15 min and washed with IMB2 (10 mM MES pH 6.5, 60 mM KCl, 0.32 mM EDTA, 3 mM MgCl2, 10% glycerol, 0.1 mg ml–1 BSA and 0.02% Igepal). Biotinylated antibodies were incubated on the surface in IMB2 for 30 min, followed by washing with IMB2. Next, the plasma sample was added to the flowcell and incubated on the surface for 30 min, followed by three washes with IMB2 to allow binding of target proteins. Fluorescently labelled antibodies (detection antibodies) were introduced to the surface for 60 min, washed with IMB2 and imaged.

In a recent development, imaging was performed on a TIRF microscope manufactured by Nikon (Eclipse Ti2-E LU-N4 TIRF) with a CFI apochromat TIRF ×60 objective lens and TRF49904, TRF49909 and TRF89902 filter cubes (Chroma) for the 488 mm, 561 mm and 647 nm lasers, respectively. Images were taken with the ×1.5 magnification setting, which resulted in fields of view (FOVs) of 148 µm × 148 µm using an Andor Zyla 4.2 Plus camera. At least 50 FOVs were imaged per lane.

PEGylated-poly(T)-coated coverslips were assembled into an Ibidi flowcell (Sticky Slide VI hydrophobic, IBIDI), generating a 6-lane flowcell and further passivated with 5% BSA for at least 30 min.

In a recent development, plasma nucleosomes were processed as previously described28 with minor modifications. Nucleosomes were polyA tailed by the following reaction: 20 µl plasma was mixed with 10 µl of 10× Green buffer (Enzymatics), 416 µM CoCl2 (Enzymatics), 1:60 protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma), 83.3 µM dATP (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 5 µl Klenow Fragment (3′→5′ exo-, NEB), 3 µl T4 polynucleotide kinase (NEB) and 4 µl terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT, Enzymatics). Following incubation at 37 °C for 1 h, TdT in the samples was inactivated by the addition of EDTA at final concentration of 5 mM.

Next, plasma samples containing polyA-tailed cell-free nucleosomes were incubated with antibodies (final concentration 1:60) for 30 min at room temperature to allow for the formation of antibody–cell-free nucleosome complexes. Next, samples were loaded on the surface and incubated for 15 min to allow hybridization of polyA tails to dT50 oligonucleotides. The flowcell was washed once with IMB (12 mM HEPES pH 8 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 40 mM Tris pH 7.5 (Gibco), 60 mM KCl (Sigma), 0.32 mM EDTA (Invitrogen), 3 mM MgCl2 (Sigma), 10% glycerol (Bio-Lab), 0.1 mg ml–1 BSA (Sigma) and 0.02% Igepal (Sigma)), and cell-free nucleosomes were visualized by hybridizing 25 pM Cy3-dT23 in IMB to the free portion of polyA tails for 10 min. We supplemented Cy3-dT23 solution with TetraSpeck beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific), used as fiducial markers to allow correction for stage drift in image analysis. The flowcell was washed once with IMB, then filled with IMB, followed by time-lapse imaging of 5 cycles every 15 min with the 3 laser channels across all positions.

Industry observers note that imaging was performed on a TIRF microscope as described above obtaining 100 FOV (148 µm2) images per lane or on a high-throughput single-molecule imaging system at Epivision obtaining 100 FOVs (200 µm2) images per lane. The focus was maintained throughout the run using IR-assisted autofocus system.

Sources indicate that image analysis was performed with the open-source software CellProfiler (v.3.1.9; http://www.cellprofiler.org/) as previously described28. In brief, time-lapse images of antibody-binding events and TetraSpeck beads were aligned, stacked and summed to one image. Antibody spots can be differentiated from TetraSpeck bead spots based on spot size and intensity. Summed antibody images were aligned with cell-free nucleosome images to count colocalization events. For biomarkers analysis, antibody binding events were quantified. To minimize the surface batch effects, signals were normalized to the surface activity (average antibody signal across all lanes of the surface).

PPS analysis on the data was conducted using a previously published algorithm (https://github.com/8080labs/ppscore). In brief, by calculating a cross-validated decision tree (repeated (10,000) 4-fold cross-validation) for the target variable (for example, diagnosis) using only one of the markers, it is possible to determine which of the markers in the datasets contributes most to the target variable.

XGBoost classifier was applied to the data, using all features measured and their combinations. Feature contribution was assessed by SHAP.

It has been revealed that for ROC curves, for each classification task, the most important features were selected using the Boruta algorithm (with a random forest classifier)121. An additional feature engineering step was used to generate combinatorial combinations (multiplication, division and SQRT) of the selected features, and another round of feature selection was performed using Boruta. The final features selected were used either in a random forest classifier or in a soft voting classifier consisting of RF, XGBoost and LDA classifiers. The final classifier was used to generate a ROC curve with the associated confidence intervals using 10-fold cross-validation and 1,000 bootstrap repeats.

According to recent reports, to enable comparison across independently processed EPINUC cohorts, batch correction was applied to account for differences in antibody labelling degree. In brief, the reference dataset was subsampled to balance group sizes, and feature-wise means and standard deviations were calculated. The independently processed cohort was first standardized and subsequently rescaled to match the mean and variance of the reference dataset. This approach allowed alignment of feature distributions across cohorts while preserving relative differences between samples.

Recent findings suggest that histones were enriched from FFPE tissues as previously described122. Approximately 4 µg of histone octamer was mixed with an equal amount of heavy-isotope labelled histones, which were used as an internal standard123, and separated on a 17% SDS–PAGE gel. Histone bands were excised, chemically acylated with deuterated acetic anhydride and in-gel digested with trypsin124. The samples were separated by reversed-phase chromatography, acquired on a Q Exactive HF instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and analysed using MaxQuant and QualBrowser, as previously described124. For each histone modified peptide, a percentage relative abundance (%RA) value for the sample (light channel) or the internal standard (heavy channel) was estimated. Light to heavy ratios (log2 transformed) of %RA were then calculated and are reported in Supplementary Table 8.

Latest Update: Barnsley developments hand Sheffield United & Derby County clear Reyes Cleary boost

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Barnsley, Reyes Cleary, Sheffield United, and Derby County could all become central to an interesting January transfer situation, with the talented winger attracting attention from higher up the football pyramid.
  • Reyes Cleary has emerged as one of the most exciting attacking players in League One with Barnsley, and it is hardly surprising that Championship clubs are monitoring his situation again after having interest in the 22-year-old in the summer.
  • Industry observers note that both Sheffield United and Derby County have reason to strengthen their attacking options, while Barnsley face an increasingly important period in their own campaign.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barnsley, Reyes Cleary, Sheffield United, and Derby County could all become central to an interesting January transfer situation, with the talented winger attracting attention from higher up the football pyramid.

Reyes Cleary has emerged as one of the most exciting attacking players in League One with Barnsley, and it is hardly surprising that Championship clubs are monitoring his situation again after having interest in the 22-year-old in the summer.

Industry observers note that both Sheffield United and Derby County have reason to strengthen their attacking options, while Barnsley face an increasingly important period in their own campaign. There could be some significant developments at Oakwell over the coming weeks ahead of January.

Reyes Cleary is arguably one of the most exciting and explosive wide players in League One, so it is little surprise that the likes of Sheffield United, Derby, and Bristol City have been credited with an interest in securing his services.

It's evident that he has the individual quality to make the step up to the Championship and would represent an exciting addition for any of the sides keen on him at a higher level.

However, Barnsley's latest defeat to Wigan Athletic has made their league position even more precarious, with the threat of relegation to League Two becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

That could have significant implications for Cleary's future. Barnsley adopted a hardball stance during the summer and priced interested clubs out of a move, but their current predicament makes that approach considerably harder to justify.

According to recent reports, cleary might be vital to their survival hopes, but they cannot necessarily expect to retain him on their terms if Championship interest intensifies in January. Barnsley are now second-bottom and three points off safety, albeit with games in hand on some of the sides above them.

Barnsley deserve considerable credit for identifying Cleary's potential in the first place. He had shown promise during his time with Hartlepool United in the National League, but not many League One clubs would have taken the gamble of recruiting somebody two divisions higher and backing him to make the step up.

It has proved to be an inspired decision, although Barnsley now face a difficult situation with just 18 months remaining on his contract come January. Sheffield United and Derby are unlikely to be the only Championship clubs interested, either, with Bristol City also keen.

West Bromwich Albion should also have serious regrets about allowing Cleary to leave as early as they did. He looks every bit a player capable of establishing himself in the Championship, and a return to The Hawthorns could even be something worth exploring if they recognise their previous mistake.

Recent findings suggest that that said, Barnsley have to be braced for offers and interest again, with it becoming increasingly to stand in the player's way if he is determined to test himself in the second tier. That said, Barnsley will be desperate to keep hold of arguably their best player.

There is, of course, another side to this argument. If Barnsley cannot turn their fortunes around and ultimately suffer relegation to League Two, Cleary's market value could fall considerably for clubs like Derby and Sheffield United, particularly with only 12 months remaining on his contract next summer.

From a financial perspective, January might just be their best opportunity to secure a substantial fee. However, selling him could also be a grave sporting mistake, too. Cleary is arguably Barnsley's most talented player and possesses the individual quality to help drag them away from the relegation places.

How likely is Reyes Cleary to remain at Barnsley after January? Comment below!

Losing that sort of match-winner midway through a difficult campaign could make an already challenging situation considerably worse. The Tykes have to weigh up the financial benefits of cashing in against the very real possibility that they need Cleary more than ever to preserve their League One status.

There are only three players with more than three goal involvements for Barnsley in all competitions this season, including Vimal Yoganathan with five, as well as both Cameron McGeehan and Cleary with nine apiece. No one can better Cleary's three assists, either.

Bradford City's prospective new owners could face a £10m stadium complication

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are rumours that Bradford City could be up for sale, but any prospective newly introduced buyers of the club should be warned that any purchase of the club could come with one significant complication.
  • For several seasons, it looked rather as though Bradford City were living in some sort of footballing purgatory.
  • According to recent reports, at the end of the 2024-25 season, though, that run came to an end.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are rumours that Bradford City could be up for sale, but any prospective newly introduced buyers of the club should be warned that any purchase of the club could come with one significant complication.

For several seasons, it looked rather as though Bradford City were living in some sort of footballing purgatory. Trapped in League Two and watched by huge crowds for that division despite barely challenging for promotion, the club seemed stuck in a loop which was proving extremely difficult to escape from.

According to recent reports, at the end of the 2024-25 season, though, that run came to an end. Bradford were promoted back to League One following an absence of six years, and they marked their first season back by finishing in fourth place and securing a play-off place, where they lost 2-0 over two legs to Bolton Wanderers.

Sources indicate that that form has broadly followed them into League One this season. The departure of manager Graham Alexander to Preston North End at the start of October was a major loss, and their form has dipped since then. Prior to that, though, the Bantams soared to the top of League One, again demonstrating that this is a club with untapped potential, and this in turn has reportedly attracted the interest of investors from abroad.

Recent reports from journalist Alan Nixon have confirmed that there is interest in buying Bradford City from a consortium of Thai investors who are seeking a route into the English game, with Nixon writing that, "Bradford could be for sale at the right price and the Thais, who have an intermediary with inside knowledge, are considering an official offer.".

Recent findings suggest that stefan Rupp has been the public face of the club's ownership since 2016, and Rupp has been clear that he will only sell to the right buyer. Speaking to the Bradford Telegraph & Argus after the end of the 2025-26 season, Rupp said, "I'm the keeper of the keys and I would never hand it over to somebody where I have the impression he can't do any better.".

According to recent reports, how would you redevelop Valley Parade further to match Bradford City's growing ambitions? Let us know in the comments below!

Industry observers note that on the surface, there are plenty of good reasons to have an interest in buying Bradford City. The days of them being underachievers in League Two already feel like a rapidly fading memory, and even though they've had a dip in form since the departure of Alexander, they remain one of the promotion contenders in League One again this season.

Crowds remain extremely healthy, at just shy of 20,000, and Valley Parade is a stadium which hosted Premier League football for two seasons at the turn of the century, representing a city of half a million people in which they remain the only professional football club.

But when The Athletic's Matt Slater reported on the possibility of the Bantams being sold in March 2026, he mentioned a potential sale price of around £10 million. This seems very low for an upwardly mobile League One club, but there's a very good reason for this modest valuation, and it comes down to what the club doesn't own.

In an era during which a Championship striker is having a £70 million price tag slapped on his head to deter predators, spending £10 million to buy an entire football club sounds like a bargain, but with the sale of any football club it can be beneficial to pay attention to the detail of what's actually being bought or sold.

Sources indicate that and in the case of Bradford City, the club owns neither Valley Parade nor their training ground. Valley Parade belongs to former chairman Gordon Gibb's family pension fund. Bradford reportedly pay more than £500,000 annually to lease the ground, with the existing agreement due for renewal in 2028. Bradford have been giving consideration to possibly leaving the ground over the cost of the rent for at least a decade and a half.

And in the lower reaches of the EFL, the pure real estate value of the ground can be the biggest single cost aspect of any potential takeover. Without that, any newly introduced owner is essentially buying the player and staff contracts along with a license to operate the club in the EFL, and Bradford City, like the overwhelming majority of clubs, are not a profitable enterprise, with the last available set of manufacturer accounts showing a £3 million loss on a revenue of £8.6 million.

Earlier this year, the Bantams Supporters Trust entered into a consultation period with fans over what to do about the stadium, with a valuation of it put at between £8 million and £10 million. It's not known whether there are covenants limiting its use. But regardless of this, the Trust confirmed that they believe that the club's intention is to seek to continue to lease the stadium when that renewal comes up.

In a recent development, it would be advantageous to any new owners to take ownership of the ground itself. To do so would save them more than they're paying their highest-earning player every year, while its value would increase as land prices increase, and it would allow the club to redevelop the site more easily if they were looking to increase their revenues another way round.

But throwing the ground into the sale mix could double that original £10 million valuation, and although that would still represent stunning value for money were the club able to fight their way back to the Premier League, sale prices can vary wildly even within League One.

Recent findings suggest that when Rob Couhig bought Reading from Dai Yongge in May 2025, for example, it was reported that the sale price was £30 million, but this included the Select Car Leasing Stadium and the club's training ground. But when Leicester City were put up for sale in September 2026, it was for a staggering £224 million, though this did include state-of-the-art training facilities, land around the stadium for redevelopment, and Leicester's Belgian sister club, OH Leuven.

Buying a football club at any level of the game can be a gamble, and the recent IFR report into the state of football finances stated that two-thirds of club have liabilities which exceed their assets and rely on owner funding to survive - making them technically insolvent - while only seven of the 116 professional clubs in the top five men’s divisions did not record a loss for the last available financial year.

According to recent reports, all of this means that, while £10 million to buy a football may sound like a bargain, it's almost certain that this price is reflective of the extreme likelihood being that the cost to any new owner wouldn't end at that point. In the case of Bradford City, it wouldn't include the stadium itself, and this would likely double that price, while the new owner would also be on the hook for covering the club's losses, which at the last available count amounted to £3 million for one year.

According to recent reports, even at a sale price of £20 million to £30 million, buying Bradford City could prove to be a bargain. But so lop-sided are the finances of the majority of English football clubs that they may have to get the club all the way to the Premier League to turn a serious profit on their investment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:30 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026.

Whatever concerns there may legitimately be about the limited progress seen in Sebastien Pocognoli’s brief time in charge of Scotland, the Belgian has hardly been blessed with good fortune.

Industry observers note that in five matches to date in the Nations League, the manager has not yet been able to select the same back-three in two consecutive outings. Injuries and suspensions have seen to that.

For all that, you sense that even if he’d had a full quota of players to choose from, Pocognoli would still be figuring out his preferred defensive grouping.

In a recent development, this does feel like a time of opportunity for those who are fresh on the scene. Catch the eye and there’s a real chance to become established as a mainstay of the team moving forward.

Luke Graham did his chances of doing just that no harm at all in his first start and second cap for his country on Friday.

Playing in between Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney, the Stoke City man made a compelling case to stay there with a strong and diligent display.

Luke Graham enjoyed a composed debut for Scotland as they recorded a much-needed win.

On the back of a summer move from Dundee to the English Championship, Graham appears to have taken the step-up to international level in his stride.

‘It’s something I’ve always wanted to do since I was growing up, so I have to be ready for the moment and take it when it comes,’ he said.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I think there’s good competition. We have a lot of good centre-halves. Obviously, it was unfortunate for Welshy (Stephen Welsh) and Binksy (Luis Binks) to go out with injury, but that opens up a space for me to come in and try to cement a place.

Recent findings suggest that ‘When you’re out on that pitch, you have to do everything you can to try and stay in the team. I gave my all and I’ll just need to wait and see what happens going forward.’.

According to recent reports, timing can be vital in football. And it’s conceivable that Graham’s might just propel him to become a Scotland regular.

While playing at Dens Park saw him mentioned in dispatches with regards to a call-up, his move to England, coming just before Pocognoli was announced as Steve Clarke’s successor, has seen his dream swiftly become reality.

‘I’ve always mentioned that one thing I wanted to do in my career was play for Scotland, so to get it over the line was pretty special,’ he reflected.

Former Dundee defender Graham proudly belts out the national anthem ahead of kick-off.

‘Not much is going wrong for me at the moment, so it’s just about maintaining that and keeping it going every week.

‘I wouldn’t say I merited a start as we have a lot of good players in the camp. It’s up to the manager to pick the team and, luckily, he gave me the chance.

Recent findings suggest that ‘He just said to go out and enjoy it and do what you’re doing every week at Stoke. I think I did all right.’.

Notwithstanding how limited the North Macedonians were on the night, Pocognoli was entitled to take encouragement from the way the back three acquitted themselves.

According to recent reports, playing closer to each other than we’d seen in the previous matches, they were rarely unpicked by balls through the middle. Angus Gunn was not overworked in goal. Tellingly, the only concession of the night came when Scott McTominay lost his man at a corner.

‘I think a lot of it is just being brave,’ Graham reflected. ‘It’s about bravery in going man-to-man with the striker, being brave on the ball, trying to break the lines and keeping possession.

‘So, I think bravery is the main thing and concentration as well.’.

Graham keeps a close eye on North Macedonian danger man Elmin Rastoder at Hampden.

Industry observers note that with the defence solid enough, Pocognoli had a platform for a much-needed win. While the narrow scoreline made the final moments more anxious than they should have been, on balance, Scotland were deserved winners.

According to recent reports, ‘It’s just about winning games at this stage of the competition, so that was good,’ said Graham. ‘I think, if I’m being harsh, we should have killed the game off before it got to 1-1. We had a few good chances to put them to bed.

‘Then we kinda shot ourselves in the foot by conceding from a set piece. But Ben Gannon-Doak does well for the penalty and for us to go 2-1 up and see it out was good.’.

No one would dispute that the display was a long way from perfect. There’s significant room for improvement ahead of the concluding group match with Switzerland on Monday.

Recent findings suggest that ‘We’re going through a bit of a transitional spell at the minute, so it’s not going to be all smooth sailing from the get-go,’ Graham said. ‘It’s about adjusting and trying to build on performances in every game. I think it’s going to take time.

‘It’s a different style, a different manager and we just have to keep being patient. You look at the squad now and there’s a lot of new, young players coming through. It’s just about encouraging us young boys and showing we can get a place in the squad.

‘It is going to take time but, once we get there, we’re going to do really well and compete right at the top of the game.’.

Graham has been a huge success in Stoke's flying start to the Championship season.

Industry observers note that graham does look like he’s moving in the right direction. From watching Scotland compete at the World Cup on licensed premises five months ago, he hopes he too can be the toast of the nation one day.

‘I didn’t go. It was too expensive for me,’ he explained. ‘I think I was just like everyone else, watching in the pub with their mates. It was pretty amazing and hopefully I can be part of something like that one day.

It has been revealed that ‘I wasn’t too far away (previously), I think. Steve Clarke, the former manager, told me that. It’s just about trusting myself now and hopefully getting there one day.

‘There’s been a lot of hard work and dedication which has led me to this point. I’m very grateful to a lot of people who have helped me in my career so far and just to get this chance is amazing.’.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the news of the latest company leading AC Milan, Gerry Cardinale has offered a few words about what it means for the project.

It has been revealed that in recent minutes, RedBird have announced a latest parent tech giant for Milan, aptly named ‘Milan Sports & Entertainment’. It’s a project that aims to put all of the club’s investments under one umbrella, whilst also allowing further investment into the city.

The new stadium is believed to have played a big part in this decision, and the Rossoneri will hopefully benefit significantly from this move.

As MilanNews relays, Cardinale offered some words in the announcement about the creation of the organization, what it means to the city and for Rossoneri fans, what it means for the club.

“Over the past 25 years, we have worked alongside rights holders in the sports and media sectors to create innovative businesses that have transformed their respective industries.

“This evolution is based on a deep respect for the intellectual property assets that underpin these businesses, a long-term partnership with rights holders, and the ambition to fully unlock the potential of these teams and leagues, both on and off the pitch.

It has been revealed that “Milan Sports & Entertainment represents the culmination of this journey and the work we have carried out since we first invested in AC Milan four years ago. Becoming a club owner has given us an even deeper understanding of what creates long-term value: winning, serving fans, and investing in the communities that give these institutions meaning.

Sources indicate that “Today, we apply this experience on a different scale: not just to a single club, a single sport, or a single facility, but to an entire city and a portfolio that spans sports, lifestyle, and entertainment. I have known Brett Yormark and worked with him for 25 years.

“We’ve been working with Milan for years, and I can’t imagine a better executive in the international sports industry to help execute this strategy. Thanks to Brett, we can bring the best of American sports and live entertainment to Milan, helping write a new chapter in the city’s growth and international success.

“With AC Milan as our cornerstone, which will always be the driving force behind all our initiatives, we intend to build a world-class sports and entertainment platform capable of shaping the future of Milan and European sports, and bringing it back to the forefront of the global stage.”.

Considering how much attention Cardinale has paid to the future of the Diavolo, and taking them back to the top level, it’s nice to hear it referenced once again in his latest statement. Hopefully this move is another step towards that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swansea City are facing another fight to retain the services of head coach, Vitor Matos, with it emerging that French top-flight side, RC Strasbourg, have approached the Welsh side for his services.

The Swans have enjoyed an impressive start to the Championship season, as they sit sixth in the table after 15 games on 26 points, despite losing three of their last five encounters.

Matos' side were narrowly defeated before the November international break by current leaders, Birmingham City, at St. Andrew's @ Knighthead Park despite being a man down for the vast majority of the contest, and it may transpire that the loss in the West Midlands could be the 38-year-old's final game in charge.

Speculation involving the former Liverpool coach is nothing new to supporters in this part of South Wales in recent weeks, but one positive has emerged should Matos decide to move on to a third managerial role within the space of 12 months.

Matos was appointed by Swansea on November 24th of last year, three weeks after the Welsh outfit parted organization with Alan Sheehan.

Jürgen Klopp's former Anfield assistant was lured from Maritimo through a reported £880,000 compensation fee, and subsequently transformed the Swans' form for the remainder of the season as they finished 11th - nine points outside the play-offs whilst boasting Golden Boot winner, Zan Vipotnik.

Having signed a one-year contract extension until June 2030 on July 31st, a strong first pre-season and summer transfer window has been backed up by a positive start, but it emerged on Monday that Strasbourg have approached Swansea over the potential appointment of Matos, with his compatriot, Hugo Oliveira, under pressure after just three wins this season.

Strasbourg are 13th in Ligue 1 at present, but would be forced to part with a significant sum of cash if they were to instill the highly-rated head coach at the Stade de la Meinau, and it has since been suggested that the figure being negotiated is in the region of £4m as Matos braces for his latest managerial change.

Matos won 22 of his first 47 matches in charge of Swansea, boasting a win percentage of 47%, following on from a 54% total in just 13 matches at his previous employers, Maritimo.

It is a testament to the work put in by the Portuguese that clubs are looking to poach him away from Swansea, and that recently included the Premier League's bottom club, Crystal Palace.

The Eagles were recently credited with interest in the Portuguese and Middlesbrough head coach, Kim Hellberg, before opting to confirm Thomas Frank as Pierre Sage's replacement at Selhurst Park on Monday afternoon.

Despite losing Ethan Galbraith to Stoke City for £10m, Matos changed the outlook of his Swansea side with 11 newly introduced recruits, with the likes of Joseph Opoku, Moussa Yeo and Stephen Welsh, already earning rave reviews.

Such a strong recruitment drive came after the penning of Matos' contract extension, after which he explained his sudden connection towards all aspects of the club as he aimed to drive the Swans forward.

"From the moment I arrived here, I have sensed how powerful the connection between Swansea City and the fans and community is," Matos remarked.

"This is something very special, it is a feeling myself and the players love, and the desire to keep building that and sharing great moments together is one of the key motivations in extending my contract with the club.".

Former Spurs midfielder Redknapp felt United struggled to connect their midfield with the rest of the team during the opening stages.

Industry observers note that he added: “I didn’t see enough connections in that midfield in the first hour. Baleba came on and did OK and highlighted a bit more.

“They look devoid of any confidence, any idea, any patterns of play, playing out from the back. Tottenham were much better than them in every single department.”.

While Carlos Baleba was a particular highlight on the day, he indicated great potential when brought on. He brought a new sense of energy in the midfield and sent a few balls over the top for a couple of quick counterattacks as well.

Redknapp also pointed to the physical demands of modern Premier League football, arguing that United cannot afford to be outworked by their opponents.

Tottenham ran a staggering 5 km more than Manchester United, something Redknapp felt was a pattern.

"Spurs ran 5km more than Man United… it's like that EVERY GAME!"Jamie Redknapp is less than impressed with the lack of ground covered this season by Manchester United 😬 pic.twitter.com/BxWkFuyGJ1.

“There is a pattern that I don’t really like when I watch teams, and that’s when every time the stats don’t lie and the other team runs more than you.

According to recent reports, “I feel in Premier League football right now there are a couple of non-negotiables, and one is you have to run more than the other team if you want to win or at least get close enough. Tonight Spurs ran 5km more than Manchester United.”.

He believes Tottenham’s pressing exposed the lack of pace in United’s midfield, making it difficult for the hosts to move the ball safely through the centre.

“In terms of how they played today, I think they have an problem with Tielemans and Mainoo in midfield. I don’t see enough energy in there. Baleba will add a lot and will give them a tremendous amount of energy but right now, when things aren’t going well… and Tottenham knew it!

“Every time United played the ball out from the back they pounced. They pressed them because they knew United don’t have the pace and speed in midfield to get away.”.

Industry observers note that “In isolation, one of them is absolutely fine, the two of them together doesn’t work for me. They haven’t got the pace or the energy to get around the pitch for 90 minutes.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senne Lammens believes Manchester United must learn to finish games off after their late collapse against Tottenham Hotspur.

The result left the goalkeeper frustrated at Old Trafford despite leading the game and with a player more on the field.

Manchester United looked set for three points after Bryan Mbeumo put them ahead in the second half, but Dominic Solanke’s stoppage-time equaliser denied Michael Carrick’s side a much-needed victory.

Speaking to MUTV, Senne Lammens admitted the team had struggled early on but had done enough after the break to put themselves in a winning position.

“Football can be a bit cruel at times,” the Belgian goalkeeper stated. “There are a lot of ups and downs, especially in a game like that.”.

Senne Lammens felt United failed to take advantage of Tottenham’s red card, allowing the visitors too much space to find a late equaliser.

“We’ve won a lot of games against 10 men [in the past], but you also know there can be a tricky situation when you’re playing against 10 men, because they have nothing to lose and they know that.”.

He added that United should have scored again to put the result beyond doubt or, at the very least, prevented Tottenham from creating further chances.

“I think that’s what we did wrong. We gave them a little bit too much breathing room to create those chances, and then one ball has to go right for them, one bounce has to go their way, and they can score like that.”.

The goalkeeper also pointed to similarities with United’s earlier disappointment against Everton, where points slipped away late in the match.

“You feel like those games just slip away from you, and there are one or two situations where you don’t really have control,” he said.

Industry observers note that “I think there’s a lot to learn from today. It wasn’t all negative, not at all, but especially the way it ended left a very bad feeling.”.

“I think the easy answer is that we have to be able to kill the game faster and not put ourselves in that position to give them a chance.”.

Despite the frustration, Lammens mentioned there were positives to take from the performance. However, the late goal had left a bitter feeling, and United now need to turn those lessons into better results.

According to recent reports, neves had given the visitors the lead with a trademark free-kick, but Cardiff missed the chance to equalise in stoppage time when Gary Madine saw his effort saved by John Ruddy. Incredibly, the Bluebirds would be awarded another spot-kick, but Junior Hoilett hit the bar with the last kick of the game.

That prompted wild celebrations, with Cardiff boss Neil Warnock famously snubbing Nuno’s offer of a handshake after the game.

So, it’s a stadium that will hold many memories for all Wolves fans, and Neves is back in the Welsh capital with Portugal, as Jorge Jesus’ side prepare to take on the Dragons in the Nations League.

Inevitably, Neves was questioned about coming back to the Cardiff City Stadium, and he told BBC Wales that it remains one of the ‘craziest’ games he has ever been involved in.

In a recent development, “I remember (it) very well! It was a crazy match, one of the craziest matches in my life, and fortunately we won that match.

“I scored a free-kick, and then in the last minutes they had two penalties, they missed both penalties, and of course, after that there was a bit of confusion on the pitch because the emotions were high.

“But it was a fantastic match, and it’s a stadium that brings me good memories.”.

This is nice for Wolves fans to hear, as they still love Neves, and it will be great for them to see that he still looks back on his time at the club fondly, with all supporters hoping that he might one day return for a second spell at some point before he retires.

Obviously, the Cardiff game is one that will live long in the memory, and it’s no exaggeration to say that it was an ending to a match that you rarely ever see.

It was a huge disappointment for Cardiff at the time, but, to their credit, the Bluebirds did manage to put the defeat behind them, as they went up automatically with Wolves - and they did actually beat them at home in the top flight.

But, that night was pivotal for Wolves, and, even after everything Neves went on to achieve at the club, and in his career, it was clearly a game that stands out.

So, he will have fond memories of Cardiff, and Neves will hope to leave with another win with Portugal against Wales on Tuesday night.

The Bournemouth youngster had an up-and-down evening in Friday’s 2-1 Nations League win over North Macedonia, getting into numerous promising positions on the right flank and winning the penalty – dispatched by John McGinn – which decided the game.

But, as has been the case throughout his Scotland career, the 21-year-old’s final ball in key moments left a lot to be desired.

Pocognoli is under no illusions that Gannon-Doak still has plenty to improve on, but insists that it won’t be long before things start to click for the talented youngster.

Sources indicate that ‘On Friday, he had great opportunities. We know that he needs to improve on the end product, but he created a penalty and against Slovenia and North Macedonia away he created a number of unbelievable one v ones.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets Ben Gannon-Doak as he is substituted at Hampden.

It has been revealed that ‘He did that last night as well. We know he can be good if we dominate the game and he can get in good positions if we control the ball. I am happy with his performance.
