‘I believe if he is playing every game he can make many decisions. He will know that in the next game he will have to do it again.

‘If he knows that he only has to play a game every two weeks, sometimes he can think, “This is my moment”.

Industry observers note that ‘It is a process. He will become older and at some point will become relaxed in his decision making, but at this very young age what he is producing is very good.

‘I say exactly the same thing to him after training on the pitch. I say, “Ben, this is the next step”. He knows that and it is vital he knows that.’.

Scotland conclude their Nations League campaign in Switzerland on Monday knowing that only a victory against the group winners will be enough if they are to have any chance of leapfrogging Slovenia – currently one point better off ahead of their trip to North Macedonia – into second spot.

According to recent reports, ‘We are still alive in this competition,’ remarked Pocognoli, who celebrated his first win at Hampden on Friday at the third time of asking. ‘We know we have to do more than this competition. This competition is about trying to build something.

‘It is part of the process to play away against a top team. That is not something we have done yet. The approach will be different and, for me as a coach, it is a game with a lot of responsibility.’.

Saturday's 4-1 loss against the high-flying Mariners was also Swindon's third on the spin, having been eliminated from the FA Cup against League One side, MK Dons, as well as losing in the EFL Trophy to Plymouth Argyle.

Supporters in Wiltshire have grown increasingly frustrated with the club's recent situation, as the club have continued to stagnate in the fourth tier in the five years of Clem Morfuni's ownership.

Holloway recently surpassed two years in charge at the County Ground, but after finishing 12th in his first full season last term, there are concerns as to whether his team can show any signs of progress based on their recent form.

Holloway is, arguably, the EFL's most experienced manager at present, having taken charge at matches across all levels for 30 years, including Premier League spells with Blackpool and Crystal Palace.

The 63-year-old has gained a strong reputation for various incidents over time, and this season, that has been no exception for the Swindon boss.

Recent findings suggest that after slamming Manchester City for their alleged financial misconduct, Holloway claimed last month he was a "Dead. Man. Walking," within a viral interview clip, which he was reminded about by the supporters of his former club as David Artell's side ran riot, with Aaron Drinan's goal for the hosts a mere consolation after strikes from Andy Cook, Josh Andrews and a brace from Iwan Morgan.

Hollowaytook charge of Grimsby between December 2019 and 2020, winning 13 of his 39 matches in charge, accumulating a 33 percent win ratio in the process.

The experienced figure resigned at Blundell Park following a 2-1 loss to Bradford City which had the club lying 20th in League Two at the time, and the Mariners were eventually relegated back to the National League months later, albeit for a solitary season.

As such, the North Lincolnshire fanbase are not particularly fond of Holloway, who, in return, criticised their actions in his post-match interview.

“On that performance, it is what we deserved, and that hurts me bitterly, because that was a club that I used to work for," he said.

“You wouldn’t think so, would you? The use of language [from their fans] was disgusting, in my opinion, but that is what happens in modern-day football.

It has been revealed that “They didn’t say a word when we beat them 4-0 up there two years ago, did they? It is what it is," he added.

Discussing the action in League One and League Two from across the weekend, EFL pundits, Tom Garratt and Callum Fowler, were amongst those debating whether Holloway's future in the Swindon job is presently jeopardised.

According to recent reports, "Another man who should be under pressure, Ian Holloway. Swindon 1-4 Grimsby," said Garratt on the Pyramid podcast.

"He's just a 'dead man walking', that's what the Grimsby fans were singing to him," Fowler immediately responded.

"Swindon's four-game unbeaten run ends at the hands of Grimsby who have won their last three, scoring 13 goals in that time.".

Recent findings suggest that later discussing Holloway's immediate future, Garratt asked: "is he under pressure?" to which Fowler added: "100%. He's a nutter.".

In a recent development, "I'm amazed he's still got a job. Get him gone," the former then stated.

Industry observers note that swindon fans, is Ian Holloway the right man to lead the Robins forward? Comment below!

It remains to be seen where the Robins go from here, with the next opportunity for Holloway to turn the tide being Saturday's trip to Newport County, who sit two places above Swindon on goal difference.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Now Manchester United need to think about who should control the club in the future.
  • The journalist believes the change in ownership has had a lasting effect on United, with the club still feeling its consequences today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Glazers took control of Manchester United in 2005. That takeover has since caused so many disruptions and protests by the fans over massive debts and insufficient backing of the team in the transfer market, despite successful periods in the Premier League and Europe.

Now Manchester United need to think about who should control the club in the future. Laurie Whitwell has now shared his views on why Manchester United need an ownership change. He simply wants the Glazers gone from Old Trafford. However, he also recognizes that replacing the current ownership doesn’t automatically mean things will improve for United.

The journalist believes the change in ownership has had a lasting effect on United, with the club still feeling its consequences today. A fresh start might be welcome, but the identity of the next owners would matter just as much as the departure of the existing ones.

“Personally, I would like to see the Glazers gone from Manchester United,” Laurie Whitwell mentioned on The Rest is Football podcast with Gary Lineker.

“That change, you know, just really affected and still impacts United now.”.

The desire for different ownership is one thing, but finding people capable of taking the club forward is another.

Whitwell admitted there is no perfect answer when it comes to who should take charge.

That leaves United facing a difficult choice. A sale could offer the chance to change how the club is run, but simply bringing in a latest owner would not guarantee better decisions or a brighter future.

Industry observers note that whitwell also raised the idea of United supporters having a greater say in the club’s ownership and decisions, much like the Barcelona model where fans own the club itself. However, he highlighted that the Barcelona model isn’t ideal either and has its own shortcomings.

Changing the names at the top would only be one part of the change. The club would also need an ownership structure capable of making sound decisions and providing a direction.

The problem of ownership goes beyond whether the Glazers should stay or leave. Manchester United needs to find the right people and the right model to secure the club’s future. Getting that decision wrong could leave them facing the same circus the fans are enduring under the Glazers.

Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 94 min read (18894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~94 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1,2,3,4,5.
  • Recent findings suggest that functional cellular heterogeneity is well documented in hepatocytes, driven by liver zonation7, and in muscle fibres, shaped by local environmental cues, particularly motor neuron activity8.
  • Thermogenic adipose tissue undergoes adaptive thermogenesis and is crucial for energy expenditure and thermoregulation1,2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1,2,3,4,5. We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells)6. Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 (Rgs2), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.

Recent findings suggest that functional cellular heterogeneity is well documented in hepatocytes, driven by liver zonation7, and in muscle fibres, shaped by local environmental cues, particularly motor neuron activity8. Single-cell technologies have revealed extensive latest patterns of heterogeneity of specific cell types within the same tissue9, yet their biological importance remains largely undetermined.

Thermogenic adipose tissue undergoes adaptive thermogenesis and is crucial for energy expenditure and thermoregulation1,2. Its specialized metabolism and precise responses to environmental and physiological stimuli make it an ideal model for studying functional cellular heterogeneity. Thermogenic capacity declines substantially with age in rodents and humans, leading to age-related cold sensitivity and metabolic disorders3,4,5, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

According to recent reports, BAs and beige adipocytes mediate UCP1-dependent non-shivering thermogenesis10. Although substantial progress has been made in identifying the key pathways that activate thermogenesis, most studies have been conducted at the whole-tissue level, leaving the mechanisms governing its activation, maintenance and deactivation incompletely understood.

Recent findings suggest that the heterogeneity of BAs within the same brown adipose tissue (BAT) and beige adipocyte cluster within inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) has been characterized by our group6 and others5,11,12,13,14. We found that BAs heterogeneously express UCP1 and classified those with low expression as BA-L cells and those with high expression as BA-H cells6. At room temperature, BA-H cells constitute 30–50% of all BAs; BA-H cells predominate after cold exposure, whereas BA-L cells predominate under thermoneutral conditions6. This raises questions of why BA heterogeneity exists, and whether it reflects random variation along a thermogenic continuum or spatially organized, tightly regulated states within the tissue.

Here we identify dynamic bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity controlled by the spatial proximity of BAs to IL-1β puncta through a neuronal–immune regulatory mechanism. This regulation becomes dysfunctional during ageing, leading to cold intolerance in older adults. These findings highlight how different cell types collectively control cellular heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner, integrating environmental and internal cues to regulate tissue metabolism and function.

Reanalysis of our previous single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset6 revealed enrichment of glucocorticoid signalling and GR-target genes in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Top BA-L-cell-enriched genes include H6pd, Rgs2 and thioredoxin-interacting protein (Txnip), whereas BA-H cells were enriched for thermogenesis-related genes, including Ucp1 and cytochrome c oxidase 6B1 (Cox6b1) (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,d–f). Nr3c1 was similarly expressed in BA-H and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f).

It has been revealed that we generated Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice for inducible labelling of Ucp1+ cells by crossing the Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Rosa-stop-mT/mG mouse lines (Extended Data Fig. 2a). After 1 week of feeding on a doxycycline diet at room temperature (24 °C), GFP+ and GFP− BAs revealed a patchy distribution (Fig. 1a), consistent with BA heterogeneity in AdipoChaser mice6. The Ucp1-rtTA mice used a relatively weak 5 kb Ucp1 promoter15 so GFP is only expressed in UCP1high-expressing BAs (BA-H cells), while Ucp1-cre mice have a strong bacterial artificial chromosome-based Ucp1 promoter that drives Cre expression in all BAs16. Immunofluorescence (IF) staining confirmed selective H6PD expression in BA-L cells (Fig. 1a); 50% of BAs were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD−, 45% were UCP1−(GFP−)H6PD+ and 5% were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD+ (Fig. 1b). Similar heterogeneity was observed in iWAT after 1 week of cold exposure (6 °C) (Fig. 1c), with 45% of these beige adipocytes being UCP1+H6PD−, 49% UCP1−H6PD+ and 6% UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1d). Human BAT showed a similar reciprocal UCP1 and H6PD pattern in multilocular brown–beige adipocytes (Fig. 1e), 45% of BAs were UCP1+H6PD−, 47% were UCP1−H6PD+ and 8% were UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1f). Western blotting confirmed more than twofold higher H6PD in BA-L cells than in BA-H cells and more than fourfold higher UCP1 in BA-H cells than in BA-L cells, while H6PD was enriched in mature BAs relative to in the stromal vascular fractions (SVFs) (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Together, these data identify H6PD as a BA-L marker.

It has been revealed that to enable real-time labelling of BA-H cells, we generated Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mice by inserting a P2A-mGFP cassette after Ucp1 exon 6, immediately upstream of the stop codon (Extended Data Fig. 2d). These mice displayed robust BAT GFP fluorescence without altered UCP1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f). GFP IF staining revealed a heterogeneous distribution of GFP+ and GFP− BAs (Extended Data Fig. 2g). In vitro-cultured BAs and beige adipocytes revealed selective H6PD expression in GFP− BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 2h), validating our in vivo findings.

Sources indicate that we next investigated UCP1-independent thermogenesis through the futile creatine cycle17,18,19,20,21. Tissue-non-specific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP) and creatine kinase B (CKB) protein levels increased 4.8-fold and 2.5-fold, respectively, in BAT during cold exposure and were enriched 2.9-fold and 2.0-fold in BA-L cells versus in BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b), consistent with higher Ckb mRNA in BA-L cells6. IF staining further highlighted TNAP enrichment in BA-L cells (H6PDhigh BAs) in BAT and H6PDhigh beige adipocytes in cold-exposed iWAT (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). In vitro-differentiated BAs also displayed selective TNAP expression in BA-L cells (GFP− BAs) (Extended Data Fig. 3e), indicating that the futile creatine cycle is more active in BA-L cells.

Regarding the metabolic differences between BA-L cells and BA-H cells, BA-L cells have half the basal respiration, but similar maximal respiration compared to BA-H cells, indicating similarly high mitochondrial potential6. Using in vivo [U-13C]glucose tracing22, we recently highlighted that BAT has the most active glucose oxidation among metabolically active tissues, while in vitro tracing confirmed active glucose oxidation in differentiated BAs23. To characterize BA-L metabolism, we performed [U-13C] glucose and [U-13C] palmitate tracing in freshly isolated BA-H cells and BA-L cells, followed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Fully labelled (m+16) free palmitate (C16:0) was about twofold higher in BA-L cells, indicating greater fatty acid uptake (Extended Data Fig. 4b), while fully labelled total palmitate was sixfold higher, suggesting preferential fatty acids storage in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 4c). BA-L cells also showed lower citrate enrichment from both tracers, indicating lower glucose and fatty acid oxidation (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Thus, BA-L cells exhibit greater fatty acid uptake and accumulation but lower fatty acid and glucose oxidation, consistent with their lower basal respiration6.

We next examined whether H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells. H6PD depletion in BAs differentiated from BAT SVFs of Ucp1-mGFP mice increased Ucp1 expression sixfold (Fig. 1g), indicating that H6PD negatively regulates Ucp1. Conversely, H6pd overexpression by lentiviral injection into BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 4e,f) significantly reduced the proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 1i,j). Thus, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L that regulates UCP1 expression and BA heterogeneity.

In a recent development, H6PD localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and generates endoplasmic reticulum-resident NADPH, distinct from cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)24. H6PD primarily determines the reductase activity of endoplasmic reticulum-localized 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD11B1), which converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol25. GR protein levels were similar between BA-H cells and BA-L cells, indicating that GR signalling is not regulated by receptor abundance (Extended Data Fig. 3b). We next investigated whether GR signalling regulates UCP1 expression. Simultaneous treatment of BAs differentiated from the SVFs of wild-type (WT) mice with 11-dehydrocorticosterone (11-DHC), a natural substrate for active glucocorticoid biosynthesis25, and noradrenaline (NA) substantially increased UCP1 protein (Fig. 2a). However, 24 h 11-DHC pretreatment blunted NA-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2b). Thus, prolonged activation of GR signalling suppresses BA responsiveness to NA, maintaining BA-L cells in a stable, low-thermogenic status.

Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (a–h, j and m), unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-tests (i (GR) and k) and unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests (i (IgG)); ***P < 0.001. NS, not significant. For a–g, i–k and m, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bar, 50 μm (h).

Forskolin activates adenylyl cyclase (AC) to generate cAMP26. 11-DHC pretreatment also blocked forskolin-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2c), suggesting inhibition of AC activity or downstream cAMP signalling. To determine where GR signalling acts within the canonical β-adrenergic receptor–cAMP–PKA pathway that controls UCP1 expression27, we measured PKA activity in in vitro-differentiated BAs after 24 h of 11-DHC pretreatment, followed by NA, forskolin or 8-BrcAMP (a cAMP derivative). 11-DHC pretreatment markedly reduced NA- or forskolin-induced PKA activity (Fig. 2d,e), but not the response to 8-BrcAMP (Fig. 2f), indicating that downstream cAMP signalling is not affected by GR activation. Thus, GR signalling potentially suppresses UCP1 expression by inhibiting AC-mediated cAMP production.

Recent findings suggest that whereas 11-DHC requires conversion to active glucocorticoids, dexamethasone (DEX) directly activates GR. In contrast to the delayed effect of 11-DHC, DEX suppressed NA-induced UCP1 expression after co-treatment (Fig. 2g), an effect that was abrogated by the GR antagonist mifepristone (RU-486) (Fig. 2g). Similarly, in the in vitro-differentiated BAs, CL-316,243 increased Ucp1 expression about 3-fold, whereas DEX pretreatment reduced this induction to about 1.6-fold (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Together, these data support the conclusion that GR activation maintains BA-L cells in a low-UCP1-expressing state by suppressing cAMP production.

Recent findings suggest that we next investigated how GR signalling regulates BA heterogeneity. DEX is commonly used in adipogenic differentiation cocktails; its withdrawal increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.8-fold in BAs differentiated from BAT SVF of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Conversely, 11-DHC and the active glucocorticoid corticosterone decreased the BA-H/BA-L ratio compared with in the DEX-free control, independent of differentiation efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In WT mice, DEX induced BAT whitening and reduced the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 74% (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Thus, manipulating GR signalling alters BA heterogeneity both in vitro and in vivo.

In a recent development, to determine how GR signalling inhibits cAMP production, we examined other BA-L-enriched genes. Rgs2 was highly expressed in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,e,f). RGS2 binds to the C1 domain of AC III, V and VI, attenuating Gαs-dependent cAMP accumulation28. IF staining confirmed selective RGS2 expression in BA-L cells, with 40% of BAs being UCP1+(GFP+)RGS2−, 55% UCP1−(GFP−)RGS2+ and 5% UCP1+(GFP+)RGS2+ (Fig. 2h). RGS2 was also selectively expressed in GFP− BA-L cells in in vitro-differentiated BAs (brown and beige) (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). Analysis of published GR chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) followed by sequencing datasets29 identified GR occupancy within the promoter and intronic regions of Rgs2 (Extended Data Fig. 5i). ChIP–quantitative PCR (qPCR) in in vitro-differentiated BAs confirmed GR binding at the Rgs2 promoter, which was enhanced by DEX (Fig. 2i). Lastly, DEX increased Rgs2 mRNA 2.2-fold in freshly isolated BAs (Fig. 2j), supporting Rgs2 as a GR target. Thus, RGS2 is a GR target in the BAs that inhibits cAMP production. Knocking down Rgs2 in in vitro-differentiated BAs (Fig. 2k) did not affect PKA activity in response to NA alone (Extended Data Fig. 5j,k). However, Rgs2 knockdown abrogated the inhibitory effect of 11-DHC pretreatment on NA-induced PKA substrate phosphorylation (Fig. 2l,m). Rgs2 is therefore a GR target in BAs that suppresses Ucp1 expression by inhibiting AC activity, and BA-L cells are stabilized in the low-thermogenic state through the GR–RGS2–AC signalling axis.

H6PD protein levels in BAT changed inversely with UCP1 across environmental temperatures, while GR protein was only slightly elevated at thermoneutrality (30 °C) (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Cold exposure reduced H6PD protein by 1.8-fold in iWAT, but not in gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c), suggesting thermogenic-depot-specific regulation. CL-316,243 similarly decreased H6PD and increased UCP1 protein levels in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d). H6pd mRNA decreased rather than increased with rising temperature in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6e), indicating post-transcriptional regulation. Thus, H6PD protein levels, but not mRNA levels, change dynamically in BAT in response to fluctuating environmental temperatures, which may be essential for altering the BA-H/BA-L ratio in response to thermogenic demand.

It has been revealed that sympathetic neurons secrete NA to activate BA thermogenesis. We next tested whether sympathetic innervation mediates cold-induced H6PD protein reduction using unilateral BAT denervation, validated by reduced tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) protein (Fig. 3a). Cold exposure increased BA-H cells from 31.1% to 85.6% (Fig. 3b), as previously reported6. Denervation prevented the cold-induced reduction of H6PD (Fig. 3a), and although there was an increase in the BA-H/BA-L ratio, the proportion of BA-H cells was 66% lower than the sham group during cold exposure (29.1% versus 85.6%) (Fig. 3b). The low BA-H/BA-L ratio was accompanied by BA whitening (Extended Data Fig. 6f), a feature associated with impaired thermogenesis30. Notably, H6PD consistently labelled BA-L cells regardless of the variable BA-H/BA-L ratio at different environmental temperatures (Fig. 3b). Thus, sympathetic innervation is required to reduce H6PD protein and raise the BA-H/BA-L ratio after cold exposure.

Recent findings suggest that cold exposure also downregulated GR target genes, including Rasd1, Fkbp5, Pik3r1, Tsc22d3 and Rgs2 in BAT, whereas denervation blunted these effects (Extended Data Fig. 6g), supporting the involvement of GR signalling in raising the BA-H/BA-L ratio. We next tested whether the opposite occurred when shifting mice from cold to thermoneutrality. H6PD protein increased 2.1-fold in BAT, while GR protein remained unchanged (Fig. 3c). Transitioning cold-exposed mice to 30 °C also restored GR target gene expression in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6h), indicating that H6PD and GR signalling dynamically respond to temperature fluctuations to regulate BA heterogeneity.

We next tested whether blocking GR during the transition from cold to warmer temperatures prevents BA-H cells from switching to BA-L cells. We generated a BA-H-specific, inducible Nr3c1-knockout model by crossing Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Nr3c1flox/flox mice (Fig. 3d). Mice were first exposed to 6 °C for 1 week to raise the BA-H/BA-L ratio, followed by 1 week of doxycycline diet under cold conditions to induce Nr3c1 deletion in BA-H cells (Ucp1-Nr3c1flox/flox turning into Ucp1-Nr3c1−/−), and were then returned to room temperature with the doxycycline diet for another week. One week is long enough for the mice to reduce thermogenesis according to the rise in environmental temperature. IF staining confirmed Nr3c1 deletion in most BAs (Fig. 3e), consistent with 86% of BAs being BA-H cells during cold exposure (Fig. 3b), and western blotting highlighted reduced GR and RGS2 in isolated BAs (Fig. 3f). We previously showed that BA-H cells contain smaller lipid droplets and therefore have higher density, whereas BA-L cells have larger lipid droplets, lower density and float after mild centrifugation (like white adipocytes)6. Notably, BAT from Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice sank in PBS, whereas control BAT floated (Fig. 3g), suggesting a higher density and a higher BA-H/BA-L ratio. Consistently, Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice showed browner BAT with smaller lipid droplets, increased iWAT beiging (Fig. 3h) and a higher proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 3i). Metabolic cage studies further showed increased energy expenditure and oxygen consumption in Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice, without changes in body weight (Fig. 3j,k and Extended Data Fig. 6i), body composition, food intake, respiratory exchange ratio or locomotor activity (Extended Data Fig. 6j–n). As the controls were metabolically healthy young adults, Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice showed no further improvements in glucose tolerance or insulin sensitivity (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). These data highlight stage- and cell-subtype-specific requirements for GR signalling to regulate bistable BA states and thermogenesis. Inhibition of GR reactivation during the transition from cold to room temperature preserved a high BA-H/BA-L ratio and persistent thermogenesis despite reduced environmental thermogenic demand. These data not only confirm that we can block the BA-H-to-BA-L switch by inhibiting GR signalling, but also indicate that manipulating BA heterogeneity can increase thermogenesis and significantly boost whole-body energy expenditure.

In a recent development, to elucidate the sympathetic regulation of H6PD protein, we treated in vitro-differentiated BAs with NA but observed no change in H6PD protein (Fig. 4a), suggesting that other cell types and factors are involved in sympathetic regulation of H6PD. We next assessed cytokine expression in BAT and found that Il1b exhibited the greatest reduction (by 53%) after cold exposure (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7a), and the greatest induction (by 3.3-fold) when mice were shifted from cold to thermoneutrality (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7b). Cold-induced Il1b suppression was blunted by BAT sympathetic denervation (Fig. 4b), while NA reduced Il1b expression in BAT explants (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Il1b was predominantly expressed in SVFs rather than in mature adipocytes (Fig. 4d) and its expression changed with environmental temperature (Fig. 4d). qPCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) analysis further confirmed the predominant expression of Il1b in CD45+ SVFs (Fig. 4e), indicating an immune cell source. By contrast, systemic IL-1β levels remained unchanged across environmental temperatures, suggesting local regulation of IL-1β levels in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 7d).

Notably, IF staining revealed that BA-L cells clustered around IL-1β puncta, whereas BA-H cells formed clusters further away (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 7e), a pattern that was observed across room temperature, during cold exposure and after denervation (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Quantification indicated that IL-1β puncta and GFP+ cells (BA-H cells) show a significant negative Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC = −0.5 ± 0.1), suggesting a mutually exclusive pattern between these two factors at room temperature (Extended Data Fig. 7f). During cold exposure, this pattern persisted but was weaker (PCC = −0.2 ± 0.1), as fewer IL-1β puncta were available for quantification (Extended Data Fig. 7f). BAT denervation prevented the reduction in IL-1β puncta, maintained a low BA-H/BA-L ratio and preserved a strong negative correlation with GFP+ cells (BA-H cells) (PCC = −0.45 ± 0.1). Thus, across all three conditions, BA-L cells were consistently close to IL-1β puncta, indicating a strong correlation between IL-1β and BA heterogeneity.

Sources indicate that we next tested whether IL-1β regulates H6PD protein levels in BAs. Among the proinflammatory cytokines tested, TNF and IL-1β increased H6PD protein levels by 1.8- and 3.5-fold, respectively (Fig. 4g), without increasing H6pd mRNA (Extended Data Fig. 7g), confirming a post-transcriptional regulation of H6PD. Combined IL-1β, TNF and IFNγ treatment did not further increase H6PD protein beyond the effect of IL-1β alone (Fig. 4g). IL-1β increased H6PD protein in a time-dependent manner (Fig. 4h). During cycloheximide (CHX) treatment, H6PD abundance decreased by 30% and 50% at 6 and 12 h, respectively, whereas IL-1β prevented this decline (Fig. 4i), indicating increased H6PD protein stability from degradation. IL-1β is known to activate multiple downstream pathways, including JNK, MEK–ERK, p38–MAPK and IKK–NF-κB. Among inhibitors targeting these pathways, only the MEK and ERK inhibitor U0126 attenuated IL-1β-induced H6PD upregulation (Extended Data Fig. 7h,i), indicating that MEK–ERK mediates IL-1β-induced H6PD stability.

We next examined whether IL-1β regulates UCP1 expression. IL-1β did not alter UCP1 expression in the in vitro-differentiated BAs in the absence of 11-DHC, but reduced UCP1 protein levels by 53% in the presence of 11-DHC (Extended Data Fig. 7j,k), indicating that IL-1β suppresses UCP1 through GR signalling.

Industry observers note that adipose-tissue-resident immune cells can regulate sympathetic innervation31,32,33. However, TH and synaptophysin staining showed similar sympathetic innervation of BA-H cells and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 7l,m), indicating that IL-1β regulates BA heterogeneity independently of differential sympathetic innervation.

It has been revealed that to identify the immune cells that secrete IL-1β in BAT, we integrated multiple published BAT scRNA-seq datasets14,34,35,36,37 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). β-Adrenergic receptors were expressed in CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), suggesting potential sympathetic regulation. Subclustering analysis revealed that Il1b was enriched in neutrophils (CD45+CD11b+F4/80−CXCR2+), monocytes (CD45+CD11b+F4/80−Ly6C+), and macrophages (CD45+CD11b+F4/80+) (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). Flow cytometry confirmed that IL-1β was mainly produced by CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a,b), with IL-1β+ cells predominantly comprising neutrophils and macrophages, but not monocytes (Extended Data Fig. 9c–e). IL-1β+ cells represented 10% of neutrophils and 1% of macrophages, indicating that IL-1β production is restricted to specific subsets (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Despite the low frequency, the greater abundance of macrophages resulted in substantial numbers of IL-1β+ macrophages, with IL-1β+ neutrophils only 1.7-fold more abundant (Extended Data Fig. 9e), indicating that both cell types are major IL-1β sources. IF staining further confirmed IL-1β colocalization with subsets of CXCR2+ neutrophils and F4/80+ macrophages in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 9f,g).

Recent findings suggest that depletion of CD45+ immune cells from BAT SVFs increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.7-fold without affecting overall differentiation efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j), supporting a role for immune cells in regulating BA heterogeneity. To further confirm the role of local IL-1β in thermogenic regulation, we injected lentivirus encoding Il1rn (encoding IL-1RA), a naturally occurring inhibitor of IL-1 receptor signalling, or an mCherry control directly into BAT (Extended Data Fig. 10a). IL-1RA increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio twofold in mice housed at room temperature (Fig. 4j,k). In in vitro-differentiated BAs, Il1r knockdown attenuated IL-1β-mediated suppression of UCP1 expression, indicating a direct effect of IL-1β on BAs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Moreover, in vivo pharmacological inhibition of IL-1β production using the caspase-1 inhibitor VX-765 increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.2-fold (Extended Data Fig. 10c,d), further demonstrating a functional role for IL-1β in regulating BA heterogeneity.

In a recent development, we next investigated how temperature fluctuations regulate IL-1β in BAT. Il1b expression in primary BAT SVFs was temperature-dependent (Fig. 4d), whereas IL-1β+ immune cell numbers remained unchanged across housing temperatures (Extended Data Fig. 10e–h), indicating regulation independent of immune cell recruitment. NA directly suppressed Il1b expression in BAT-derived CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 10i), suggesting adrenergic regulation of IL-1β production. Consistent with adrenergic receptor expression in CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), scRNA-seq analysis showed selective expression of Adrb1 and Adrb2, but not α-adrenergic receptor genes, in Il1b-expressing immune cell populations (Extended Data Fig. 11a). We further examined adrenergic regulation of Il1b using bone marrow-derived neutrophils. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced Il1b expression dose dependently (Extended Data Fig. 11b), whereas NA pretreatment suppressed this induction in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). This effect was reversed by the non-selective β-adrenergic receptor antagonist propranolol, but not by the non-selective α-adrenergic receptor antagonist phenoxybenzamine (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Consistently, propranolol administration, but not phenoxybenzamine, increased Il1b expression in BAT in vivo (Extended Data Fig. 11g,h), supporting β-adrenergic suppression of IL-1β production.

Decreased BA thermogenesis has been reported with obesity38 and ageing3. However, high fat diet- (HFD)-induced obese mice were completely cold-tolerant, with 100% survival after 7 days of cold exposure (Fig. 5a,b). HFD feeding decreased H6PD and increased UCP1 protein levels (Fig. 5c), indicating preserved BAT thermogenic potential. By contrast, aged mice exhibited cold intolerance, with reduced body temperature and a 25% mortality within the first 2 days (Fig. 5d,e), suggesting impaired thermogenesis. Aged mice indicated a 2.3-fold increase in H6PD and a 40% decrease in UCP1 (Fig. 5f), suggesting a reduced BA-H/BA-L ratio. GR was modestly reduced by HFD feeding but unchanged with ageing. These differences suggest that cold-induced thermogenesis is more severely impaired with ageing than with obesity at a young age, and that the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying impaired thermogenesis may differ substantially.
