Sources indicate that in young Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice, BA-H cells increased from 28.8% at 24 °C to 61.7% and 89.7% after 1 and 3 days of cold exposure, respectively. In aged mice, the baseline BA-H/BA-L ratio at 24 °C was extremely low (0.31%), and BA-H cells increased to 15% and 50.9% after 1 and 3 days of cold exposure, respectively (Fig. 5g,h), suggesting delayed BA bistable regulation in response to cold stimulation. H6PD progressively decreased during cold exposure in both young and aged mice (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 11i), but its level at cold exposure in aged mice was comparable to that in young mice at 24 °C (Extended Data Fig. 11i). UCP1 was also reduced in aged mice, consistent with the lower BA-H/BA-L ratio (Extended Data Fig. 11i). Despite increased BA-L abundance, cold-induced TNAP expression was also blunted with age, although TNAP remained enriched in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 11j), suggesting impaired futile creatine cycle activation. Aged mice also exhibited a 1.8-fold increase in BAT corticosterone (the active form of glucocorticoid in mice) in BAT, but not serum corticosterone (Extended Data Fig. 11k,l), and a sixfold increase in BAT Il1b expression arising from SVFs (Extended Data Fig. 11m,n). Together, these results suggest that elevated local IL-1β and H6PD-mediated overactivation of the GR–RGS2–AC axis lower the BA-H/BA-L ratio, therefore impairing cold-induced thermogenesis in aged mice.

Lastly, we investigated whether GR inhibition could restore BA bistable regulation and thermogenesis in aged mice. One week of RU-486 treatment increased the proportion of BA-H cells in aged mice from 0.5% to 8.3% at room temperature and from 10.6% to 32.8% after 1 day of cold exposure (Fig. 5j–m). RU-486 also reduced lipid droplet accumulation within BAs and improved BAT whitening (Fig. 5n), increased rectal temperature during the cold tolerance test and reduced body weight in the first few days of cold exposure (Extended Data Fig. 11o,p). Metabolic cage studies revealed that RU-486 treatment increased energy expenditure and oxygen consumption across the day–night cycle, without changes in respiratory exchange ratio, locomotor activity or food intake (Extended Data Fig. 11q–u). Thus, GR antagonism increases energy expenditure in aged mice, potentially due to elevated UCP1-dependent thermogenesis in BAT.

We found that the two BA subtypes are spatially organized and tightly regulated. IL-1β stabilizes surrounding BAs in the low-thermogenic state (BA-L cells) by extending H6PD protein half-life. H6PD facilitates active glucocorticoid production, which suppresses UCP1 expression through the GR–RGS2–AC axis (Extended Data Fig. 12a). BAs further from IL-1β puncta are stabilized in the high-thermogenic state (BA-H cells) with low H6PD protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 12b). During cold stimulation, activated sympathetic neurons secrete NA, which suppresses IL-1β production by immune cells. Low IL-1β levels promote H6PD degradation and switch BA-L cells into BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 12a,b). After cold stimulation, this process is reversed, restoring a lower BA-H/BA-L ratio. Age impairs the flexibility to alter BA heterogeneity due to IL-1β overload in BAT, which significantly contributes to the age-related decline in thermogenesis (Extended Data Fig. 12b).

Recent findings suggest that the advantages of this spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity are multifaceted. First, it enables a dual-layered response: an immediate, acute response through readily active BA-H cells, and a longer-term, chronic response that involves shifting cellular heterogeneity. Second, it facilitates communication between different cell types through spatial proximity, thereby integrating stimuli from multiple systems, combining environmental and internal cues, and enabling precise regulation of cell states. Third, shifting between BA-H and BA-L states preserves BAs from oxidative damage associated with sustained high thermogenesis.

Although this study primarily focused on UCP1-dependent thermogenesis, UCP1-independent mechanisms are also critical for thermogenic adipose tissue function and whole-body metabolic homeostasis39,40,41. We observed that TNAP, a key component of the futile creatine cycle, is enriched in BA-L cells. Cold exposure increased the proportion of BA-H cells while inducing CKB and TNAP expression in BAT42, reflecting enhanced futile creatine cycle activity either specifically in BA-L cells or across all BAs, with BA-L cells retaining higher activity. Importantly, cold-induced TNAP expression was compromised with age, while remaining enriched in BA-L cells. These results suggest that both UCP1- and futile creatine cycle-dependent thermogenesis are impaired with age.

According to recent reports, BAT has long been recognized as a target organ for glucocorticoids, but their precise role remains unclear. Some studies indicate that glucocorticoids suppress UCP1 expression and/or BAT activity43,44,45,46, whereas others reach the opposite conclusions47,48,49. Glucocorticoids have also been implicated in warm-induced beige adipocyte whitening50. This study highlights that GR signalling in BAT regulates BA heterogeneity by locking BAs in the BA-L state and reducing their responsiveness to NA. Active glucocorticoid levels are regulated locally, independent of systemic levels25. Thus, systemic glucocorticoid treatments may not alter active glucocorticoid levels in individual BAs, potentially explaining previous conflicting observations. Importantly, inducible GR deletion in BAs during the transition from cold to room temperature sustained the high BA-H/BA-L ratio and thermogenesis. The stage- and cell-subtype-specific requirement of GR signalling explains why Nr3c1-knockout mice do not exhibit altered BAT development or thermogenesis51,52, and indicates that targeting GR at selective timing could profoundly manipulate thermogenic activity.

Our study highlighted that BA heterogeneity is determined by communication from sympathetic neurons to immune cells, rather than by direct communication from sympathetic neurons to BAs. NA, the primary neurotransmitter from sympathetic nerves, has been shown to modulate immune cell response by regulating cytokine production by immune cells in the liver and adipose tissue53,54. We found that NA directly suppresses Il1b production in immune cells through β-adrenergic signalling, thereby modulating BA heterogeneity. Notably, a recent study showed that cold-induced β3-adrenergic activation transiently recruits neutrophils predominantly to white adipose tissue (WAT), particularly the visceral depot55. These infiltrating neutrophils produce IL-1β, which suppresses local lipolysis by attenuating cAMP-dependent signalling, thereby limiting excessive lipid mobilization. Based on our findings in BAT, IL-1β may similarly suppress lipolysis through the H6PD–GR–RGS2–AC axis in white adipocytes. Notably, Il1b expression in WAT exhibits transient kinetics, peaking at 12 h after stimulation and returning to basal levels at 24 h. Given that NA suppresses Il1b expression in BAT, it may similarly suppress Il1b expression in newly infiltrated neutrophils in WAT.

It has been revealed that it remains unclear why in vitro-differentiated BAs exhibit heterogeneity. BAs may intrinsically differentiate into cells with varying UCP1 levels to preserve thermogenic flexibility or maintain metabolic balance. Cross-talk between BAs and IL-1β+ immune cells in vivo may further reinforce and spatially organize this heterogeneity. Alternatively, IL-1β+ immune cells in SVFs during differentiation may influence the local environment. Indeed, depletion of CD45+ immune cells from SVFs before differentiation substantially increased the proportion of BA-H cells, suggesting that SVF immune cells reduce the BA-H/BA-L ratio. Future efforts with cell type-specific receptor knockout mouse models will help to validate and further elucidate how sympathetic innervation regulates IL-1β secretion and how IL-1β regulates H6PD protein stability.

In a recent development, decline of thermogenesis and age-related adiposity56 contribute to age-related metabolic disorders. Previous studies suggest that reduction in thermogenic activity may be due to impaired beige adipogenesis5,57, declined mitochondrial fuel oxidation3, reduced adrenergic receptors, altered other master regulators of thermogenesis58 and compromised sympathetic innervation due to infiltration of senescent immune cells59. Our study revealed that Il1b is increased in aged BAT, consistent with previous studies reporting increased immune cell infiltration and upregulated cytokines in aged BAT59. Increased IL-1β stabilized large amounts of BAs in the BA-L state and suppressed thermogenesis in aged mice. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of GR signalling by a GR antagonist raised the BA-H/BA-L ratio and improved cold-induced thermogenesis in aged mice, indicating that BA-specific GR signalling could be targeted to correct age-related cold intolerance and significantly increase basal metabolism. However, given the systemic effects of RU-486 (ref. 60), other tissues and cell types may also contribute. Future efforts will focus on the effects of targeted inhibition of GR signalling specifically in thermogenic cells.

All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of City of Hope (protocol 17014). Mice were maintained under a 12 h–12 h dark–light cycle in a temperature-controlled facility with ad libitum access to water and food. The diets included a standard chow diet (5053, Lab diet), an HFD (D12492, Research Diets) and a chow diet supplemented with 600 mg per kg doxycycline (S4107, Bio-Serv), as described for individual experiments. The Ucp1-rtTA mouse line was generated as previously described15,61. The Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mouse line was created by Biocytogen through microinjection of CRISPR components and a donor vector into C57BL/6J zygotes. The single guide RNA targeted the junction of the exon 6 coding region and 3′ untranslated region (UTR) (CTTCCTCCAAGTTGCTTATG + TGG) of the Ucp1 gene, and a P2A-mGFP cassette was inserted at the 5′ end of the 3′ UTR, immediately upstream of the Ucp1 gene stop codon. TRE-Cre (B6.Cg-Tg(tetO-cre)1Jaw/J, 006234), Rosa26-loxp-STOP-loxp-mT/mG (B6.129(Cg)-Gt (ROSA)26Sortm4(ACTB-tdTomato,-eGFP) Luo/J, 007676) and Nr3c1-floxed (B6.Cg-Nr3c1tm1.1Jda/J, 021021) mouse lines were purchased from the Jackson Laboratories. To generate mice lacking GR proteins selectively in BAs, Ucp1-rtTA and TRE-Cre mice were crossed with Nr3c1-floxed mice. Littermates lacking TRE-Cre were used as control mice. All mice were maintained on a pure C57BL/6J background. The sample sizes for animal experiments were determined based on previous studies. Experimental groups were randomly assigned. Investigators were blinded to group allocation during rectal temperature measurement, but blinding was not feasible for other experiments.

Unilateral denervation of BAT was performed as previously described62. In brief, 8-week-old male mice were anaesthetized with 5% isoflurane and placed onto a warm surgical platform. The interscapular surgical region was shaved and sterilized with 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol and iodine. A 1 cm lateral incision was made from the scapula to the neck, and the interscapular BAT depot was carefully detached from the underlying muscle layer and retracted cranially over the head using toothed forceps. Five branches of the intercostal sympathetic nerve bundles innervating the left and right BAT lobes were exposed. Unilateral denervation was achieved by cutting the nerve bundles on the left side, while the right nerve bundles were exposed and touched as a sham-operated control. The BAT lobes were repositioned, and the incision was closed using absorbable 5.0 sutures. Mice were allowed to recover for 2 weeks before undergoing further experimental procedures.

Industry observers note that to construct the H6pd-expressing lentiviral vector, the mouse H6pd complementary DNA (cDNA) (NM_173371.4) was amplified using primers with 5′ BamH I and 3′ Sal I restriction sites. To construct the Il1rn-expressing lentiviral vector, the mouse Il1rn cDNA (NM_031167.5) was amplified using primers with 5′ BamH I and 3′ Sal I restriction sites. The PCR products were cleaved with BamH I and Sal I and ligated into the pLenti-mCherry vector (36084, Addgene) to generate the pLenti-mH6pd lentiviral vector or pLenti-mIl1rn lentiviral vector. Lentiviral particles were produced by co-transfecting HEK293T (ATCC) cells with the pLenti-mCherry, pLenti-mH6pd, or pLenti-mIl1rn transfer plasmids, along with the packaging psPAX2 (12260, Addgene) and envelope plasmids pMD2.G (12259, Addgene) at a 1:1:1 ratio, using PEI (1 μg DNA to 3 µl PEI). HEK293T cells were not independently authenticated but were regularly tested for mycoplasma contamination, with negative results. After 72 h, the supernatant containing lentiviral particles was collected, filtered through a 0.45-μm PES filter and concentrated using the Lenti-X concentrator (631232, Takara Bio). The concentrated lentivirus was resuspended in PBS, stored at −80 °C and titrated using an RT-PCR Titration kit (631235, Takara Bio). Lentivirus administration in BAT was performed as described previously63. In brief, 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP or Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice were anaesthetized with 5% isoflurane. A small lateral incision (~0.5–0.8 cm) was made in the interscapular area to expose BAT. Then 10–20 μl of either pLenti-mH6pd lentivirus, pLenti-mIl1rn lentiviral or a negative control lentivirus (109 IFU ml−1) was directly injected at three distinct sites into each interscapular BAT lobe.

For three-dimensional fluorescence imaging of BAT, we used the Adipo-Clear method as described previously64. In brief, 8-week-old male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice were fed a doxycycline diet for 3 days at 24 °C. Mice were anaesthetized and perfused with cold PBS containing 100 U ml−1 heparin (H3149, Sigma-Aldrich), followed by ice-cold 4% PFA. The BAT was then dissected and post-fixed in 4% PFA at 4 °C overnight. After fixation, the tissue was washed with PBS, trimmed and delipidated using a graded series of methanol–B1n buffer, followed by 100% dichloromethane. After delipidation, the BAT was washed with a graded series of methanol–B1n buffer, followed by PTwH buffer. The sample was then incubated with primary rabbit anti-TH polyclonal antibody (1:200, ab152, Abcam) or rabbit anti-synaptophysin antibody (1:200, ab32127, Abcam) along with chicken anti-GFP antibody (1:200, ab13970, Abcam), diluted in PTxwH buffer at room temperature for 3 days. After incubation with primary antibodies, the sample was washed with PTxwH buffer and then incubated with secondary antibodies: Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31573, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Cy3 AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragment donkey anti-chicken IgY (IgG) (H+L) (703-166-155, Jackson Immuno Research) secondary antibodies at room temperature for 3 days. The sample was dehydrated through a series of methanol and 100% dichloromethane and then cleared with dibenzyl ether. Three-dimensional imaging of the cleared BAT was performed using tile scanning with a confocal laser-scanning microscope (LSM 880, Zeiss) at ×10 and ×20 magnifications, with image acquisition and analysis conducted using the Zeiss Zen black software.

The SVF of BAT was isolated from the interscapular BAT of mice on postnatal day 7, while the SVF from iWAT was obtained from 5-week-old male mice. In brief, dissected BAT or iWAT was minced and digested for 45 min at 37 °C in a digestion buffer containing 1.5 mg ml−1 collagenase D (11088882001, Sigma-Aldrich) in an isolation buffer (0.123 M NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 1.3 mM CaCl2, 5 mM glucose, 100 mM HEPES and 4% BSA). The cell–tissue mixture was filtered through a 70-μm cell strainer (08-771-2, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove undigested fragments, then centrifuged for 5 min at 300g at 4 °C. The resulting cell pellet was resuspended in growth medium (DMEM, 10566016 Life Technologies; 1% penicillin–streptomycin, SV30010 Hyclone; 0.1% gentamicin, 1855724 Life Technologies and 20 mM HEPES, Sigma-Aldrich, H3537) containing 20% FBS (16H328, Sigma-Aldrich) and filtered again through a 40-μm cell strainer (08-771-1, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove clumps and adipocytes. The flow-through was centrifuged for 5 min at 300g at 4 °C, and the SVF pellet was resuspended in SVF growth medium and plated onto a 12-well tissue culture plate for RNA and protein extraction or onto a 35 mm glass-bottom tissue culture dish for IF staining. For differentiation into brown and beige adipocytes, SVF cells were switched to fresh induction medium (DMEM plus DEX (1 μM), insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), isobutylmethylxanthine (0.5 mM), T3 (1 nM), indomethacin (0.125 mM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS on day 0 (2 days after reaching confluence). After 2 days, the medium was replaced with maintenance medium (DMEM with insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), T3 (1 nM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS, and this maintenance medium was changed every 2 days until further use.

For glucocorticoid treatment, SVF cells from the BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice were cultured and differentiated as described. During differentiation, cells were treated with or without 1 μM corticosterone (16063, Cayman Chemical), 1 μM DEX (D4902, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM 11-DHC (32907, Cayman Chemical) in the induction medium. On differentiation day 6, the density of GFP fluorescence was assessed under a microscope (BZ-X710, Keyence) to quantify the BA-H/BA-L ratio. For the PKA activity assay, on differentiation day 6, primary BAs differentiated were pretreated with 1 μM 11-DHC or vehicle for 48 h, followed by incubation with 1 μM NA (A0937, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM forskolin (F6886, Sigma-Aldrich) or 500 μM 8-Br-cAMP (B7880, Sigma-Aldrich) for 30 min. PKA activity was measured by western blot analysis using antibodies specific to phosphorylated PKA substrates. For the H6PD half-life assay, BAs differentiated from primary BAT SVFs were pretreated with 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β (401-ML-005, R&D Systems) or vehicle for 4 h, followed by exposure to 50 µg ml−1 CHX (C1988, Sigma-Aldrich) with IL-1β or saline for various timepoints (0, 3, 6 and 12 h) at 37 °C, with H6PD quantified by western blot analysis. For cytokine treatment, on differentiation day 6, primary BAs were treated with saline, 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β, 20 ng ml−1 TNF (410-MT-010, R&D Systems) and 10 ng ml−1 IFNγ (485-MI-100, R&D Systems) alone or in combination for 48 h. For IL-1β signalling inhibition, BAs were treated with saline, 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β or IL-1β in combination with 10 μM p38 kinase inhibitor SB203580 (559395, Sigma-Aldrich), 5 μM NF-κB inhibitor BAY11-7082 (196871, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM JNK inhibitor SP600125 (420119, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM ERK inhibitor U0126 (662005, Sigma-Aldrich) or 5 mM IKKβ inhibitor aspirin (A5376, Sigma-Aldrich) for 48 h, with inhibitors administered 1 h before IL-1β treatment. To test the effect of IL-1β on UCP1 expression, BAs on day 6 were switched to culture medium containing charcoal-stripped FBS and then treated with vehicle or 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β for 48 h in the absence or presence of 1 μM 11-DHC. For DEX and RU-486 treatment, the BAs on day 6 were pretreated with vehicle or 10 μM RU-486 for 1 h, followed by treatment with 1 μM NA in the presence or absence of 1 μM DEX for 24 h. The concentrations of UCP1, H6PD and β-actin were quantified by western blot analysis. To assess the effect of immune cells on BAs heterogeneity, SVF cells from the BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice were cultured and differentiated as described, with or without CD45+ immune cells. CD45+ immune cells were depleted from SVFs using PE-anti-CD45 antibody (103106, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies).

Mature BAs from the interscapular BAT of 10-week-old male mice were obtained as described before. In brief, BATs were dissected, cleaned of contaminating muscle and WAT, minced into small pieces, and digested in collagenase-dispase buffer (17703034, Gibco) for 1 h at 37 °C with shaking at 110 r.p.m. The cell suspension was filtered through 100-μm cell strainers (08-771-19, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove undigested tissues, washed with 3 volumes of DMEM/F12 medium (10565018, Life Technologies) containing 10% FBS and centrifuged at 100g for 5 min at room temperature. The floating BAs were transferred and resuspended in PBS wash buffer three times. After quantification, 5 × 105 BAs were suspended in Matrigel (Corning, CB-40234C) at a 1:1 volume ratio and seeded into 6-well tissue culture dishes. The plates were incubated at 37 °C for 15 min to induce gel formation. Maintenance medium (DMEM with insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), T3 (1 nM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS was then added to the wells with either vehicle, 1 μM DEX, 10 μM CL-316,243 (C5976, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM DEX combined with 10 μM CL-316,243 for 24 h. For the separation of BA-H and BA-L cells, we modified our previous protocol6 by adding additional steps to further deplete contaminating SVFs in BA-L cells. In brief, floating BAs were collected as BA-L cells, and the pellet containing BA-H cells and SVF was further separated using the EasyPlate magnet-based method. The cell suspension was incubated with PE-conjugated antibodies against immune cells (PE-anti-CD45, 103106, BioLegend), endothelial cells (PE-anti-CD31, 102408, BioLegend), fibroblasts (PE-anti-CD140a, 135905, BioLegend) and pericytes (PE-anti-CD146, 134704, BioLegend) and processed using EasySep reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Freshly isolated BA-H and BA-L cells (1 × 105 per condition) were incubated in tracing medium (D5030, Sigma-Aldrich) containing either 5 mM [U-13C]glucose or 0.5 mM [U-13C]palmitate for 2 h and 6 h. After incubation, cells were washed with NaCl and collected with cold 50% methanol as before22,23. Metabolites were extracted and analysed by GC–MS.

Recent findings suggest that mice were anaesthetized and perfused with PBS, followed by 10% formalin fixative buffer. The interscapular BAT, iWAT and gWAT were carefully dissected and post-fixed in 10% formalin buffer overnight at 4 °C. After dehydration, paraffin embedding and sectioning, tissue sections were stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E).

Sources indicate that for human samples, adipose tissue was collected during thyroid surgery. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients. Supraclavicular adipose tissue was removed as waste biological material from subjects undergoing surgery at the General Hospital (AOU; Ancona, Italy) for thyroid diseases. Ethical approval was obtained from the specific Commission within the Azienda Ospedaliero Universitaria delle Marche (University Hospital of the Marche Region). The ethical approval protocol code is 208156. Immediately after removal, tissue pieces were fixed overnight at 4 °C by immersion in 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). They were then dehydrated, cleared and paraffin embedded. Sections from three levels (100 μm apart) were stained with H&E to assess morphology and BAT presence for UCP1-immunohistochemistry.

According to recent reports, for IF staining of mouse and human tissues, paraffin-embedded sections of Ucp1-mGFP and Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice and human BAT slides were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated using a graded ethanol series to double-distilled H2O. The slides were immersed in 10 mM sodium citrate buffer (C9999, Sigma-Aldrich) and boiled for 30 min for antigen retrieval, then blocked in PBST containing 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% BSA. Primary antibodies used were as follows: perilipin (1:500, NB100-60554, Novus and ab61682, Abcam), UCP1 (1:200, ab23841, Abcam and MAB6158, R&D Systems), GFP (1:200, ab13970, Abcam; and 2956S, Cell Signaling Technology), mCherry (1:200, ab167453, Abcam), H6PD (1:200, ab170895, Abcam; and 15255-1-AP, Proteintech), TNAP (1:200, AF2910, R&D Systems), GR (1:200, 12041S, Cell Signaling Technology), RGS2 (1:200, NBP1-32284, Novus), IL-1RA (1:100, MA5-35068, Thermo Fisher Scientific), IL-1β (1:50, AF-401-NA, R&D Systems), F4/80 (1:100, ab6640, Abcam) and CXCR2 (1:100, 20634-1-AP, Proteintech). Secondary antibodies (1:200 dilution) used were Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (A31571, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31572, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31573, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated donkey anti-goat IgG (H+L) (A32814, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated donkey anti-rat IgG (H+L) (A48270, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-goat IgG (H+L) (A21447, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Cy3 AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragment donkey anti-chicken IgY (IgG) (H+L) (703-166-155, Jackson Immuno Research). Slides were counterstained with 1 μg ml−1 DAPI (D9542, Sigma-Aldrich) and mounted with prolonged Anti-Fade mounting medium (P36931, Invitrogen). Bright-field and fluorescence images were acquired using an inverted fluorescence phase-contrast microscope (BZ-X710, Keyence).

Fluorescence microscopy images were acquired for three experimental conditions: room temperature, cold exposure and cold exposure with denervation. For each condition, dual-channel fluorescence images were collected with UCP1 labelled in the green channel and IL-1β labelled in the magenta channel, along with corresponding autofluorescence reference images for cellular region identification. All image analysis was performed using custom Python scripts using the tifffile, numpy, scipy and pandas libraries. To restrict analysis to cellular regions and exclude background artifacts, autofluorescence images were Gaussian-smoothed and used to generate binary masks with a threshold of 50 arbitrary units applied to autofluorescence intensity values65, ensuring that correlation analysis was performed exclusively on biologically relevant areas. To eliminate low-intensity noise and focus analysis on meaningful fluorescence signals, intensity-based thresholds were applied to both channels: UCP1 (green channel) at 70 arbitrary units and IL-1β (magenta channel) at 20 arbitrary units. Pixels were retained for analysis if they exceeded the threshold in either channel, using a logical OR to preserve regions with specific labelling while maintaining sensitivity to differential expression patterns. Co-localization between UCP1 and IL-1β was quantified using the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC), calculated pixel-wise across filtered cellular regions66. After masking and thresholding, images were vectorized by flattening two-dimensional pixel arrays into one-dimensional arrays. The PCC was computed using scipy.stats, providing both the correlation coefficient and associated P value for each image pair. Statistical comparisons between experimental conditions were performed using Welch’s t-tests for independent samples with unequal variances. This approach accounts for potential differences in variance between experimental groups while providing robust statistical inference. Results were compiled into structured data frames and visualized using bar plots with error bars.

Total RNA was extracted from tissues or cultured cells using either TRIzol reagent (15596026, Thermo Fisher Scientific) or RNAqueous-Micro Total RNA Isolation Kit (AM1931, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The first-strand cDNA was synthesized using the iScript cDNA synthesis kit (1708891, Bio-Rad) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. qPCR was performed using the SYBR Green PCR system (A25742, Applied Biosystems) with Tbp as the internal control. A list of all of the primer sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

In a recent development, adipose tissues, cultured adipocytes and isolated mature BAs were collected and lysed in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer (20-188, Sigma-Aldrich) containing protease inhibitor cocktails (11836170001, Sigma-Aldrich) and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails (P5726, P0044, Sigma-Aldrich). The extracted protein samples were loaded onto and separated on a 4–15% gradient SDS–PAGE TGX stain-free gel (4568086, Bio-Rad) and transferred to a PVDF membrane (1620177, Bio-Rad). The membranes were incubated with specific primary antibodies against H6PD (ab170895, Abcam and 15255-1-AP, Proteintech), UCP1 (ab23841, Abcam), GFP (2956S, Cell Signaling Technology), phosphorylated PKA substrates (RRXS*/T*) (9624S, Cell Signaling Technology), TH (ab152, Abcam), TNAP (AF2910, R&D Systems), CKB (18713-1-AP, Proteintech), GR (12041S, Cell Signaling Technology), IL-1R1 (PA5-97866, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and β-actin (4970 and 58169, Cell Signaling Technology). HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (1706515, Bio-Rad) and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (1706516, Bio-Rad) were used as secondary antibodies. The immunoreactive signals were detected using the Pierce ECL Western Blotting Substrate (32209, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and SuperSignal West Pico PLUS Chemiluminescent substrate (34577, Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Industry observers note that mature BAs were reverse-transfected with dsiRNA as described previously67. In brief, on differentiation day 5, BAT-derived primary BAs were trypsinized using 0.25% trypsin (25200, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 15 min. The cells were then resuspended in culture medium and seeded onto gelatin-coated cell culture plates that had been pre-incubated with a pool of 50 nM H6pd dsiRNAs, 50 nM Rgs2 dsiRNAs, 50 nM Il1r1 dsiRNAs or relevant control dsiRNAs (Integrated DNA Technologies), mixed with 5 μl ml−1 of Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (13778075, Thermo Fisher Scientific) diluted in Opti-MEM medium (31985070, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The final density of BAs was 2.5 × 105 cells per cm2 of culture plate. Mature BAs were treated or collected 2 days after transfection. A list of all of the dsiRNA sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

It has been revealed that mice were housed individually in temperature- and light-controlled rodent incubators (Powers Scientific) set to either thermoneutrality (30 °C) or cold (6 °C), with ad libitum access to food and water. For the β3-adrenoceptor agonist treatment experiment, mice were maintained at thermoneutrality for 1 week, followed by daily intraperitoneal injections of CL-316,243 in PBS at 1 mg per kg body weight for an additional 7 days. For adrenoceptor antagonist treatment, mice were exposed at 6 °C for 16 h, followed by intraperitoneal injections of propranolol (10 mg per kg; P0884, Sigma-Aldrich) or phenoxybenzamine hydrochloride (5 mg per kg; HY-B043A, MedChemExpress) in PBS for 4 h.

Sources indicate that for flow cytometry analysis, SVF cells were blocked with anti-mouse-CD16/32 (1:500, 101302, BioLegend) for 10 min, and then stained with anti-mouse-CD45-BV605 (1:400, 103155, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CD11b-APC (1:100, 101212, BioLegend), anti-mouse-F4/80-488 (1:100, 123120, BioLegend), anti-mouse-Ly6C-PE/Cy7 (1:400, 128018, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CXCR2-PE (1:20, 149304, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CD3-488 (1:100, 100210, BioLegend) and anti-mouse-CD19-PE (1:200, 152408, BioLegend) for individual experiments for 20 min on ice. After antibody incubation, the cells were washed once with 2% FBS–PBS. For intracellular staining, cells were stained with LIVE–DEAD fixable dead cell stain (65-0868-14, Invitrogen) for 30 min on ice. After washing with PBS, cells were fixed and permeabilized using a fixation/permeabilization kit (554714, BD bioscience) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, cells were fixed with fixation–permeabilization solution for 15 min on ice, followed by a wash with PBS and 1× perm–wash buffer. Cells were stained with anti-mouse-IL-1β-APC/eFluor 780 (1:80, 47-7114-82, Invitrogen) in 1× perm–wash buffer for 30 min on ice. After staining, cells were washed once with 1× perm–wash buffer and analysed by BD Fortessa cytometer. The flow plots were analysed by FlowJo (v.10).

In a recent development, eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were subcutaneously (s.c.) injected with either vehicle or 5 mg per kg per day water-soluble DEX (D2915, Sigma-Aldrich) dissolved in PBS for 2 weeks. Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice aged 10 weeks were maintained on doxycycline chow diet and administered vehicle or VX-765 (HY-13205, MedChemExpress, 50 mg per kg per day), dissolved in 20% (v/v) Cremophor EL, through daily intraperitoneal injection for 1 week. Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG or WT mice aged 70–75 weeks were injected s.c. with 60 mg per kg mifepristone (RU-486) (HY-13683, MedChemExpress) dissolved in DMSO–corn oil or with DMSO–corn oil alone daily as controls for 1 week. Body temperature was recorded daily throughout the treatment period. After the final RU-486 or vehicle injection, mice were individually housed and exposed to a cold environment (6 °C). Rectal temperatures were measured at the indicated timepoints using a rodent thermometer (Bioseb, TK8851). For metabolic phenotyping, 72-week-old male WT mice were s.c. injected with either vehicle or RU-486 (60 mg per kg per day) for 1 week, followed by metabolic phenotyping with continuing daily vehicle or RU-486 injection for an additional 3 days. During the metabolic cage study, energy expenditure, oxygen consumption, RER, locomotor activity and food intake were recorded. At the end point, the mice were perfused with PBS and 10% formalin and processed for H&E and IF staining as described above.

Sources indicate that male Ucp1-rtTA;TRE-cre;Nr3c1flox/flox or control littermates aged 10 weeks were fed a doxycycline diet at 6 °C for 1 week, then continued for an additional week after being moved back to 24 °C, followed by glucose tolerance tests and insulin tolerance tests. For the glucose tolerance test, mice were fasted for 12 h before intraperitoneal injection of glucose (2 g per kg body weight). For the insulin tolerance test, mice were fasted for 6 h before intraperitoneal injection of insulin (0.75 U kg−1, Eli Lilly). Tail vein blood samples were collected at 0, 15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min after injection, and blood glucose levels were measured using a Contour glucometer (Bayer).

In a recent development, BAT depots were dissected from the interscapular BAT of male C57BL/6J mice exposed to 30 °C for 1 week and minced into 1–2 mm3 explants. The explants were washed three times with PBS and transferred to a six-well plate containing DMEM with 10% FBS. BAT SVFs were isolated as described above, and CD45+ immune cells were enriched using PE-anti-CD45 antibody (103106, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies). Explants were incubated in saline or 10 mM NA (A0937, Sigma-Aldrich) for 24 h and CD45+ immune cells were treated with saline or NA (1 μM) for 4 h. After incubation, explants and CD45+ cells were collected for RNA extraction.

Bone marrow neutrophils were isolated from 10-week-old male WT mice. In brief, femurs and tibias were flushed with PBS containing 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS using a 23-gauge needle, and the cell suspension was filtered through a 70-μm strainer. Cells were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min, and the pellet was resuspended in red blood cell lysis buffer (R7757, Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 min at room temperature, followed by neutralization with PBS containing 2% FBS. Neutrophils were enriched using PE-anti-Ly6G antibody (127608, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies). Neutrophils were cultured in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 2% FBS. Neutrophils were stimulated with LPS (0–1,000 ng ml−1; L4391, Sigma-Aldrich) for 6 h or pretreated with NA (0–10 μM) for 30 min before 100 ng ml−1 LPS stimulation. For time-dependent experiments, neutrophils were treated with LPS with or without 1 μM NA pretreatment for 1–9 h. For adrenergic blockade experiments, neutrophils were pretreated with 1 μM propranolol (P0884, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM phenoxybenzamine (HY-B0431A, MedChemExpress) for 60 min, followed by 1 μM NA and 100 ng ml−1 LPS stimulation. For IL-1β measurement, 10 μM nigericin (HY-100381, MedChemExpress) was added 30 min before sample collection. Neutrophils were collected for RNA extraction, and the supernatants were collected for enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) analysis.

Sources indicate that blood samples were collected between 08:00 and 10:00, then centrifuged at 2,000g and 4 °C for 20 min to separate the serum. BAT was homogenized in a TissueLyser with 1 ml of 80% methanol on ice. The samples were then subjected to 3–5 freeze–thaw cycles and centrifuged at 4 °C and 13,000 r.p.m. for 15 min. The supernatant, which contains sterols, was collected, evaporated and dissolved in an assay buffer. Serum and tissue corticosterone levels were measured using a corticosterone ELISA kit (ADI-900-097, Enzo Biochem). Serum IL-1β levels were measured using an IL-1β ELISA kit (ab197742, Abcam). Neutrophil supernatant IL-1β was measured using an IL-1β ELISA kit (MLB00C-1, R&D Systems).

scRNA-seq data from the non-adipocyte fraction of BAT of C57BL/6J mice maintained at room temperature were obtained and selected from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under accessions GSE207707, GSE177635, GSE160585 and GSE161447. Data processing and analysis were conducted using Seurat v.4.0.6 in R v.4.1.2. Each dataset was imported, converted to Seurat objects, normalized and then variable features were identified. Integration anchors were computed to merge the datasets into a unified Seurat object. Quality control involved filtering out cells with fewer than 200 detected features and those with mitochondrial gene content exceeding 10%. The integrated data were scaled, and principal component analysis was performed. Clustering was performed using the Louvain algorithm with a resolution of 1.0. For visualization, t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding was used to depict cell clusters. Identification of each cell type was determined by comparing cell cluster-specific marker genes with known cell type-specific markers from the literature. Immune cell clusters were further identified and subclustered based on the expression of Ptprc, and non-immune cell types, including erythrocytes (Hba-a1 and Hba-a2), capillary endothelial cells (Pecam1 and Gpibp1), smooth muscle cells (Acta2) and adipose progenitor cells (Pdgfra and Col3a1), were excluded from the analysis.

Industry observers note that to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and enriched pathways between BA-L and BA-H cells, scRNA-seq data deposited in the NCBI GEO database under accession number GSE125269 were analysed. Adipocyte clusters were selected based on Plin1 expression, while contaminating endothelial cells (Pecam1) were excluded from the analysis. BA-L and BA-H cell populations were identified as described previously6. These populations were further compared to identify DEGs using the FindMarker function, which applied the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, with a log-transformed fold change threshold of 0.25 and a minimum detection fraction (min.pct) of 25%. To control the false discovery rate, P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and genes with an adjusted P of <0.05 were considered statistically significant. Visualization of the top 50 upregulated DEGs in both BA-L and BA-H cells was generated using the DoHeatmap function. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed on the top 75 upregulated and downregulated DEGs in BA-L cells using Gene Ontology Biological Processes. The analysis used Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P values to identify significantly enriched pathways. Pathways with an adjusted P of <0.05 and containing at least three enriched genes were considered significantly enriched. The top 20 enriched pathways were determined based on adjusted P values. Dot plots of these pathways were generated to visualize the enrichment results, with specific pathways of interest highlighted for enhanced interpretability.

After the vehicle and DEX treatment, in vitro-differentiated BAs were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde (15714-S, Electron Microscopy Sciences) for 10 min at room temperature and quenched with 125 mM glycine for 10 min. Cells were then incubated with ice-cold nucleus preparation buffer (10 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM KCl, 250 mM sucrose, 0.1% NP-40, 0.2 mM DTT, protease inhibitor cocktails) and homogenized using a KIMBLE Dounce tissue grinder (D8938, Sigma-Aldrich). The nuclei were collected by centrifugation at 1,000g for 10 min, washed with PBS containing protease inhibitor cocktails (11836170001, Sigma-Aldrich) and then resuspended in 250 μl nuclear lysis buffer (10 mM Tris, pH 8, 1 mM EDTA and 0.1% SDS). The chromatin was fragmented using the Bioruptor sonicator (Diagenode) for 30 cycles, 30 s on–30 s off with the maximum power setting to generate DNA fragments of 200–500 bp. The sheared chromatin was centrifuged at 13,000 r.p.m. for 10 min at 4 °C to remove debris and diluted tenfold with ChIP dilution buffer (16.7 mM Tris (pH 8), 1.2 mM EDTA, 167 mM NaCl, 1.1% Triton X-100, 0.01% SDS, protease inhibitor cocktail), with 10 μg chromatin for each ChIP. An aliquot of 10% was used for the input control. Then, 5 μg anti-GR antibody (NBP2-42221, Novus Biologicals) or normal rabbit IgG (2729S, Cell Signaling Technology) was added for overnight rocking at 4 °C. Next, 40 μl protein A/G Dynabeads (26162, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added to the ChIP samples and rotated for 2 h at 4 °C. The Dynabeads were washed in low-salt wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 2 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), high-salt wash buffer (20 mM Tris (pH 8), 2 mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), LiCl wash buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 1 mM EDTA, 1% NP-40, 1% sodium deoxycholate, 250 mM LiCl) and TE buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 1 mM EDTA) twice at each step. The antibody–chromatin complex was eluted and reverse-cross-linked in 200 μl elution buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 50 mM EDTA, 0.1% SDS, 300 mM NaCl, 0.8 mg ml−1 proteinase K and 10 μg ml−1 RNase A) by incubating at 50 °C for 2 h and subsequently at 65 °C for 8 h. The immunoprecipitated DNA fragments were purified using the MiniElute PCR Purification Kit (28004, Qiagen). ChIP–qPCR was performed using the primers listed in Supplementary Table 1. ChIP enrichments were calculated relative to the input DNA control.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism v.10. Results are presented as mean ± s.e.m. All measurements were obtained from individual samples. For each two-group comparison, equality of variances was first assessed using the F test. An unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used when the F test indicated equal variances, whereas Welch’s t-tests were used when the assumption of equal variances was not met. For one-way ANOVA, Tukey’s multiple-comparison test was used when variances were equal, whereas Dunnett’s T3 multiple-comparison test was used when variances were unequal. For two-way ANOVA, Tukey’s or Šídák’s multiple-comparison test was selected according to the experimental design. The statistical tests used are specified in the corresponding figure legends. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Exact P values for all statistical comparisons are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

a, Heatmap of genes differentially expressed in BA-L cells and BA-H cells in BAT, with H6pd, Rgs2, and Ucp1 highlighted with a red asterisk. Data were obtained from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) (accession GSE125269). b, Heatmap of genes related to thermogenesis and GR signalling that are differentially expressed in BA-L cells and BA-H cells, with Ucp1 and H6pd highlighted in red. c, Top pathway enrichment analysis for BA-L cells compared with BA-H cells, including upregulated and downregulated biological processes, with glucocorticoid-related pathways highlighted in red. The “Gene Ratio” represents the ratio of the number of input (differentially expressed) genes associated with a given pathway to the total number of input genes. p-values are shown in standard scientific notation; dot colour indicates the adjusted p-values (the brighter red indicating greater significance), and the dot size reflects the number of enriched genes. d, UMAP plots of the adipocyte fraction from BAT of WT mice maintained at room temperature. e, Distribution of the expression of Ucp1, Cox6b1, H6pd, Rgs2, Txnip and Nr3c1 within UMAP plots. f, Violin plots showing the expression and distribution of Ucp1, Cox6b1, H6pd, Rgs2, Txnip and Nr3c1.

It has been revealed that a, The Ucp1-Chaser-mTmG mouse model is generated by crossing Ucp1-rtTA transgenic mice with TRE-Cre and Rosa26-loxP-STOP-loxP-mT/mG transgenic mice. In Ucp1-Chaser-mTmG mice, all cells express tdTomato. When mice are put on a doxycycline diet, UCP1-high-expressing cells will start rtTA expression; rtTA will then bind to the TRE promoter, inducing Cre expression. Cre will specifically excise the floxed membrane-localizing Tomato (mTomato) sequence, initiating expression of membrane-localizing GFP (mGFP). b, BA-L cells and BA-H cells were freshly isolated from the BAT of WT mice. In a recent development, a, Molecular mechanism for the maintenance of the BA-L state. BA has two stable states, low and high thermogenesis, based on UCP1 expression. BA states are governed by their spatial proximity to IL-1β+ immune cells (mainly neutrophils and macrophages), which integrate signals from sympathetic neurons and immune cells to determine whether H6PD protein levels should be stabilized or degraded. Green arrows illustrate how BA-L cells are stabilized in a low-thermogenic state: IL-1β enhances the protein stability of H6PD in thermogenic adipocytes, thereby boosting the production of active glucocorticoids. Glucocorticoid activates the expression of its target RGS2, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and reduces cAMP production, thereby reducing UCP1 expression. Red arrows illustrate how BA-L cells switch into BA-H cells upon cold exposure: cold stimulation activates sympathetic neurons, which decrease local BAT IL-1β levels; lower IL-1β levels lead to H6PD protein degradation, turning BA-L into BA-H. The purple arrow illustrates that in aged individuals, IL-1β is elevated in BAT. High IL-1β levels persistently prevent H6PD degradation, desensitizing BAs’ cold response by locking them in BA-L states. Illustration created with BioRender; Wang, Q. https://BioRender.com/basqx8x (2026). b, Bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner governs thermogenic activity. We report that IL-1β-secreting immune cells, mainly neutrophils and macrophages, stabilize the surrounding BAs in a low-thermogenic state by preventing H6PD degradation; BAs farther from IL-1β+ cells are stabilized in a high-thermogenic state. Specifically, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells and boosts the production of active GC. GC then activates the expression of its target, RGS2, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reducing cAMP production and, in turn, UCP1 expression. This bistable regulation dynamically and precisely controls cellular heterogeneity in response to signalling from sympathetic nerves and the immune system, managing thermogenesis at the tissue level. Increased IL-1β levels in the BAT of aged individuals lock BAs in a low-thermogenic state, thereby lowering thermogenic activity and leading to cold intolerance. Illustration created with BioRender; Wang, Q. https://BioRender.com/mj195m9 (2026).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb.

“It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play,” McBurnie told BBC Scotland.

Recent findings suggest that “We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored. I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this UEFA Nations League B, Group 1 match as Slovenia host Scotland at Stozice Stadium in Ljubljana.

Scotland qualified for their first World Cup in 28 years this summer, but they exited the tournament with a whimper after failing to finish as one of the best third-place group sides. Steve Clarke’s men beat tournament debutants Haiti 1-0 in their opening match, before falling to defeats without scoring against Morocco and Brazil.

Following the World Cup, Clarke stepped down as Scotland’s head coach, ending a seven-year tenure, and was replaced by Belgian manager Sebastien Pocognoli. The former Monaco boss will take charge of his first game in his fresh role today and will be itching to make an encouraging start in a new era for Scottish football.

Over this extended international break, Pocognoli’s side will also face Switzerland and North Macedonia, as well as a return fixture against Slovenia in Scotland on October 6 to round off a busy period.

While Scotland took part in the World Cup, Slovenia were reflecting on their hugely disappointing qualification performance, where they finished third in their group behind Switzerland and Kosovo without winning and netting just three goals across six matches.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko – Slovenia’s star man and most well-known player – withdrew from Bostjan Cesar’s squad earlier this week after the recurrence of a shin injury caused the 23-year-old to completely miss the 1-1 draw against Fulham last Sunday.

Scotland have a few notable absences, with Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland all unavailable, but Billy Gilmour returns to the fold after missing the World Cup through injury, Oli McBurnie has been recalled and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure has received his first senior call-up.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

5 managers Blackburn Rovers must eye now after devastating Tony Mowbray news

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Just a couple of years after stepping down as the head coach of Birmingham City to battle bowel cancer, Mowbray has had to make the unfortunate decision to step down from his role as Blackburn boss due to health issues.
  • Mowbray issued a heartfelt message to Rovers supporters upon the announcement of his resignation, which can only be described as an incredibly difficult situation for everyone involved, as we at Football League World wish him the best.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tony Mowbray has stepped down as Blackburn Rovers head coach due to health issues, and the hunt for his replacement has begun at Ewood Park.

Just a couple of years after stepping down as the head coach of Birmingham City to battle bowel cancer, Mowbray has had to make the unfortunate decision to step down from his role as Blackburn boss due to health issues.

Mowbray issued a heartfelt message to Rovers supporters upon the announcement of his resignation, which can only be described as an incredibly difficult situation for everyone involved, as we at Football League World wish him the best.

Blackburn travel down the road to Burnley next for an enthralling encounter at Turf Moor, with Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds taking charge of first-team duties until a newly introduced head coach can be appointed.

As the hunt for a upcoming boss begins, FLW has taken a look at five potential candidates who could realistically assume control at Ewood Park next.

Former Irish forward Damien Duff began his coaching career with Shamrock Rovers in his native country before working as an assistant coach for both Celtic and the Republic of Ireland men's national team.

He took his first steps as a head coach with Shelbourne in 2021, spending three and a half years in charge of the club and guiding them to a first league title in 18 years in 2024.

Duff, who made 220 appearances for Blackburn during his playing career, more than any other club he represented, joined Keith Andrews' coaching staff at Brentford in the summer of 2026, but would surely be tempted by the Blackburn job.

Someone who knows the club inside and out and can seamlessly take the wheel from Mowbray, Duff could be an excellent fit for Blackburn, and simply must be considered.

Austrian coach Gerhard Struber began his career on the touchline in his native country with RB Salzburg, their feeder club, FC Liefering, before joining Wolfsberger and then Barnsley in November 2019.

He would help to keep the Tykes in the Championship in dramatic fashion before leaving Oakwell for the Substantial Apple with Latest York Red Bulls just 11 months later, as spells back in Salzburg and then FC Köln preceded his move to Bristol City in the summer of 2025.

After starting bright at Ashton Gate, things rapidly derailed, and he was dismissed in March 2026; he has been out of work since, and though likely not a standout candidate for the Blackburn job, he would certainly make for an interesting pick, to say the least.

A name that will be well-known to supporters of Middlesbrough, Nottingham Forest, and Birmingham City, Aitor Karanka is a fairly left-field suggestion, though his connection with Blackburn's current Head of Football Operations, Rudy Gestede, makes him an interesting candidate.

The Spaniard helped to guide Middlesbrough to the top flight in 2016, as spells with Forest, Birmingham, Granada, and Maccabi Tel Aviv followed, where he now works as a Director of Development for the Spanish national team, taking that role in 2025.

Whether he would be open to a return to management at this stage, especially in the Championship, remains to be seen, but his connection with Gestede during their time together with Boro makes him an interesting candidate.

Rob Edwards is a name that will be linked with almost all Championship jobs that become available until he eventually takes on another role, having been dismissed from his post at Wolverhampton Wanderers unexpectedly over the summer.

The Welshman has spent time in charge of the likes of Forest Green Rovers, Watford, Luton Town, Middlesbrough, and Wolves throughout his coaching career, helping to guide Luton to the Premier League in 2023, which remains his most notable achievement in the technical area at this stage.

Edwards reportedly turned down the opportunity to take the Burnley job over the summer, and should he decide that Ewood Park is his next destination, he will almost immediately have the backing of Rovers supporters for his previous decision to reject the Clarets.

Having taken charge of Luton in November 2022 before guiding them to the top flight, Edwards has the opportunity to do the same with Blackburn, and his name will surely be touted for the position.

What do you make of Mowbray's decision to step down? Who would you like to see in charge of Blackburn following this news? Share your thoughts below!

David Wagner is a name that will put a smile on the faces of many Huddersfield Town supporters, having guided the Terriers to a historic promotion to the Premier League in 2016 before keeping them up against the odds the following campaign.

The German, who was the best man to Jürgen Klopp at the former Liverpool boss' wedding, would spend time with Schalke and Young Boys after Huddersfield before landing at Norwich City in January 2023, helping the Canaries to the Championship play-offs in 2024 before missing out to Leeds United.

He left shortly after the defeat and has been an academy manager at RB Leipzig since 2025, but with an excellent record in the Championship, he would make an interesting candidate and one Blackburn must consider.

  • Martinez had questioned whether Carrick was backed enough in the summer and suggested the club needed changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Argentinian defender has also apologized to the United higher ups as well over his comments, as shared by Fabrizio Romano.

Lisandro Martinez has held discussions with Jason Wilcox and Michael Carrick after speaking out following United’s 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid.

Martinez had questioned whether Carrick was backed enough in the summer and suggested the club needed changes.

Fabrizio Romano has now confirmed that United consider the matter resolved for now and expect Martinez to remain available for selection.

Speaking about the situation on his YouTube channel, as quoted by Football 365, Romano explained why Martinez’s comments caused concern inside the club.

Industry observers note that “He spoke very strongly after the game against Atletico Madrid, which Man Utd lost. It was a very negative moment for the Red Devils. We know that Licha was very strong in his comments. He said that Michael Carrick was not backed enough during the summer transfer window.”.

Romano added that Martinez had spoken directly to those at the club after the incident.

“Licha apologised to Man Utd as a club. He spoke to the directors, he spoke to Jason Wilcox, and he spoke to Michael Carrick, who was also involved in this conversation.”.

Recent findings suggest that “So, the underlying message remains the same. Lisandro is apologising for the way he expressed himself after a game during a difficult moment for Man Utd, but there was a discussion about the substance of what he stated.”.

Sources indicate that romano also revealed that United had imposed a financial penalty on the centre-back. However, the punishment does not appear to involve removing him from the squad.

“According to the information available tonight, Lisandro Martinez has been fined.”.

He added that Martinez is expected to return to the squad as normal, with the fine considered sufficient punishment for the incident.

Recent findings suggest that “The internal discussion also helped to resolve all the concerns. For Man Utd, the case is closed.”.

That should bring some immediate clarity to the situation, although questions remain about how the episode could affect Martinez’s longer-term position at Old Trafford.

Romano also pointed towards Martinez’s contract, which expires next summer, with United holding an option to extend it.

“So, let’s see what is going to happen there. For sure, this is the kind of situation that will have an impact on the situation surrounding Lisandro, but we have to see what happens next in terms of future transfers and everything else.”.

Lisandro Martinez could return to Manchester United’s starting line-up against Leeds United this weekend, with the defender reportedly available for selection after the controversy surrounding his comments about the club’s summer transfer business.

According to recent reports, TEAMtalk transfer insider Graeme Bailey has suggested Michael Carrick could bring the Argentine straight back into the team for the trip to Elland Road. The fixture is expected to be a hostile occasion, making Martinez’s potential involvement an interesting one.

“I am told that Martinez is available for selection this weekend, and there is every chance Michael Carrick starts him,” Bailey said.

The defender recently found himself in trouble after questioning whether Manchester United had done enough in the summer transfer window. He apologised to the club’s hierarchy and was fined, but the incident has not apparently created a divide between him and the manager.

Bailey also dismissed suggestions that Martinez’s comments were an attack on Michael Carrick, insisting the defender and his teammates continue to support the head coach.

Recent findings suggest that “Martinez was not critical of Carrick – far from it. This isn’t a repeat of something like Mo Salah criticising Arne Slot last season. It is almost the opposite.”.

Sources indicate that according to Bailey, the United dressing room remains firmly behind Carrick despite the team’s disappointing start to the campaign. Senior players reportedly believe the current manager is still the right person to lead the team, rather than bringing in another face to replace him.

It has been revealed that “Martinez and the squad are 100% behind Carrick. They know there is pressure after a poor start to the season, but they do not want to see a change.”.

Bailey went on to suggest that the fallout may have strengthened the bond between the players and their manager.

“Martinez and the senior players firmly believe nobody can come in and do a better job than Carrick. If anything, this has brought the group closer together.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swansea City fans were rocked by the news on Monday night that Vitor Matos was being looked at by Ligue 1 club Strasbourg, with pressure mounting on current manager Hugo Oliveira.

The Portuguese boss was recently linked with the Crystal Palace post, but after Swansea's form dipped with four defeats in five, and the Eagles appointed Thomas Frank to replace Pierre Sage, Swans supporters felt they'd be able to appreciate Matos a little longer.

Strasbourg's official approach to Matos indicates that the drop in form in the league hasn't impacted his standing amongst managerial circles, and the Ligue 1 side, who are sitting 13th with just three wins from 10, are keen on bringing him in if they pull the trigger on Oliveira.

It's not an ideal scenario for any club to be in, but after a strong start to the Championship campaign, with the South Wales side sitting sixth after 15 games, Swansea will need to act fast to bring someone fresh in if Matos decides to leave.

These four coaches should be in line to take the reins.

With Swansea's recruitment drive shifting to more of a project-based outcome in the summer, following their partnership with Tony Bloom-led Jamestown Analytics, there could be a more project-heavy hire in the dugout if Matos departs.

However, if the Swans want to keep the momentum from the first 15 games high and hire someone set to continue this promotion push immediately, Carlos Corberan should be right at the top of their list.

The Spaniard has been out of work since leaving Valencia in September. He's helped his boyhood club improve after slow starts and secure a mid-table finish in 2024/25 and 2025/26, and in the Championship, he forged a reputation as one of the better coaches in the division with both Huddersfield Town and West Brom.

Corberan took both of those to the play-offs, despite them being rather worse for wear beforehand, and at the Hawthorns, especially, had his sides playing some of the best football in the division, per the underlying numbers.

There's still plenty of room to improve in this Swansea squad, despite their position, and Corberan could be the missing piece to do so. Plus, the 43-year-old could finally become a Premier League boss in South Wales, something which has eluded him so far in his career.

Perhaps not the most popular choice among the four, but Steve Cooper was the last manager to oversee something close to a successful period at Swansea, finishing in the top six in consecutive seasons between 2019 and 2021.

According to recent reports, since then, the Swans haven't finished any higher than 10th. No parachute payments have helped, but perhaps the numerous changes in managers haven't either.

Recent findings suggest that swansea fans weren't totally enamoured with the football being played; others were totally fine with it. What's crucial, though, is that it brought about results at this level, and for a Swans side who want to maintain this play-off finish, bringing in someone who hasn't finished below the top six at this level wouldn't be a bad decision.

Cooper knows how to come in midway through a campaign and oversee results, too, having taken Nottingham Forest from the bottom of the division to play-off success in the space of eight months.

The task isn't as drastic back in South Wales, so he should be able to achieve some success.

In Matos, Swansea found success with a young, up-and-coming coach from a foreign league. Perhaps they could do so again, but this time with a name they know all too well from his time as a player in South Wales.

What Pablo Hernandez is doing in his first managerial role with boyhood club Castellón in the Spanish second tier is massively going under the radar.

He took over as interim boss in September last year, oversaw their best finish in nearly 20 years, and now has them second with nine wins in 13 games. They've conceded just five goals, which is quite remarkable, and they could be on their way to La Liga for the first time since the 1990/91 campaign.

The 41-year-old already has that connection with Swansea, spending two seasons there as a player and helping them win the EFL Cup in 2013, so he knows what it's like for the South Wales side to be in the top flight and competing regularly.

It may be difficult to persuade him to leave this project at his boyhood club, but the possibility of helping bring a team back to the Premier League could be tempting enough.

Another project-based manager could see Jack Wilshere make the step-up into the Championship after a year cutting his teeth in League One with Luton Town.

It has been revealed that the 34-year-old was unable to help the Hatters earn promotion in his first half-season in charge, but his side did show signs of excellence in the latter stages once things started to properly click. Luton went 12 games unbeaten to end the year, winning the EFL Trophy along the way.

Recent findings suggest that who do you think should replace Vitor Matos if he leaves for Strasbourg, Swans fans? Let us know in the comments.

Now, this season, Wilshere has his side playing good football; the underlying numbers have them among the best teams in the division, and they currently sit fourth, five points off Stockport County in second and with a game in hand.

Swansea haven't shied away from hiring out of the third tier. They did so with Russell Martin in the summer of 2021, and that came after he'd overseen mid-table finishes at MK Dons.

Wilshere is in a much better position as a manager now, and is one of the more promising young coaches in the EFL. He has Championship potential, and Swansea could be the side to harness that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Daniele De Rossi has looked back at Genoa’s defeat to AC Milan and how he wasn’t frustrated with his team afterwards.

Recent findings suggest that milan entered the international break with a much-needed victory against Genoa, but it wasn’t the easiest result of the season. After a disappointing defeat to Ferencvaros – which extended the midweek run of defeats – they couldn’t afford to drop points, and they succeeded, even if it wasn’t without flaw.

Recent findings suggest that with two goals inside 20 minutes, you’d be forgiven for expecting Milan to win by more than a couple. However, that was the end of their goalscoring for the afternoon and although Genoa pulled one back, they didn’t grab more than a consolation goal.

Speaking to Sky Sport – in the latest series ‘Radici’ – De Rossi looked back on the defeat to the Rossoneri, as well as a comment that stuck with him from Diego Moreira, as MilanPress have relayed today.

We indeed lost against Milan, but we lost ‘well.’ We didn’t deserve it. Three or four weeks ago, the latest results seemed like a pipe dream. I thank the players, staff, and my club for giving me faith and patience at a time when other clubs wouldn’t have had it.

“They remembered how good we did last year. I’m happy to have emerged from a difficult period and to be Genoa’s coach; I’m really happy there.”.

Industry observers note that “I’m passionate about the fans and the supporters. I’m part of a club that, in terms of fan base, is among the best in Europe. I’m passionate; I don’t punch a clock. I spend two hours with the stockman or the waitress with the same enthusiasm I spend time with the team captain. Experiencing it like that, you realise that Genoa is a great team.

“Genoa is full of Genoese fans who remind you every second how much they love their club, the pride of being the top club in Italy. The architecture of the stadium and the warmth of the fans… I’m not saying this to be a sycophant, but on Sunday Moreira came to me and mentioned, ‘I’ve never seen anything like this here in Italy.’ It’s a reality that even our opponents notice.”.

Don Goodman delivers brutal Bolton Wanderers warning

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bolton Wanderers have had a rollercoaster first third of the campaign upon their return to the Championship, and though the Trotters have impressed at the top end of the pitch, a lot has been left to desire at the back.

Bolton, following their return to the Championship for the first time since 2019, endured an incredibly busy summer transfer window orchestrated by head coach Steven Schumacher, with as many as 13 fresh arrivals heading to the Toughsheet Community Stadium.

Among those was an almost entirely newly introduced forward line, as the likes of Jayden Nelson, Ryan Hardie, Thelonius Bair, Kylianne Dong, and Samuel Iling-Junior joined the club.

Sources indicate that bolton have hit 20 goals in 15 league matches so far - a steady record. However, with 29 shipped in the other direction, improvements must be made at the back, as an EFL expert has shared their thoughts on the situation.

Former West Bromwich Albion, Sunderland, and Wolverhampton Wanderers striker Don Goodman has delved into punditry since his retirement from professional football, and has garnered a reputation as an expert on everything in the EFL.

The 60-year-old is not afraid to say exactly what he thinks about the ongoing situations at clubs across the 72, and has shared his thoughts and concerns right now at Bolton, saying: "If you go to watch Bolton Wanderers, you know you're in for a terrific match.

They have been all season. They're a great watch.

"I suspect Steven Schumacher wants them to be entertaining, but here's the issue. They are conceding way too many goals. That will prove costly over a 46-game season.

"They've conceded 29 goals in 15 games. That's almost two goals a game. It means you have to score three goals to win a match. That might happen occasionally, like when they won 4–3 away at Norwich, but it's rare you can rely on scoring three every week.

"They have to become harder to score against. If they don't, I fear they could end up straight back in League One. They're great fun to watch, but they must tighten up defensively.".

Only the bottom three of Preston North End, Burnley, and Derby County have shipped more goals than Bolton at this stage of the season, as it has become crystal clear exactly where Steven Schumacher's side needs to address if they are to be successful this year.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Published: 17:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:03 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • Amid the clamour for a change at the helm following another poor showing at a major tournament, it was easy to lose sight of the reality of the situation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:03 EST, 14 November 2026.

Amid the clamour for a change at the helm following another poor showing at a major tournament, it was easy to lose sight of the reality of the situation.

Steve Clarke didn’t crash and burn in the US because a raft of world-class talents failed to turn up on the biggest stage. It happened primarily because a limited squad was unable to outperform two top-ten nations in Brazil and Morocco who could call upon infinitely superior footballers.

Sebastian Pocognoli has since arrived on the scene having earned a stellar reputation from his title success with Union Saint-Gilloise and his less feted spell at Monaco. But he has not come armed with a magic wand.

In opening the door to a string of fresh faces and advocating the more attacking approach which so many craved, the turbulence he’s experienced to date should only have been expected.

Limited by both the standard of players who are eligible for Scotland and the time he has to work with them, only the blissfully naïve would have seen his appointment as a quick fix.

While there were some positives to be taken from the game with North Macedonia – primarily the result – it’s likely the nation will have to endure more short-term pain for long-term gain.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets his players after a satisfactory evening at Hampden.

This was always going to take time, perhaps, in the view of John McGinn, more than many may have imagined.

Sources indicate that ‘The manager’s got a great reputation, a good record at both places he’s been,’ said the Aston Villa captain. ‘The most key thing now in football is individuals don’t win you games. It’s unity, teamwork and everyone being on the same page.

It has been revealed that ‘You see how successful clubs and successful countries do it. And we want to be one of them.

‘It’s not going to happen overnight. There’s a lot to learn but we did create significant chances against North Macedonia where we could have scored three, four or five and it could be a different story.

Sources indicate that ‘But this isn’t something that gets fixed in March or even next September. It will start to build over the next 18 months.’.

Sources indicate that if that predicted time frame might raise an eyebrow or two, McGinn makes no apology for it. Call it managing expectations from the midfielder if you please. But without a degree of patience from the Tartan Army, he feels Pocognoli’s ideas won’t take root.

‘I understand it’s frustrating,’ he added. ‘It’s freezing and you want to see four, five, six goals, but the balance has got to be there.

McGinn sends his penalty home to give Scotland a deserved lead against North Macedonia.

‘They’re entitled to their opinion, but there’s got to be a mixture of patience.

‘The supporters are entitled to say whatever they like. But just as long as they hurl anything they want to shout at the experienced boys and just let the young ones flourish and try and settle into the team.’.

Sources indicate that give credit where it’s due. With Clarke accused of causing stagnation by selecting the same old faces, Pocognoli has capped five players for the first time while recalling the likes of Oli McBurnie.

The sages in the stands can’t have it both ways. If the squad was going to evolve, it was never going to be a smooth ride.

Industry observers note that ‘I think the young players are starting to show more now,’ McGinn stressed. ‘Luke Graham on Friday night, I thought he was brilliant. It’s not easy playing in the middle of a back three. He’s been waiting for his chance and the manager’s shown that if you deserve your chance you’re going to get put in there.

Industry observers note that ‘We’ve got so many players that can step up and they will. We just need to show that belief and take it to the pitch.’.

Even in victory, McGinn doesn’t dispute that there is significant scope for improvement. He’s convinced, however, that this will all come good in the end.

McGinn insists it's vital the entire Scotland squad buy into the methods of manager Pocognoli.

According to recent reports, ‘We need to play slightly better,’ he said. ‘We know that, but we’re going through a period which I’ve been used to at club level, a lot of changes, a lot of detail that we need to try and remember and get used to.

‘And it’s about sticking at it. We’re keen to play a style of football that’s not easy but is going to get bums off seats. It’s important that everyone believes in it because if one person drops off or doesn’t believe in it, that’s when it all starts to fall apart.’.

Industry observers note that friday was another memorable night on a personal level for McGinn. Having broken the tension with the opener only to see North Macedonia level, he held his nerve to put Scotland back from the penalty spot.

The brace put him on 24 international goals, now within six of Denis Law and Kenny Dalglish. But all of that is for another day.

It has been revealed that ‘It feels a bit strange, but at the minute that’s gone to the back burner,’ he stressed. ‘I had a wee chat with Scott (McTominay) about the penalties. I was designated penalty taker but, to be fair, he’s not missed one I don’t think in his career.

‘So, we had a wee chat and I think we both mentioned the most key thing was just no matter who hit it, hit the back of the net.’.

McGinn is eyeing three points against Switzerland in St Gallen to close the campaign on a high.

Recent findings suggest that tomorrow, the equation is clear. To finish second in the Nations League group and secure a place in pot two for the Euro draw, Scotland must beat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t beat North Macedonia.

Even if everything clicks for Pocognoli’s side, it will be the tallest of orders.

‘Difficult,’ remarked McGinn. ‘I know they drew on Friday night (with Slovenia) but they’ve got a couple of players back that they were missing last time.

Industry observers note that ‘It is a tough one but we want to be competing against these teams away from home. It’s not going to be perfect for a while, but we’ll stick at it.’.
