📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A York City star could be facing the threat of potential jail time for a shock incident that actually occurred on the pitch - and it's causing quite the reaction as a controversial legal battle begins to gather pace.

York finally ended their ten-year exile from the EFL in emphatic fashion at the end of the previous campaign by finishing at the summit of the National League table on 108 points and just two clear of second-placed Rochdale, who would resort to gaining promotion through the play-offs following a dramatic final-day clash for the ages between the two sides.

With the league title on the line for the victors, the encounter played out on a knife-edge at the Crown Oil Arena and 95 minutes of football were played before the deadline was broken when Emmanuel Dierseruvwe appeared to have won the contest for the hosts when he struck past York's Harrison Male.

The Ministermen only needed a point from proceedings, though, and capped off one of English football's most pulsating final-day showdowns after Josh Stones buried an all-important equaliser in the last kick of the game to shatter Rochdale hearts and take the fifth-tier title back to Yorkshire instead.

However, a major flashpoint emerged prior to Stones' leveller in the wake of Dieseruvwe's opening strike, which led Rochdale supporters to believe that they had won the affair in the very closing stages.

Dale fans promptly stormed the pitch in celebration, and in all the commotion, one of York's promotion heroes in Hiram Boateng appeared to have been pushed to the ground before retaliating in a manner that now leaves the midfielder shrouded in legal trouble.

Widely-shared social media footage at the time revealed Boateng on the floor in the wake of Rochdale's goal, with the 30-year-old having seemingly been pushed over and subsequently goaded by celebrating supporters - and pinned down on the floor, too, it has been claimed.

The scenes were unsavory to say the least, as Rochdale fans invaded the pitch to taunt and antagonise York players despite the game still having numerous minutes of additional time to be played out.

As stewards acted to break up the fracas, Boateng responded by punching a home fan, who promptly fell to the floor himself.

It was promptly disclosed afterwards that the FA would be investigating the matter, and proceedings have now been taken up a notch.

That's because a fresh report published by The Sun on Monday evening has revealed that Boateng, who has made just four appearances for Scott Lindsey's side in League Two so far this season, could face jail after being charged with a criminal offence.

The investigation has been taken to court, where Boateng has been charged with using threatening, abusive or insulting behavior with intent to cause fear of or provoke violence.

It's stated that the Crystal Palace academy product's case was heard with no pleas on Monday morning at Manchester magistrates' court, with the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) confirming the charges brought against the player in question.

Whether Boateng will actually spend time behind bars remains to be seen, of course, but the legal battle remains at large and it's caused quite the reaction from the many backers he has in his corner at York.

The former Exeter City and MK Dons star has retained the full backing of everybody at the LNER Community Stadium since the altercation, and club chairman Matt Uggla is among those to have spoken out in support of the popular midfielder.

Boateng, having joined York in the summer of 2025 following his departure from League One outfit Mansfield Town, played a leading role in the Ministermen's successful title charge during his debut campaign and has barely kicked a ball in anger this time around, with injuries limiting the well-travelled midfielder to just two fourth-tier starts.

Ironically, however, York faced Rochdale for the first time since the promotion-defining battle back in April, and with the fixture having been carried out in Greater Manchester, Lindsey's side would come out on top when Ollie Pearce scored the only goal of the game after 56 minutes, and Boateng himself was in the starting lineup.

Now, with the investigation against Boateng beginning to intensify following fresh developments, Uggla has responded to show his support and dismay at the charges being brought against the City starlet.

Speaking via his X account yesterday evening, Uggla wrote: "A fan runs onto the pitch to deliberately antagonise a player, yet it's Hiram who ends up facing a criminal charge.

"Where's the accountability for the person who invaded the pitch and provoked the situation? Absolutely ridiculous.

Uggla, of course, is far from the only figurehead to reserve strong backing for Boateng, who many believe was firmly within his right to retaliate after Rochdale supporters had committed a criminal offense in the first place by invading the field of play to antagonise opposition players.

Echoing the school of thought of many, this one fan called for the case to simply be thrown out of court in argument of injustice towards Boateng.

Another referred to the situation as "scandalous", citing the inarguable fact that one person had the right to be on the pitch and the other simply did not.

Indeed, the case has prompted cries for an enhanced systemic approach towards player safety and welfare in which greater protection and prevention from such events is provided, with several fans asking why the Dale supporter has not been identified and publicised for their own offences.

An Oldham Athletic supporter, meanwhile, has called for the fan to feel the same legal repercussions in an impassioned rant.

Whether or not Boateng was right for hitting out a fan has been hotly-debated online - and will be in the courts, of course - but this punter feels as though the midfield man did nothing wrong in the first place and the pitch-invader received just what they deserved in an act of "self defence" from York's promotion-winner.

However, not everybody has spoken in defence and support of Boateng.

It's clearly the general consensus, though others have argued that Boateng did not need to retailiate in such a fashion.

What do you make of the case? Was Hiram Boateng in the right here and should the York City midfielder's actions go unpunished, or does he deserve the legal charges? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

Rather interestingly, one York fan hopped over the other side of the fence and, in a claim that has not gone down too well among the City faithful, explained how Boateng's punch was unnecessary in spite of the wrongs of the aggravating supporter.

Whereas some Rochdale fans have slammed the behaviour of one of their own, others have taken a less-sympathetic stance towards Boateng and believe that his actions - regardless of whether the supporter was right to be on the pitch or not - cannot be allowed to go unpunished.

It's a controversial old case, and the direction of its travel will only be determined in due course.

For now, at least, all York supporters and power-brokers alike will intend on doing is continuing to defend the well-liked midfielder against the charges, which the overwhelming majority believe to be unjustified in light of what led to his actions.

Rio Ferdinand has admitted he is disappointed that Manchester United failed to sign Ayyoub Bouaddi, with the highly-rated midfielder now making an impression at Manchester City.

Manchester City beat several rivals to secure Bouaddi’s signature over the summer in a deal worth £86 million. The Morocco international became the Premier League’s most expensive teenager, and Rio Ferdinand believes Manchester United missed out on a special talent.

The former United defender was particularly impressed by Bouaddi’s second-half cameo during City’s Champions League defeat to Paris Saint-Germain last week. His performance reminded Rio Ferdinand why he had been talking about the youngster throughout the previous year and during the summer transfer window.

Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ferdinand highlighted how Bouaddi was the highlight of the game against PSG and who they missed.

“He came on and showed PSG that they may have missed out on someone who was on their doorstep when he was playing in France,” Ferdinand said.

The former England international also confirmed that Manchester United had been interested in bringing the midfielder to Old Trafford, but the transfer fee was too expensive.

“Manchester United were in for him, 100%, but the fee was just too much,” he added.

Ferdinand was left frustrated by what he saw from the teenager, who turned 19 this month.

“Just that little cameo against PSG makes you go, ‘oh, I can’t believe we missed out on that. I can’t believe it.’ I’m so gutted, so gutted. He’s bad! He’s so calm under pressure.”.

Rio Ferdinand suggested Bouaddi’s quality could soon make the midfield position in a packed Manchester City his regular role.

City already have Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez among their midfield options, but Ferdinand believes Bouaddi has the ability to stand out alongside them.

“They’ve got Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez in that midfield as well but this kid could be the best of the three, easily.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham United have had quite a rocky introduction to life back in the Championship, sitting outside the play-offs completely after 15 games.

The Hammers came down to the second tier with some of the best individuals that the division has ever seen, and they've proven their quality going forward, with their 37 goals an EFL best and a couple of six-goal hauls already.

It has been revealed that however, there are some concerns about the overall balance of the side and a lack of a strong spine in the squad. Scott Parker has replaced Nuno Espírito Santo to try and fix that, and the international break couldn't have come at a better time to try and implement an identity.

The upcoming January transfer window can help with that, too, with a focus on bringing in players who can make a long-term impact in the side, both in the rest of this season and then in what is hoped to be Premier League campaigns in the future.

Industry observers note that with 2026 drawing to a close, fans across the EFL are starting to think about what an ideal transfer window would look like in January. For West Ham, FLW's Hammers fan pundit, Ryan Horn, wants to see the spine of the midfield fixed.

West Ham broke the Championship transfer record by signing midfielder Arne Engels from Celtic for £22 million, but in terms of out-and-out defensive options, they don't have many available.

Tomas Soucek is still on his way back to full fitness, but he turns 32 in February, while Edson Alvarez hasn't been seen all season and, up until Parker's first game in charge at Cardiff City, neither had Soungoutou Magassa.

"Hopefully, by the time January comes, we'll be a lot closer to the top of the table, but there is a midfielder I'd really like us to sign, who'd solve all our challenges," Horn noted.

Recent findings suggest that "With the future of Magassa and Alvarez in doubt at the moment, and with Soucek only just coming back from injury and getting on a bit in age, our midfield is lacking. There's this young midfielder I really like called Luca Weinhandl, who plays in the Austrian Bundesliga for Sturm Graz.".

Recent findings suggest that 2009-born Weinhandl has been one of the key parts of Fabio Ingolitsch's side since he took charge on January 1st this year. The 17-year-old was handed his debut by the current boss, and this season, he's been one of their most consistent players.

He's started all but one league game for Sturm Graz, and all but one in their Europa League campaign, too, assisting in their 1-0 win over Marseille last month.

"He's 17, six-foot-three and doing brilliant there," Horn continued. "He'd just be one of those sort of niche signings that clubs such as Brighton and Brentford pick up out of nowhere and turn into £70 million, £80 million players.

"Bournemouth are buying players for good money now, but they, like Brighton, are competing at the top and in Europe, while Brentford have had a lot of good seasons in the Premier League now.

"But it's the modern-day football approach, and one that West Ham need to take. Weinhandl would be that kind of player.".

With Weinhandl not turning 18 until mid-January, he has the entirety of his career ahead of him. If he continues on his current path, he could end up playing right at the top of the game.

The midfielder is one of the tougher-tackling engine room men in the Austrian Bundesliga this season, winning the most duels in the division and sitting inside the top 13% of defensive midfielders for tackles won, according to FotMob.

However, he's also right near the top for the number of dribbles he's completed and the number of fouls he's won. He has plenty of strings to his bow already, and could be a vital player in the future of any football club. Horn hopes it's with West Ham.

"He could form a solid spine next to Engels, or Kante and Magassa in front of him and be a key part of it for years to come, and then we don't have to worry about our midfield every single year," the fan pundit continued.

"Last year it was overrun, then we sold Potts, and this year, we have key players who have first-team and Champions League experience not being picked because of off-field challenges.

Recent findings suggest that "Having a younger player coming in, under Parker and [Mark] Noble, as well as Soucek, [Jarrod] Bowen and other experienced players, it'd be a dream. He's definitely one I'd sign. I don't think we will, but that's my realistic pick.".

While Weinhandl would be a brilliant pickup for any English side looking to grow and develop a young midfielder, the 17-year-old may already have too much potential to be signed by a team in the Championship.

Murmurs in mid-September had the Australian linked with moves to Aston Villa, Brighton and Arsenal, so if he did move to the second-tier, it may be via a loan move after being signed by a side further up the pyramid.

It has been revealed that do you think Luca Weinhandl has the Premier League in his future? Let us know in the comments.

Weinhandl isn't as much of a hidden gem anymore, having been called up to the Austrian senior squad for the first time for the ongoing break. Ralf Rangnick opted not to debut him against the Republic of Ireland, but could do so on Tuesday night against Israel.

The 17-year-old is a Graz native, too, and growing up through the academy to become a club legend there could appeal to him and seeing a possible move from a side like West Ham seem impossible.

He's definitely one to watch, and it wouldn't be a surprise to see him in the Premier League in the future, but for now, the Hammers may find it difficult to tempt this wonderkid over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michael Carrick has come under immense pressure as a disjointed Manchester United sit just two places above the relegation places.

Despite the scrutiny and the news of a possible sacking, Michael Carrick has been given another chance at Manchester United.

Michael Carrick will remain in charge of Manchester United for their Premier League trip to Chelsea on Saturday after the club decided to give their under-pressure head coach another opportunity to turn things around.

United have gone eight games without a win in all competitions, with Sunday’s humiliating 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth leaving them 16th in the Premier League table, just one point above the relegation zone.

Carrick’s position looked increasingly uncertain after the Bournemouth loss. As a result, United chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox were at Carrington on Monday to discuss the situation.

It has been reported by Sky Sports that United have considered other options internally as well to replace Micahel Carrick but for the weekend, they are sticking with Michael Carrick.

Carrick took training on Tuesday and the decision means he has at least one more match to convince the club’s hierarchy that he can get United back on track.

Gary Neville admitted he was surprised that Carrick had survived the immediate threat of losing his job, although he welcomed the decision.

“I am surprised, but I am happy because I was absolutely certain that what I witnessed on Sunday would be the end of Michael,” Neville mentioned in Sky Sports.

The former United captain explained that Carrick’s actions after the Bournemouth defeat had made him think the manager was preparing to say goodbye to the supporters.

“It looked like he was walking round at the end on his own with the players behind him, like it was almost a goodbye lap,” Neville added.

Fans continued singing the manager’s name after the final whistle, while the rest of the team drew boos.

Despite his surprise, Gary Neville hopes Micahel Carrick can use the extra time to get a response from his squad.

“I hope he can somehow get those players to start playing for him again because they haven’t played for him in the last few weeks,” he said.

The trip to Chelsea now becomes a crucial test for Micahel Carrick but United need a result and a far better performance to ease the pressure at Old Trafford.

Chelsea Could Claim Share of £164m Compensation

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readchelsea

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, chelsea fans have followed Manchester City’s financial rules case for years.
  • Recent findings suggest that reports now suggest an independent panel has reached a decision.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Premier League charged Manchester City with 115 alleged breaches of financial regulations in February 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, chelsea fans have followed Manchester City’s financial rules case for years. Everyone at Stamford Bridge knows a guilty verdict could cost City serious money, and much of it could end up with rivals lower down the table.

Recent findings suggest that reports now suggest an independent panel has reached a decision. If that holds up, the scale of any Chelsea Manchester City compensation payout could run into tens of millions of pounds for the Blues alone.

Recent findings suggest that the Premier League charged Manchester City with 115 alleged breaches of financial regulations in February 2023. That followed a four-year investigation into the club’s accounts. The case has hung over the competition ever since. Every top-flight club knows the outcome could change how recent Premier League seasons are remembered.

This matters directly to Chelsea. If City are found to have broken spending and disclosure rules, clubs who finished below them could argue they lost out on prize money and European qualification. Chelsea have competed directly with City for top four places and cup competitions throughout that period.

In a recent development, according to The Athletic, Manchester City were found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges by the independent panel. The Premier League has not confirmed the verdict or issued a statement.

Manchester City have not accepted any suggestion of guilt. The club released a statement addressing the ongoing process directly.

Industry observers note that “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023. ‘The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.'”.

That statement makes clear the club does not see the case as settled. Until the Premier League confirms a result, the reported verdict will linger on for official sentencing.

According to recent reports, data specialists at OLBG have estimated the potential Chelsea Manchester City compensation windfall if City are found guilty. They believe City could owe domestic rivals well over £500m in lost Premier League prize money if the charges are proven.

According to recent reports, within that total, London clubs are remarked to be due around £164m between them. Chelsea, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur are among the clubs who could be entitled to a share. Other Premier League sides could benefit too, depending on where they finished compared with City in the seasons in question.

Industry observers note that prize money in the Premier League is tied closely to league position. If City gained points unfairly, that would have pushed a rival down the table and cost them money too. That is the basis for the OLBG figures, and it explains why the sums involved are so large.

In a recent development, for Chelsea, even a share of that £164m pot would be a big boost. It could help fund fresh signings, or simply ease the pressure around the kind of transfer valuations at Stamford Bridge the club faces every window.

Industry observers note that city chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak has already made clear the case is far from finished. He described the process as having “a long way to run.” That points to appeals and further legal steps, whatever the panel has decided.

According to recent reports, chelsea, for their part, carry on with life under Xabi Alonso regardless of how the case unfolds. Attention stays on squad rotation and Xabi Alonso’s squad management strategy, not on any potential windfall. The financial case will not change anything on the pitch in the short term.

According to recent reports, the Premier League has stayed silent on the reported verdict, and confidentiality remains strict around the process, according to reports from Football.London. Chelsea fans should expect a long wait before any compensation, if it comes at all, reaches the club’s accounts.

#14702. Tech Report: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion

Tech Report: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 38 min read (7530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~38 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9.
  • The increasing integration of renewable energy calls for sustainable electrochemical energy storage systems beyond lithium-ion batteries1.
  • Industry observers note that the crux of iodine conversion chemistry lies in interfacial reactions, where electrolyte composition and interfacial microenvironment govern reaction pathways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

The increasing integration of renewable energy calls for sustainable electrochemical energy storage systems beyond lithium-ion batteries1. Aqueous metal–iodine batteries offer a promising platform for large-scale energy storage by combining earth-abundant electrode materials, aqueous electrolytes and conversion-type iodine chemistry2,3. Unlike intercalation-type positive electrodes, iodine positive electrodes store charge by reversible valence-state changes, offering access to multi-electron redox chemistry with increased capacity and redox potential4. Most studies have focused on the two-electron I−/I0 redox couple, with a theoretical capacity of 211 mAh g−1 at a redox potential of 0.54 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode10. Extending iodine conversion to the successive I−/I0/I+ redox couples doubles the theoretical capacity to 422 mAh g−1 while introducing the I0/I+ redox process at a higher redox potential of 1.07 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode11. However, despite this potential, achieving reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous environments remains a fundamental challenge3,7.

Industry observers note that the crux of iodine conversion chemistry lies in interfacial reactions, where electrolyte composition and interfacial microenvironment govern reaction pathways. Electron-deficient I+ is strongly electrophilic and susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water, resulting in hydrolysis and poor reversibility in aqueous environments9,12. Previous studies have achieved four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries by stabilizing reactive I+ through interhalogen complexes (for example, ICl2 or IBr2) in highly concentrated chloride- or bromide-containing electrolytes5,6,13. In these systems, electrophilic I+ coordinates with two nucleophilic halide ions (Cl− or Br−) through non-covalent interactions8,14. However, at water-enriched interfaces, hydration of nucleophilic species (Nuc) competes with these interactions and destabilizes I+ complexes (Fig. 1a). Highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes mitigate this competition by reducing water activity and increasing halide availability, but their high salt contents and corrosivity constrain broader implementation (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1), necessitating new electrolyte chemistry and a mechanistic framework that move beyond reliance on halogen-containing electrolytes and conventional interhalogen stabilization5,8.

a, The mechanism of the competition between halogen bond and hydrogen bond. b, The conventional interhalogen stabilization mechanism in highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes. c, The KA–PA–Nuc framework levering anionic chemistry and halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free electrolytes. IHP, inner Helmholtz plane; OHP, outer Helmholtz plane.

Given the competition between I+ stabilization and hydration at water-enriched interfaces, overcoming this challenge requires simultaneous regulation of the interfacial environment and water–Nuc interactions. Anionic chemistry offers a powerful lever to coordinate these interfacial and molecular interactions15,16,17,18. Herein we establish a kosmotropic anion (KA)–polar anion (PA)–Nuc electrolyte framework for reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes (Fig. 1c). Systematic experiments and theoretical calculations reveal how the synergistic effects of PAs and KAs coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, thereby stabilizing interfacial electrochemical behaviour and promoting reversible four-electron iodine conversion. The applicability of this electrolyte framework is demonstrated across four halogen-free Nuc (urea, acetamide, pyridine and nicotinamide) and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Beyond establishing a halogen-free electrolyte chemistry, this work reveals how electrolyte chemistry governs iodine conversion across interfacial, molecular and electrochemical scales, providing a mechanistic basis for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

Stabilizing I+ against hydrolysis is essential for reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous electrolytes. Previous studies have relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes for interhalogen stabilization19,20, whereas more recent studies have explored specific additive-halogen nucleophilic substitution reactions21,22. These approaches primarily address I+ stabilization through specific molecular interactions, whereas how electrolyte chemistry collectively regulates the interfacial microenvironment, molecular stabilization and the resulting iodine conversion pathways remains less understood. This work establishes a mechanistic framework that integrates anionic chemistry with halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, strong PAs establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interface, whereas KAs weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding to facilitate halogen-bond stabilization of I+. These complementary effects underpin the halogen-free KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, whose composition was subsequently optimized (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4) and exhibits sufficient electrochemical stability (Supplementary Fig. 5) for four-electron iodine conversion.

a, Molecular interplay governed by anionic chemistry and halogen bonding. b, Cyclic voltammetry profiles of iodine conversion reaction using urea as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. c, Cyclic voltammetry profiles using acetamide as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. d, Cyclic voltammetry profiles using nicotinamide as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. e–g, Corresponding GCD profiles for b–d at 1 A g−1, respectively. All electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2.

Industry observers note that the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework was validated in aqueous Zn–I2 batteries across four different Nuc (Supplementary Fig. 6). Electron-deficient I+ can interact with two electron-rich Nuc molecules to form linear Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. These halogen bonds provide the molecular basis for I+ stabilization, as supported by Nuc-free controls, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and theoretical calculations23 (Supplementary Figs. 7–11). Using urea (U) as a representative Nuc, KA–U exhibits only the I−/I0 redox process, whereas PA–U enables further I0/I+ oxidation but with poor reversibility (Fig. 2b,e). The excessive capacity at the second charge plateau is attributed to irreversible iodine oxidation coupled with parasitic water oxidation (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). Combining KA and PA in KA–PA–U produces two reversible redox peaks and corresponding charge–discharge plateaus, demonstrating their synergistic role in enabling reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion (Supplementary Fig. 14). Replacing U with acetamide (AE), nicotinamide (NA) or pyridine (PD) shows the same phenomenon, with reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion achieved only in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes, including under identical ionic strength conditions, indicating the broad applicability of this electrolyte framework (Fig. 2c,d,f,g and Supplementary Figs. 15–18).

According to recent reports, to isolate the role of PAs in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, SO42− was maintained as the KA, whereas structurally related CF3SO3−, CF3COO− or CH3COO− was introduced as the second anion. Density-functional-theory calculations reveal a polarity sequence of CH3COO− > CF3COO− > CF3SO3− (Supplementary Fig. 19), providing a basis for examining how anion polarity influences interfacial behaviours24,25. Molecular-dynamics simulations show similar water-enriched bulk environments across the three electrolytes (Supplementary Figs. 20–22), but distinct interfacial structures (Fig. 3d). CH3COO− reduces the interfacial water density while increasing anion enrichment, whereas CF3COO− and CF3SO3− retain high interfacial water intensity (Fig. 3e,f). In situ attenuated total reflection infrared (ATR-IR) spectroscopy further supports this interfacial redistribution. The δ-HOH vibration at 1,640 cm−1 remains pronounced with CF3SO3− or CF3COO− (Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Fig. 23), but is suppressed with CH3COO− alongside pronounced anion-associated signals26,27,28,29 (Fig. 3i). Notably, highly concentrated ZnCl2 retains a water-enriched interface despite its water-deficient bulk environment (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25). Differential capacitance measurements indicate stronger interfacial adsorption of CH3COO− than of CF3COO− and CF3SO3− (Supplementary Figs. 26 and 27), linking preferential adsorption of strongly PAs to the formation of a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment30.

Recent findings suggest that a, Cyclic voltammetry profiles in electrolytes with different anions. b, GCD profiles in electrolytes with different anions. The rising and falling voltage curves correspond to charging and discharging processes, respectively. c, Cycling stability in electrolytes with different anions, with upper and lower curves representing Coulombic efficiency and specific capacity, respectively. Electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2. d, Schematic snapshot of the interfacial structure in the electrolyte with CH3COO−. e, Corresponding interfacial cumulated density profiles of H2O in electrolytes with different anions, with the grey shaded region highlighting interfacial variations. f, Corresponding interfacial cumulated density profiles of anions in electrolytes with different anions, with the pink shaded region highlighting interfacial variations. g–i, In situ ATR-IR spectra in the electrolytes with CF3SO3− (g), CF3COO− (h) and CH3COO− (i).

In a recent development, these polarity-dependent interfacial structures lead to distinct iodine conversion behaviour. CF3SO3− reveals a negligible I0/I+ process, whereas CF3COO− enables I0/I+ oxidation but with limited reversibility. By contrast, CH3COO− supports reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion with improved stability and capacity (Fig. 3a–c and Supplementary Fig. 28). In situ ultraviolet–visible spectra and micro-computed-tomography analyses further link these differences to iodine species distribution, showing that CH3COO− confines iodine species within the electrode and suppresses their migration into the bulk electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 29 and 30). Together, these results establish a mechanistic relationship between anion polarity and the resulting water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment that governs the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Building on the understanding of PAs, the critical role of KAs in the KA–PA–Nuc framework was further explored. Nuc stabilize I+ through electron-rich nitrogen or oxygen centres, which also interact with water through hydrogen bonding and therefore compete with halogen-bond formation (Supplementary Fig. 31). Inspired by anion-specific effects on water–solute interactions, SO42−, CH3COO−, NO3−, CF3SO3− and ClO4− were compared in the same PA–Nuc baseline31,32,33,34 (Supplementary Fig. 32). Although these anions have little effect on the initial capacity, they produce different cycling stability (Supplementary Fig. 33). SO42− maintains nearly overlapping galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) profiles, whereas CH3COO− and CF3SO3− show intermediate cycling stability and ClO4− undergoes rapid deterioration (Fig. 4a–c and Supplementary Fig. 34), giving a stability sequence of SO42− > CH3COO− > CF3SO3− > ClO4−. NO3− deviates from this sequence owing to its limited electrochemical stability within the applied voltage range35 (Supplementary Fig. 35a,b).

a, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing SO42− at different cycles. b, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing CF3SO3− at different cycles. c, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing ClO4− at different cycles. Electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2. d, 2H NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. e, 1H NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. f, 13C NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. g, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing SO42−. h, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing CF3SO3−. i, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing ClO4−.

NMR spectroscopy and molecular-dynamics simulations reveal the molecular origin of these electrochemical differences. The 2H chemical shift follows SO42− > CH3COO− > NO3− > CF3SO3− > ClO4− (Fig. 4d), indicating progressively stronger anion-induced water polarization and restructuring of the aqueous hydrogen-bond network36,37. These differences in water–anion coordination translate into distinct water–Nuc interactions. The corresponding 15N chemical shifts, together with the inverse trends observed in 1H and 13C chemical shifts, indicate that KAs such as SO42− polarize hydration water and thereby weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding, whereas chaotropic anions such as ClO4− interact directly with the Nuc backbone and facilitate Nuc hydration32 (Fig. 4e,f, and Supplementary Figs. 32 and 36–38). Nuc solubility measurements, two-dimensional 1H–15N heteronuclear multiple bond correlation (HMBC) NMR spectra, and calculated Nuc–water distances and hydrogen-bond populations further support this interpretation (Fig. 4g–i, and Supplementary Figs. 35c, 39 and 40). By weakening Nuc–water interactions, SO42− increases the availability of Nuc for halogen-bond stabilization of I+, thereby promoting reversible iodine conversion. These results reveal how anionic chemistry regulates molecular water–Nuc interactions to govern the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

In a recent development, having established the complementary roles of PA and KA in interfacial and molecular regulation, we next examined how these effects manifest in the electrochemical processes governing iodine conversion. In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) combined with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis was used to decouple the complex impedance response and identify individual electrochemical processes38,39,40 (Supplementary Figs. 41–43). In the absence of either KA or PA, the DRT responses evolve distinctly with additional competing interfacial processes, whereas their combined presence maintains stable interfacial electrochemical behaviour throughout iodine conversion41,42 (Extended Data Fig. 1). Rate-dependent analysis identifies charge transfer, rather than ion transport, as the dominant kinetic contribution to iodine conversion in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 44–50). In situ Raman spectroscopy further links these electrochemical processes to iodine chemistry, revealing the reversible evolution of the Nuc–I+–Nuc species during cycling (Supplementary Figs. 51 and 52).

According to recent reports, the KA–PA–Nuc framework supports four-electron iodine conversion across different operating conditions and cell configurations. Zn–I2 cells retain 96% of their capacity after 1,000 cycles at 1 A g−1 and 94% after 2,000 cycles at 2 A g−1, while sustaining four-electron conversion at iodine loadings up to 12.2 mg cm−2 (Supplementary Figs. 53–55, 58a and 59). This electrolyte framework is also compatible with different current collectors and pouch-cell configurations and extends to aqueous Al–I2 cells using Al–Zn alloy negative electrodes (Supplementary Figs. 56–58b,c, 60 and 61). A techno-economic analysis under standardized modelling assumptions further illustrates its theoretical cost-reduction potential by avoiding highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes and costly current collectors (Supplementary Fig. 58d–f and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Mechanistic and post-mortem analyses further reveal that the apparent low Coulombic efficiency and capacity fading involve coupled reversible and irreversible iodine inventory loss, with the latter becoming more pronounced at increased iodine loading (Supplementary Figs. 62–67 and Extended Data Figs. 2–4). Together, these results clarify the iodine conversion pathways while defining the applicability and remaining limitations of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, showing that sustained reversible four-electron iodine conversion requires not only stabilization of hypervalent iodine species but also broader management of the entire iodine inventory.

It has been revealed that all chemicals were used as received without further purification unless otherwise stated. The manufacturer and purity of each material are specified at its first occurrence in Methods and are not repeated thereafter unless a different source or purity was used.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes were prepared by dissolving KA, PA and Nuc into deionized water at room temperature. For aqueous Zn–I2 batteries, KA and PA were 1.5 M ZnSO4 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M Zn (CH3COO)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich), respectively. To demonstrate the broad applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, various Nuc were used, including 2 M urea (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich), 2 M acetamide (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.2 M pyridine (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) or 0.4 M nicotinamide (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich). To explore the role of PAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 1.5 M ZnSO4 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. Zn(CH3COO)2, Zn(CF3COO)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) or Zn(CF3SO3)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 0.5 M to obtain electrolytes containing different PAs. To evaluate the role of KAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. ZnSO4, Zn(NO3)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), Zn(CF3SO3)2 or Zn(ClO4)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 1.5 M for comparative analysis. To compare electrolytes performance under a standardized ionic strength condition, the ionic strength of each electrolyte was calculated according to the equation:.

According to recent reports, where Ci and Zi represent the molar concentration and charge number of ion i, respectively. For aqueous Al–I2 batteries, the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte was prepared by dissolving 1.5 M Al2(SO4)3 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.5 Mg (CH3COO)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M nicotinamide into deionized water.

Industry observers note that iodine-activated carbon (I2–AC) composites were prepared using an evaporation–adsorption method. In brief, 0.5 g iodine (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) and 0.5 g activated carbon (AC; YP-80F, purity not specified, Kuraray) were manually ground in an agate mortar with a pestle for 10 min under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was sealed in a Teflon reactor and heated at 120 °C for 6 h. For the preparation of iodine positive electrodes using titanium (80 mesh, >99.5%, Hebei Conway Metal Products) or stainless steel mesh (80 mesh, 316L, Hebei Conway Metal Products) as the current collector, I2–AC, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, 60 wt% dispersion H2O, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P (purity not specified, Canrd) were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 40 mg I2–AC, 5 mg Super P and 5 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using a roller press (Etelux) and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The areal iodine loading was controlled by adjusting the thickness of the composite film. The dried film was then pressed onto the titanium or stainless steel mesh using the roller press. The resulting electrodes were punched into 12 mm disks using a manual disk punch (T07, ‌Hefei Kejing Material Technology).

For iodine positive electrodes using carbon paper (TGP-H-060, Toray) as the current collector, I2–AC, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, weight-average molecular weight, Mw ≈ 534,000 g mol−1 by gel permeation chromatography, powder, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg I2–AC, 20 mg PVDF and 20 mg Super P were manually mixed with N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) using an agate mortar and pestle in ambient conditions. The resulting slurry was manually and uniformly spread onto the carbon paper using a laboratory spatula. The coated electrodes were dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 8 h and subsequently cut into 12-mm disks using the manual disk punch. Commercial Zn foils (70 µm, >99.99%, ‌Qinghe Haoxuan Metal Materials) were used as negative electrodes as received.

To assess the potential of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, a Ag/AgCl electrode in saturated KCl (Beijing Jingke Instrument Science Instrument) was used as the reference, and AC electrodes were prepared as the counter electrode. The measured potentials are reported directly versus the Ag/AgCl reference electrode. For the preparation of AC electrodes, AC, PTFE and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg AC, 20 mg Super P and 20 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle at ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using the roller press and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The dried film was then pressed onto titanium mesh using the roller press. By adjusting the electrode thickness, the capacity of the AC electrode was controlled to be much higher than that of the iodine working electrode, ensuring its capability as the counter electrode for evaluating the electrochemical performance of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte. To further validate the applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, Al–Zn alloys were fabricated as negative electrodes following a previous study43. In brief, symmetric cells were assembled using Zn foils (70 µm, 16 mm in diameter) as electrodes and 2 M Al (CF3SO3)3 (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) as the electrolyte. During charging, Al3+ in the electrolyte deposited on and reacted with the metal Zn substrate, forming the Zn-supported Al–Zn alloys.

Halogen-bond complexes were synthesized via a cation-exchange reaction using corresponding silver analogues, following a previously reported procedure with some modifications44. All operations were carried out under a standard Schlenk line. In a typical synthesis, 0.94 mmol of the corresponding silver salt (Ag2SO4, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCH3COO, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3COO, >98%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3SO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgNO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; or AgClO4, >97%, Sigma-Aldrich) was added to a 20-ml vial equipped with a stir bar. The vial was sealed with a rubber septum and evacuated. Subsequently, 6.0 ml dry CH2Cl2 (purity not specified, VWR Chemicals) and 1.90 mmol pyridine (3.80 mmol for Ag2SO4) were added at room temperature under a nitrogen atmosphere. The mixture was stirred for 10 min to form the Ag(I)–pyridine bis-coordination complex. Next, 2.00 mmol of iodine (4.00 mmol for Ag2SO4) was added, and the reaction was allowed to proceed for an additional 20 min under continuous stirring. The supernatant was then carefully transferred to another vial via cannula filtration, followed by the addition of 15 ml dry n-hexane (>99%, Macron Fine Chemicals) to induce precipitation of the halogen-bond complex. The mixture was stored at −20 °C overnight to complete precipitation. Afterwards, the supernatant was removed using a syringe, and the resulting solid was washed with 20 ml dry n-hexane to remove any residual I2. Finally, the product was dried under vacuum on the Schlenk line.

In a recent development, in situ ATR-IR spectra were recorded by a Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS50 spectrometer equipped with a liquid nitrogen-cooled MCT-A detector. Gold-coated silicon plates were used as working electrodes, with Zn foils (70 µm, 10 mm in diameter) and glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter, Whatman) used as reference electrodes and separators, respectively. To assess the critical role of the PA in the interfacial environment, 1.5 M KA electrolyte was maintained as the baseline, and 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2, 0.5 M Zn(CF3COO)2 or 0.5 M Zn(CF3SO3)2 was separately added. An electrolyte volume of 500 μl was used for each measurement. During tests, the assembled batteries were connected to a Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat to run a cyclic voltammetry programme at a scan rate of 0.2 mV s−1 for a full charge and discharge cycle. All spectra were collected at a resolution of 4 cm−1, with 50 scans per measurement. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

Raman spectra were recorded using a Bruker Senterra II Raman spectrometer with a 532-nm excitation wavelength. The in situ Zn–I2 cell comprised an iodine positive electrode (12 mm in diameter, iodine mass loading 2.2 mg cm−2), a Zn negative electrode (70 µm, 12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter). An electrolyte volume of 200 μl was used. Raman spectra were collected during GCD cycling using an external Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

FTIR spectra of various electrolytes were obtained using an ATR-FTIR spectrometer (BRUKER, Platinum-ATR). Scanning electron microscopy characterization of electrodes was performed using a JEOL 7600 microscope. Ultraviolet–visible measurements were conducted on a Shimadzu UV-3600i Plus spectrophotometer. For in situ ultraviolet–visible measurements, a two-electrode Zn–I2 cuvette cell was connected to a Neware battery test system for GCD cycling. NMR analyses, including 1H, 13C and 1H–15N HMBC spectra, were carried out on a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 500). 15N spectra were collected using a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 700). Deuterium oxide (>99.9%, Fluorochem) was used as the solvent for electrolyte characterization, and dideuteromethylenechloride (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as the solvent for characterizing halogen-bond complexes. Micro-computed-tomography imaging was conducted using a Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa system with a ×4 objective, operating at a tube voltage of 80 kV and an exposure time of 8 s, achieving a voxel resolution of 0.8 μm. For each sample, a disk with a diameter of 2 mm was prepared to balance X-ray attenuation and representative sampling volume. The acquired computed-tomography datasets were subsequently processed and analysed using Avizo software.

Electrochemical studies of halogen-free electrolytes were performed using CR2025 coin cells, whereas those of halogen-containing electrolytes were performed using Swagelok cells. For CR2025 Zn–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode, Zn negative electrode (70 µm) and separator (GF/D) had diameters of 12 mm, 16 mm and 19 mm, respectively. For Swagelok Zn–I2 cells, corresponding electrodes and separators had the same diameter of 12 mm. For CR2025 Al–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode had a diameter of 12 mm, the Al–Zn alloy negative electrode had a diameter of 16 mm, and a GF/D separator with a diameter of 19 mm was used. An electrolyte volume of 100 μl was used for each cell. Coin cells were mechanically crimped at 50 kg cm−2 using a hydraulic crimping machine (MSK-110, Hefei Kejing Material Technology) during assembly. Swagelok cells were manually tightened during assembly.

Industry observers note that for the 1.1-Ah pouch cell, 2 double-side coated iodine positive electrodes (10 × 15 cm), and 3 Zn negative electrodes (70 µm, 10 × 15 cm) were stacked alternately. The areal iodine loading of positive electrodes is controlled at 10 mg cm−2. Four glass fibre separators (GF/D, 10.1 × 15.1 cm) were utilized, and 1.5 ml electrolyte was added to each separator. The electrolyte consisted of 1.5 M ZnSO4, 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide. Titanium foils were connected to electrodes as tabs. After lamination, the assembled battery was encapsulated in an aluminium–plastic film and mechanically constrained using a customized model during electrochemical measurements. The applied pressure was not specifically quantified.

It has been revealed that GCD tests were conducted using a Neware battery test system in a room maintained at an ambient temperature of approximately 25–28 °C. All other electrochemical measurements described below were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C. Cyclic voltammetry, linear sweep voltammetry and EIS measurements were performed using a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat. For the electrochemical stability window analysis, linear sweep voltammetry measurements were performed using a three-electrode configuration consisting of a titanium mesh working electrode (1 × 2 cm), an AC counter electrode (1 × 2 cm) and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode at a scan rate of 2 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to an exposed geometric area of 1 cm², and the potentials are reported directly versus Ag/AgCl. The polarization measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti CR2025 coin cells using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter), titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter) at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to the geometric area of the titanium electrode. For in situ EIS tests, a thin Zn wire was inserted into the coin cell as an additional reference electrode to establish a three-electrode configuration. This reference electrode was placed between the positive electrode and negative electrode, separated by two layers of separators (GF/A, Whatman). For measurements of the individual iodine positive electrode, the potential is reported versus the Zn reference electrode as potential (V versus Zn/Zn²+), whereas the full-cell and Zn negative electrode responses are reported as voltage (V) owing to the voltage was applied on full cell. For peak assignment, the assembled cells were connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat to perform staircase potentio EIS with a potential range of approximately 0.6–1.8 V. For rate-step identification, the assembled cells simultaneously connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat and a Neware battery test system to conduct potentio EIS and GCD cycling, respectively. All Nyquist plots were fitted using EC-Lab software based on the equivalent circuit (R1 + Q2/R2 + Q3/R3 + W4). DRT data were calculated from EIS data using MatlabR2019 with the DRT tool developed by Francesco Ciucci’s research group. The differential capacitance was calculated using the following equation:.

Sources indicate that where C is the differential capacitance, ω is the angular frequency and Zim is the imaginary component of the impedance. In this work, a specific frequency of 1,000 Hz was used. Measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti cells assembled in CR2025 coin-cell configuration, using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter) and titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) as the two electrodes and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter). The potential was varied from 1.0 V to 1.7 V versus Zn/Zn2+. No ohmic-drop (iR) correction was applied to the potentials or voltages reported in this work.

In a recent development, all molecular-dynamics simulations were performed using the LAMMPS package45 to investigate the bulk solvation structure of various aqueous electrolytes. The initial configurations were constructed using Packmol46, which randomly packed electrolyte components into a periodic cubic box according to the target molar ratios, ensuring no initial atomic overlaps. The simulation cell was then relaxed by energy minimization before subsequent equilibration. Force-field parameters for organic molecules were taken from the OPLS-AA family47,48, whereas others were adopted from validated aqueous zinc salt parameter sets in the literature. To partially account for polarization effects in concentrated electrolytes, the atomic charges were uniformly scaled (scaling factor 0.8)49. Interaction of water was represented by TIP3P50, and all X–H bonds were constrained using the SHAKE algorithm51. Each system was first energy-minimized and equilibrated in the isothermal–isobaric ensemble (300 K, 1 atm) using a Nosé–Hoover thermostat until both the density and potential energy were stable. Subsequently, production runs were performed in the canonical ensemble for 5 ns (5,000 ps) with a 1-fs integration step to ensure complete equilibration while avoiding structural drift.

Sources indicate that radial distribution functions gij(r) were computed to analyse ion pairing and solvation structure. Coordination numbers were obtained by integrating gij(r) up to their first minimum. Both radial distribution functions and hydrogen bonds were identified using the hydrogen-bond analysis tools implemented in VMD52. Average hydrogen-bond numbers and distributions were determined over the equilibrated trajectories to characterize the reorganization of the hydrogen-bond network by different anions.

According to recent reports, to probe field-induced ion and molecular redistribution, an additional set of simulations was conducted in the canonical ensemble with a uniform static electric field applied along the z axis. The field strength corresponded to the experimentally estimated potential gradient.

Density-functional-theory calculations were performed using the Gaussian16 program package, using the M06-2X exchange-correlation functional53. Geometry optimizations were conducted using a mixed basis-set approach: the 6-311+G(d,p) basis set was applied to all elements excluding iodine54. Iodine was described using an effective core potential from the Stuttgart/Dresden group55. Solvent effects were accounted for using the polarizable continuum model, with water selected as the solvent56.

Galli pleads Milan fans to ‘have patience’ with Cardinale and Amorim: “I’m convinced”

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Filippo Galli praised Gerry Cardinale a few weeks ago, and he’s repeated the praise for the AC Milan chairman today.

At present, Milan are in a good place. Although they’ve had a few disappointing results in midweek games, they’ve largely been solid when it’s mattered and picked up several really impressive results.

Industry observers note that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

According to recent reports, for Cardinale, it’s been a great start to life under Ruben Amorim – who he backed heavily in the summer – and the hope is that it will continue for the foreseeable future. In January, more investments are planned, and the aim is to continue the upward trajectory.

Speaking to Tuttosport, Galli pleaded for patience from the fans about Cardinale and Amorim, endorsing the pair heavily, as MilanNews relayed.

“I urge the fans to have patience and faith: I’m convinced that the Cardinale-Amorim project will be rewarding. This AC Milan will return to winning ways in the coming years. Scudetto? I see Inter and Roma a step above all the others for first place.

“Also keep an eye on Lazio, who are flying and only play one game a week, but AC Milan can also have their say. As a fan, I hope the Rossoneri can compete until the end.”.

“Are there talks about Inacio, Calvani, and Reggiani for the defence? They’re excellent players, but there are those who are better than me at being responsible for the club’s transfer decisions: I trust them. I’ll just say that, after Gabbia’s injury, a reinforcement is needed in the back.

Sources indicate that “Gila at full-back? I’m really enjoying the Spaniard, even as a full-back. He’s playing his newly introduced role very well, also making a significant contribution in supporting the attack. I was sure he would establish himself quickly; already at Lazio, he proved himself to be one of the best defensive players in Serie A. Great acquisition.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jamie Gittens has withdrawn from the England Under-21 squad. He suffered an ankle injury during Tuesday’s qualifier against Kazakhstan at Molineux. The Chelsea winger left the ground on crutches. He has returned to Stamford Bridge, where the Jamie Gittens injury will now be assessed by the club’s medical staff.

Gittens picked up the knock after a challenge during the second half of England’s win over Kazakhstan. He was withdrawn as a precaution. He did not take any further part in the match. England have been careful not to overstate the problem and no further reports have come out further.

Recent findings suggest that the 21-year-old struggled to put weight on the affected ankle and was seen limping around Molineux after full time. That prompted an immediate release back to his club, rather than any attempt to assess him further in camp.

In a recent development, england Under-21 boss Lee Carsley addressed the injury directly after the game. He confirmed the nature of the knock and the decision to send Gittens home.

Sources indicate that “Jamie got a kick on his ankle,” Carsley said after the match. “We never take any risks. With the age of these players, we don’t ever keep them in camp to see how they are. He will go back.”.

England’s statement on the squad changes, detailed in a report from Football.London, confirmed the wider fallout from the fixture.

“Mukasa’s call-up follows the withdrawal of Chelsea’s Jamie Gittens and Norwich City pair Kellen Fisher and Ben Chrisene through injury,” the statement read. West Ham midfielder Divine Mukasa has been called up as cover for all three.

It has been revealed that gittens has been an unused substitute in every Premier League fixture Chelsea have played this season, with his only two appearances under Xabi Alonso coming in the Carabao Cup. Those minutes have offered him little platform after his big summer move.

Alonso’s squad selection has been a talking point since he took charge. Our earlier look at Xabi Alonso’s squad choices at Stamford Bridge covered how competitive things have become. An ankle injury will not change his pecking order in the short term. It does, though, remove any chance of him pushing his case this week.

It has been revealed that chelsea’s break has brought other headlines too. Cole Palmer also withdrew, for entirely different reasons, after his recall by senior boss Thomas Tuchel to the full England squad. Chelsea will be watching both returns closely before domestic football resumes.

Sources indicate that chelsea have not yet issued a formal revision on the severity of the injury. Any recovery timeline will depend on an assessment by the club’s medical team once Gittens is back at Cobham. Nothing beyond the crutches seen at Molineux has been confirmed.

Given his limited game time this season, the immediate concern is less about missed fixtures than a setback to his integration under Alonso. Fans can follow how the squad shapes up before the next fixtures through our recent line-up updates. Further news on Gittens is expected once Chelsea’s medical staff finish their evaluation.

Tech Report: Two days or two weeks – Michael Carrick future decision rolls into the international break

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester United will use the November international break to decide whether Michael Carrick stays on as head coach, after a three-game reprieve that delivered only one win.
  • According to The Guardian, Carrick came close to being sacked after the 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth on 25 October.
  • Director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada discussed his position at the training ground the following day and agreed to give him three matches to turn things around before the break.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United will use the November international break to decide whether Michael Carrick stays on as head coach, after a three-game reprieve that delivered only one win.

According to The Guardian, Carrick came close to being sacked after the 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth on 25 October.

Director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada discussed his position at the training ground the following day and agreed to give him three matches to turn things around before the break.

Industry observers note that those games brought a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea, a 3-2 win over Roma and a chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday. United conceded eight goals across the three fixtures, and defensive frailty remains the biggest worry.

Wilcox is now leading a review of Carrick’s position. He will consult Berrada before making a recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who oversees the club’s sporting operations. Talks are expected to begin on Monday and continue through the break.

It has been revealed that the league table makes grim reading. United sit in the Premier League relegation zone with just one league win in their last 10 matches.

In a recent development, if he does win a stay of execution, results will need to follow. Manchester United cannot be languishing in 17th place.

Carrick remains defiant. Speaking to Sky Sports News after the Villa draw, he admitted his side “haven’t won enough games” but insisted he expects to move forward.

“I’m quite clear with what direction the club needs to go in, and it’s got to win games, remarked Carrick after the late Villa draw.

“I think there’s more than enough [to turn things around].”.

Recent findings suggest that if United do make a change, former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe is reported to be Wilcox’s preferred candidate. Howe has been out of work since leaving St James’ Park during pre-season, after four and a half years in charge.

In the meantime, there are no aims to strengthen Carrick’s coaching staff.

It has been revealed that for now, Carrick is expected to be in charge for United’s next match, against Liverpool. Whether three games were enough to convince the hierarchy should become clear before then.

The trip to Anfield could be do or die for the decorated former United midfielder.

He’s not likely to survive a heavy defeat at the home of the club’s fierce rivals, but a galvanising win would surely buy him time and goodwill.

It has been revealed that that’s if he makes it through the next fortnight before then. A decision or indication could be two days or two weeks away.

The only certainty at Old Trafford is uncertainty.

Latest Update: England throw it away with defending unworthy of a top nation

📅 26 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 32 min read (6419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~32 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there had been so much talk – first raised by Thomas Tuchel after the shocking World Cup exit to Argentina – about England’s DNA.
  • The world and European champions were England’s first opponents – after the World Cup – in this Nations League campaign and came away from Wembley with a deserved win.
  • Sources indicate that mikel Oyarzabal SCORES against England AGAIN!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there had been so much talk – first raised by Thomas Tuchel after the shocking World Cup exit to Argentina – about England’s DNA. About whether they could keep the ball, pass the ball, control the ball, the way Spain do.

The world and European champions were England’s first opponents – after the World Cup – in this Nations League campaign and came away from Wembley with a deserved win. They are now 39 games unbeaten with substitute Mikel Oyarzabal, who scored the winning goal against England in the final of the last European Championship, doing so again.

Sources indicate that mikel Oyarzabal SCORES against England AGAIN! 🎯Spain retake the lead after a slick finish from the Spaniard 👏#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pPT3KvRHWl.

That may have been no surprise, even if the inevitable “olés” after Spain’s third goal will have hurt. But the nature of it? For the England manager this was another shocker. Not in the way his team went about the task. They were positive, fun, attacking. But in the way they conceded – goals and chances – and lost.

On this performance, DNA, for England, stands for Defensively Not Able, as they threw away what could have been a famous and restorative victory. Instead, with Croatia beating the Czech Republic in the other group game, England are under immediate pressure to win in Prague on Tuesday.

In a recent development, in fact, England have conceded 13 goals in their past six matches – in fairness including four in that third-place World Cup 6-4 win over France – and that is not good enough for a top-tier nation. Tuchel needs to sort it out defensively.

According to recent reports, it could have been very different if Harry Kane had not missed from the penalty spot, slipping as he struck the ball, with England improbably 2-1 ahead. “It would have been the decisive punch,” Tuchel stated. Maybe so, even if there was always the feeling that Spain could go through the gears.

It has been revealed that kane MISSES from the penalty spot! 😧Harry Kane slips when he strikes the ball, let off for Spain and Luis de la Fuente#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pvg3GGa9ma.

Industry observers note that afterwards there were claims, led by the impressive Anthony Gordon, that this was a missed opportunity for England. A bit like the World Cup. They need to shake this theme.

The irony was this was one of their best creative displays for quite some time. They took the game to Spain and could have scored more. And conceded more.

In truth it could have been Spain 4 England 0 inside half an hour and before Tuchel’s team laid a glove on their opponents.

Another let off for England 😧Ferran Torres misses another big chance one-on-one with James Trafford #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/KFkJoJUW6c.

The manager had also spoken about how England should “embrace the chaos” as their best route to success. That may appear a questionable tactic – does chaos ever win a tournament? – but England certainly did that. This was as chaotic and, admittedly, entertaining as it gets.

England attacked with pace and power with the pick of their players the two based in Spain: Gordon, who scored, and Jude Bellingham. And the defenders? This was a bad night for Marc Guéhi, his Manchester City team-mate Nico O’Reilly (cue speculation about whether they were distracted by the verdict on the Premier League charges against their club) and for Jarell Quansah at right-back who is so evidently a centre-half.

According to recent reports, A penny, once more, for the thoughts of the unused Trent Alexander-Arnold. The fourth defender, Ezri Konsa, vented his frustration at what was happening around him.

It was not just the errors but the unforced nature of them. Poor in possession with misplaced passes and defensively wide open. There is a gap between Spain and England but not as big as the gaps that were exposed in England’s back four. They endured a full house of calamities. They seemed strangely unaware – or incapable of dealing with – the danger posed by the outstanding Lamine Yamal.

Maybe because of the opposition – or the criticism – England felt the need to play out. But what an horrific start. What an inexplicable moment for Guéhi as he received the ball from O’Reilly and turned into trouble, gifting possession to Yamal who ran on and scored. Inside two minutes.

WHAT A START FROM SPAIN 🇪🇸Lamine Yamal pounces on a Marc Guéhi error to give Spain an early lead at Wembley #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/Et83EyTPlp.

Sources indicate that spain walked out with the second star on their shirt – to mark their second World Cup triumph. That was the star Tuchel had promised for England.

Industry observers note that now, straight away, they were up against it. It could have turned very ugly. Ferran Torres, who had scored the winner in the World Cup Final, had one disallowed for offside, then was thwarted by James Trafford after – inexplicably again – being played onside by Quansah.

SIGNIFICANT SAVE from James Trafford 🧤The Leeds United goalkeeper keeps out Ferran Torres#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/nj5b8AUSQU.

Then Torres was sent clear following Elliot Anderson’s poor pass, only to drag his shot wide. The third miss came from Dani Olmo, again set up by Yamal.

It could – it should – have been game over. Then England unexpectedly turned it around. They had kept attacking despite what was going on at the back and struck through a truly thrilling counter-attack, with Gordon and Bellingham combining before the Barcelona winger calmly beat goalkeeper Unai Simon.

Recent findings suggest that ENGLAND ARE LEVEL! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿A brilliant finish from Anthony Gordon after a breathtaking counter attack 👏#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/z0nSfWIHVd.

It was an exceptional goal and was quickly followed by a fortunate one as O’Reilly’s cross was met by Kane who stooped to steer in a header, only for it to strike Marc Cucurella, who made a mess of clearing, and it went past Simón.

I think we'll give that goal to Harry Kane 🎯England come from behind to lead Spain thanks Harry Kane, with assistance from Marc Cucurella ⚽️#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/X3qSOWUhVT.

The Spain left-back hit the post with a cross, misjudged by Trafford who was given this game and the next to stake his claim ahead of Jordan Pickford who has so long been the undisputed first-choice.

England dominated for a while and Bellingham won a penalty, after a VAR intervention, only for Kane to strike the crossbar.

Sources indicate that how Spain made them pay and worryingly so. O’Reilly passed the ball straight to Olmo who swept it inside. Substitute Álex Baena checked and beat Trafford from the edge of the area. Even worse was how Spain cut through the heart of England defence with Baena finding Oyarzabal. Why was no defender closer to him? What was Guéhi doing? And O’Reilly? Oyarzabal exquisitely dinked the ball over Trafford.

Thomas Tuchel does not think Manchester City’s guilty verdict over almost all of their Premier League charges distracted his England players in the Nations League defeat to Spain.

City players Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly were at fault for two of Spain’s goals and both Tuchel, the head coach, and England captain Harry Kane confirmed news of the verdict had been discussed among the squad.

Tuchel does not plan to address the issue with his players ahead of the remaining Nations League games against Czech Republic and Croatia.

In a recent development, asked if the City verdict had been a cause of discussion ahead of the Spain game, Tuchel replied: “Not for me, but I can imagine maybe for the Man City players. I won’t comment on it as it’s an ongoing case.

Industry observers note that “I didn’t make it a topic. It was not a topic for me. I’m just thinking about Spain and the team and meetings. The players have more time than me. So I can imagine they talk about it. It’s good they do. I don’t think it was a distraction for them.”.

Kane added: “There was a discussion, but when we’re with England, we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week.”.

Tuchel also refused to point the finger of blame at Guéhi, O’Reilly or Kane, who missed a penalty, for England’s defeat despite admitting his team got off to the worst possible start by conceding a goal after two minutes.

“We will focus on the positives, but also highlight the stuff we can do better,” Tuchel noted. “Not even speaking about individual mistakes because this is normal. It just happens. It should not happen, and for sure not in this amount. But there is no sense in showing the individual mistakes or telling them ‘please don’t make mistakes’. That is normal, but we can do things better. We can defend the third goal better. But we will focus on the positives. There is a lot to take away from the game.

Sources indicate that “We wanted to be the team desperately to beat them [Spain] and we think we had them. We still think we had them at half-time. That was the way the team highlighted up after half-time. So we will focus on that, but the reality is we lost and the reality is we need to prove it again.”.

Sources indicate that “It was a terrible start, the worst possible start, which makes it so difficult against a team like this. The reaction was very good. After 10/12 minutes, we were the better team but we gave away too many mistakes. We were the better team. If we had converted the penalty, it could have been the decisive moment. We have to keep going and learn from the mistakes. We could have created more if we had been more clinical in the final 20 metres. We revealed great bravery and courage with our high-ball wins. There will always be moments you suffer against teams like this. The effort and quality were there tonight but the result does not prove it today.”.

It has been revealed that “I think there is a gap [between Spain and England]. They [Spain] are the world champions and European champions. Mikel Oyarzabal was never going to miss. He was always in control of the situation. Honestly, people talk about sexy football, that is sexy football. I would watch that all night.”.

🗣️ "We went toe to toe with the European and world champions" 💪Harry Kane remains positive about England performance despite their 3-2 defeat to Spain 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿🇪🇸#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/qkhqsqmPEl.

🗣️ "You have to beat them to show people we can do this" 💪@IanWright0 reflects on England's 3-2 defeat to Spain at Wembley#ITVFootball | @markpougatch pic.twitter.com/ko2FYs4VqA.

It has been revealed that marc Guehi and Nico O’Reilly may want to look away now but Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon scored well. Our very own Mike McGrath has provided his player ratings.

Tonight: England 2 Spain 3 (H)Tuesday September 29: Czech Republic (A), kick-off 7.45pmSaturday October 3: Croatia (A), kick-off 5pmTuesday October 6: Czech Republic (H), kick-off 7.45pm.

🗣️ "I think it's a bit of a missed chance" 👀Anthony Gordon says mistakes cost England the win tonight against Spain at Wembley 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/AJBxVNjbjq.

According to recent reports, A highly entertaining game. England will probably argue the game changed on Kane’s missed penalty, but Spain missed a lot of very clear chances and will feel they deserved the victory. A losing start to the Nations League for Tuchel and his team, but there were some positives. Gordon, Bellingham and Anderson were all excellent. Some of the defending, not so excellent.

Then comes the final whistle at Wembley and the world champions Spain claim a 3-2 victory in north London. It was an absorbing game, where momentum swung one way and then the other, but it is Spain who are the victors.

Anderson is over it but his delivery is poor, easily caught by Unai Simon.
